title: Leilac calciner inside a Brevik-type amine plant: cement capture rises from 50% to about 90% with no new fuel
one_line: Replace a waste-heat-limited cement plant's precalciner with a Leilac indirect calciner. About 57% of plant CO2 then leaves pure, and the existing waste-heat-driven amine plant only has to capture the fuel CO2, which its heat budget can cover.
conventional_core: Brevik CCS (Heidelberg Materials with SLB Capturi amine; operating since June 2025). It captures 400 kt/yr, about 50% of plant CO2, and capture is capped by the waste heat available for regeneration.
graft: Leilac direct-separation (indirect) calcination, from the LEILAC-1 pilot at Lixhe and Leilac-2 at Ennigerloh (commissioning mid-2026, up to 100 kt/yr). The limestone is heated through a steel wall, so the process CO2 comes out undiluted.
mechanism: At Brevik the amine treats mixed kiln flue gas, and its reboiler heat comes from kiln waste heat, which only stretches to about 400 kt/yr. Process (calcination) CO2 is about 60% of a cement plant's direct CO2 (LEILAC 2017 design paper), and Leilac's design target is to capture 95% of it as a near-pure stream. That stream needs only drying and liquefaction: the verifier's separation floor is 0.004 GJ/t. The amine then sees only fuel CO2, about 40% of the total, in roughly 10% CO2 flue gas. Capturing 90% of that needs about 0.86-1.04 PJ/yr of reboiler heat. The heat that today supports 400 kt is about 1.08-1.28 PJ/yr (assuming 2.7-3.2 GJ/t). The existing stripper, reboiler and compressor, sized for 400 kt, already cover the 288-331 kt of fuel CO2. Only the absorber's gas-handling capacity has to grow, by about 1.6x. Uncounted upside: about 0.38 PJ/yr of high-grade heat in the hot Leilac CO2, and removal credits for the biogenic share of the kiln fuel.
target: Cement and lime plants with amine capture that is planned or already operating and capped by waste heat: Brevik, plants in the GCCA 10-plant 2030 milestone, and the Heidelberg sites hosting both Leilac and CCS. The bottleneck it removes is the map's 'waste heat limits capture to about 50%'.
quantitative_claims: Basis: an 800 kt CO2/yr plant (Brevik's 400 kt = about 50%). (1) Captured CO2 = 456 kt pure Leilac stream (60% x 95%) + 288 kt amine (90% of 320 kt fuel CO2) = 744 kt, or 93% of plant CO2. If indirect heating costs +15% fuel (my assumption), it is 787 kt of 848 kt (92.8%). (2) Amine heat needed is 0.86-1.19 PJ/yr against 1.08-1.28 PJ/yr available (need/available ratio 0.68-1.10). Only the worst corner (+15% fuel, 3.6 GJ/t needed, 2.7 GJ/t Brevik basis) overshoots, by 10%, which drops capture to about 89-90% unless the 0.38 PJ/yr of Leilac CO2 heat (900 to 150 C) is recovered. (3) Verifier floors: Leilac stream 0.004 GJ/t; 10% flue at 90% capture 0.166 GJ/t; liquefaction-pressure compression (1 to 16 bar) 0.156 GJ/t. Amine second-law efficiency is about 24-28% at 3.0-3.6 GJ/t of 125 C heat. (4) Absorber gas throughput rises 1.57x (46 to 72 Gmol/yr). Stripper and compression capacity need does not rise. (5) Hypothesis: the blended cost falls below Brevik's modelled ~EUR100/t, because about 58% of captured tonnes become concentrated-stream tonnes (IEA: $15-25/t for capture from such streams). Leilac capex is unpublished; the 2017 'no extra energy or capital cost' statement is a design claim.
who_gains: S4: Heidelberg-type producers capture about 90% instead of 50% and can sell about twice the evoZero-type volume per kiln. S6: kiln jobs are kept. S1: process-emission CCS is where CAN's objection is evidential rather than categorical, and no extra fossil fuel is burned for capture. S7: Norway, the EU and GCCA targets. S3: more demand for storage (Northern Lights).
who_loses: S10 carries first-of-a-kind risk on Leilac scale-up and indirect heat-transfer reliability. S9 pays a small cement premium (<1% of build cost per the map). S11 sees more CO2 shipping (low risk at coastal sites). Suppliers of stand-alone heat (new gas boilers for capture) lose a market.
closest_known_work: (a) LEILAC (Hills, Sceats, Rennie, Fennell, Energy Procedia 2017): 95% of process CO2, about 60% of plant direct CO2. (b) Jacob & Tokheim, Energy 2023: an electrified calciner concept for CO2 capture at a dry-process cement plant (Norwegian context). (c) Brevik CCS itself. (d) Calix/Heidelberg statements that fuel emissions are to be handled separately.
why_different: Prior work treats Leilac and amine as alternatives, or leaves fuel CO2 for later. This idea is a specific heat-budget closure: reuse the existing waste-heat-sized amine train, which is oversized for fuel CO2 alone, and add only absorber capacity. A 50% cap becomes about 90% capture with no new fuel. The claim can be checked with a heat and mass balance.
cheapest_falsifying_test: A desk heat and mass balance (spreadsheet or open-source process model, about 2 weeks) of a 3,000-4,000 t/d clinker line with Leilac replacing the precalciner, using published preheater and cooler exhaust temperatures and flows. The idea is falsified if recoverable heat at or above about 130 C after the retrofit is less than 288-331 kt x 3.0-3.6 GJ/t, or if Leilac's fuel penalty exceeds about 25%. Then ask Calix/Heidelberg for Leilac-2's measured fuel per tonne of process CO2 and its CO2 purity (one data request).

title: CO2 as voidage replacement in Smackover lithium brine fields: lithium pays for storage pressure management
one_line: Direct-lithium-extraction (DLE) projects have to replace the brine volume they withdraw, and CO2 storage projects have to withdraw brine to relieve pressure. Coupled, each project's cost becomes the other's revenue.
conventional_core: Saline-aquifer CO2 storage with brine extraction for pressure management. Brine extraction is needed at basin scale (Anderson & Jahediesfanjani 2020; Gorgon's binding constraint was produced-water handling, 25% of reservoir CO2 stored against 80% required).
graft: Oilfield-brine direct lithium extraction (Standard Lithium's Smackover demonstration at El Dorado, Arkansas; the SWA project, 22,500 t LCE/yr, reported permitted May 2026). The geothermal-brine analogue is Vulcan's lithium co-production in the Upper Rhine. Today DLE reinjects spent brine into the Smackover to keep reservoir pressure up.
mechanism: Brine is produced for lithium, and CO2 is injected in place of the Li-depleted spent brine to replace the withdrawn volume. The spent brine goes to a shallower disposal zone. Brine production stops being a cost (Anderson & Jahediesfanjani found it pays only if disposal is cheap) and becomes revenue: each tonne of CO2 stored frees about 1.54 m3 of brine worth 2.9-4.3 kg LCE. As an immiscible displacing phase, CO2 also pushes Li-rich brine toward the producers without diluting it, which spent-brine reinjection does. CO2 breakthrough is handled as in EOR, by recycling produced CO2. Unlike EOR, the product is battery lithium, not oil.
target: Li-rich saline formations with nearby concentrated CO2: the Smackover (south Arkansas, East Texas, north Louisiana), where majors are reported to hold lithium acreage (Exxon, Equinor with Standard Lithium, Chevron; unverified this run) and where ammonia, refining and gas-processing CO2 sources sit near El Dorado. Possibly also the Leduc (Alberta) and Paradox formations.
quantitative_claims: (1) Smackover Li at 400-580 mg/L (2025 East Texas average 582 mg/L, secondary source) and 90% DLE recovery (assumption) gives 1.9-2.8 kg LCE per m3, i.e. 360-522 m3 of brine per t LCE. (2) Filling that voidage with CO2 at a reservoir density of 600-700 kg/m3 (assumption) stores 216-365 t CO2 per t LCE. (3) An SWA-scale project (22,500 t LCE/yr) withdraws 8.1-11.7 Mm3/yr of brine, room for 4.9-8.2 Mt CO2/yr at full replacement and 2.4-4.1 Mt/yr at 50%. That is comparable to Northern Lights Phase 2 (5 Mt/yr). (4) Per tonne of CO2, the brine produced holds $29-64 of gross lithium value at $10-15/kg LCE (assumption), against $5-15/t CO2 to dispose of spent brine at $3-10/m3 (assumption). (5) In a 1 km2 x 30 m x 15%-porosity pattern at 30-50% sweep, CO2 breaks through after 0.9-1.5 Mt, about 4-6 years at 0.25 Mt/yr per injector. (6) Energy: verifier ideal isothermal compression to 300 bar is 0.32 GJ/t; separation is about 0 for concentrated sources. (7) Upper bound on scale: 100-200 kt LCE/yr of US Smackover output corresponds to 21-74 Mt CO2/yr of voidage.
who_gains: S3: majors and independents with Smackover acreage gain a lithium-plus-storage business that reuses reservoir skills. S7: US critical-minerals security plus 45Q storage capacity. S6: oilfield-service jobs in AR, TX and LA. S4: nearby ammonia, refinery and gas-processing emitters get storage close by. S1: storage whose co-product is battery lithium rather than oil sidesteps CAN's EOR red line. S10: two revenue lines de-risk the wells.
who_loses: S8: lithium exporters (Chile, Argentina) and hard-rock producers (Australia) lose market share. S11: spent-brine disposal raises induced-seismicity and legacy-well concerns, and Smackover brines carry H2S. The CO2-handling (recycle) and Class VI monitoring costs fall on the DLE operators. Some S1 groups oppose any new extraction in Gulf South communities.
closest_known_work: (a) Anderson & Jahediesfanjani, IJGGC 2020: net costs of brine production and disposal for basin-scale storage (Illinois Basin). (b) Jahediesfanjani, Anderson & Warwick, IJGGC 2019: brine extraction ratios as low as 1:4 suffice. (c) Hunter, Bielicki et al., Energy Procedia 2017: CO2 storage with enhanced water recovery. (d) LLNL active CO2 reservoir management, using extracted brine for water (from memory). (e) Standard Lithium/Equinor DLE with spent-brine reinjection.
why_different: Earlier brine-extraction studies treat the brine as a disposal cost or a source of fresh water. None found here prices it as lithium feedstock, or inverts DLE's pressure maintenance into a CO2 sink. The coupling makes pressure management revenue-positive in Li-rich formations.
cheapest_falsifying_test: About 1 month. (1) Pull Smackover brine Li and Ca data (USGS Produced Waters Database; Arkansas Oil & Gas Commission). (2) Run an open-source reservoir simulation (OPM Flow or MRST-co2lab) of a DLE five-spot with CO2 replacing the withdrawn volume, compared with spent-brine reinjection. The idea is falsified if CO2 breakthrough comes in under about 4 years at economic well spacing, if cumulative Li recovered per pattern falls more than 20% against reinjection, or if the overlying formations cannot accept the spent brine. A follow-up step is to call Standard Lithium/Equinor and an El Dorado CO2 emitter.

title: Gas-first DRI with its built-in CO2-removal stream shipped to storage, under a contracted switch to H2
one_line: Run new EU shaft-furnace DRI plants on natural gas now, store the near-pure CO2 they already separate, and contract a switch to H2. That gives a 66-79% cut against the blast furnace without waiting for cheap H2.
conventional_core: Gas-based shaft-furnace DRI plus EAF (Energiron/HYL-type process with selective CO2 removal in the reducing-gas loop). Salzgitter's SALCOS is reported to use Energiron (unverified), and Thyssenkrupp Duisburg is allowed to start without H2.
graft: Al Reyadah, Abu Dhabi (ADNOC/Masdar): since Nov 2016 it has compressed the DRI loop's concentrated CO2 from Emirates Steel and injected up to 0.8 Mt/yr. The CO2 goes to Northern Lights-style ship-based storage instead of EOR, which avoids S1's EOR red line.
mechanism: DRI shaft furnaces strip CO2 from the recycled top gas to keep it reducing. That stream is already about 95% CO2 or more and is vented today. Adding drying, liquefaction and a ship or pipeline connection captures it with almost zero separation work. With an EAF and a moderately clean grid, steel comes in at about 0.44-0.70 t CO2e/t with no H2. The H2-switch clause, triggered when delivered H2 falls below a set $/kg or at a set date, together with a cap on upstream methane intensity, answers the gas lock-in objection. Without the clause the idea fails S1.
target: EU blast-furnace sites converting to DRI (Salzgitter, Duisburg; Dunkirk is cancelled) within reach of North Sea CO2 export hubs. The bottleneck it removes: every $1/kg of H2 adds about $55/t of steel, and Europe's H2 flagships are stalling.
quantitative_claims: (1) Gas use of 9.6-10.5 GJ/t DRI (vendor range, assumption) means 0.54-0.59 t CO2/t DRI in total carbon. A selective-removal share of 45-60% (assumption; Al Reyadah shows Mt scale) gives 0.24-0.35 t CO2/t DRI as a stream of at least 95% CO2. (2) Verifier: separation floor 0.0065 GJ/t; compression to liquefaction pressure (1 to 16 bar) 0.16 GJ/t. (3) Net 0.44-0.70 t CO2e/t liquid steel, including 0.5-1.5% upstream CH4 leakage at GWP100 and an EAF using 0.55-0.60 MWh at 0.20-0.25 t/MWh. Against BF-BOF at 1.9-2.2, that is a 66-79% cut, zero H2. (4) Conditioning plus transport and storage at $55-105/t CO2 (assumption) costs $12-37/t steel, close to the EU ETS cost avoided (EUR15-35/t steel at EUR70-100/EUA). By comparison, H2-DRI at $5/kg against $1.5/kg costs about $190/t steel more. (5) The H2 switch later reuses the same shaft furnace, so the capital is not stranded.
who_gains: S4 keeps sites and avoids the H2 premium. S6: Salzgitter and Duisburg workforces. S3 gains gas demand plus a storage business. S7 meets ETS and CBAM obligations without a jobs shock. S9 sees under 1% per car (map arithmetic). S2 gets an early cut rather than a delayed perfect one.
who_loses: S1 objects to gas lock-in and to subsidies for fossil-linked CCS; this is mitigated only by the binding switch clause and the methane cap. Electrolyser and H2 developers lose near-term offtake. S8 green-iron exporters (Brazil, MENA) lose some early EU demand. S11 sees more CO2 transport.
closest_known_work: (a) Al Reyadah/Emirates Steel (2016-, EOR). (b) Tenova/Danieli marketing of Energiron as 'CO2 selective removal, capture-ready'. (c) HBIS Zhangxuan's Energiron plant with CO2 capture (from memory, unverified). (d) IEAGHG iron and steel CCS studies. (e) The map's open problem on gas-DRI lock-in contracts.
why_different: Prior DRI capture sends CO2 to EOR or sells it. This idea pairs the inherent stream with open-access ship storage (Northern Lights) and a contractual H2 trigger. It reframes gas-DRI as a bounded bridge that S1 can audit, and it prices the bridge against the ETS rather than against H2.
cheapest_falsifying_test: A desk mass and cost balance (1-2 weeks) using Emirates Steel and Al Reyadah public data (DRI tonnage against CO2 captured) and published Northern Lights or EU hub tariffs. The idea is falsified if the selective stream is below 0.15 t CO2/t DRI, or if transport and storage exceed about EUR150/t so that capture costs more than the ETS saving. In parallel, run a structured acceptability check: 5-10 interviews with CAN Europe-type NGOs and IG Metall on the H2-switch clause. The idea is falsified for multi-party purposes if S1 rejects every trigger design.

title: Carbfix-style CO2 dissolution into Permian produced-water disposal
one_line: Dissolve concentrated CO2 into the oilfield brine that is already being pumped down disposal wells. Carbfix's water bottleneck (25 t water per t CO2) disappears, because the Permian's problem is too much water.
conventional_core: Permian Basin saltwater disposal: existing permitted wells, pipelines and pumps that move very large produced-water volumes into deep formations.
graft: Carbfix (Hellisheiði, Iceland): CO2 is dissolved into the injection water inside the well at about 25-40 bar, so it is never a buoyant free phase. More than 95% mineralised within 2 years at pilot scale, though mineralisation is not assumed here; dissolved CO2 makes brine denser and it sinks.
mechanism: Fully saturated brine carries no buoyant plume, so security relies less on caprock. It adds only about 0.8 m3 of volume per tonne against about 1.5 m3/t as supercritical CO2, which halves the pressure build-up per tonne in a basin already struggling with overpressured disposal zones. The CO2 needs compression only to the mixing pressure (about 50 bar), not 150 bar. Mass is metered exactly at the wellhead (CO2 in, water in), which simplifies MRV. Candidate sources are vented gas-processing acid gas and other concentrated Permian streams. Revenue is 45Q at $85/t for dedicated Class VI storage, not EOR.
target: Permian operators and disposal companies, and gas processors venting separated CO2. Only disposal zones that qualify for Class VI and are not penetrated by unplugged legacy wells are eligible.
quantitative_claims: (1) CO2 solubility in Permian-type brine (2-3.5 mol/kg NaCl) at 30-50 bar and 30-40 C is about 15-30 kg/m3 (my Henry plus Setschenow estimate, +/-30%), against 33-48 kg/m3 in fresh water. That is 33-67 m3 of already-disposed water per tonne. (2) Permian disposal of 15-20 MMbbl/d (assumption) is 0.87-1.16 bn m3/yr, a technical ceiling of 13-35 Mt CO2/yr if every barrel were saturated. The realistic share is set by Class VI-eligible zones. (3) Verifier compression floor is 0.22 GJ/t to 50 bar against 0.28 GJ/t to 150 bar. Extra water pressurisation is 0-0.21 GJ/t, depending on whether the disposal wells take water by gravity. (4) Added volume is about 2% of the water stream. (5) At $85/t of 45Q, each 1 Mt/yr hub is worth $85M/yr.
who_gains: S3: Permian operators and disposal firms turn a waste-disposal cost line into 45Q revenue using permitted assets. S4: gas processors get cheap storage for vented acid gas. S6: Permian service jobs. S7: Texas and federal storage goals with no new pipelines or land fights.
who_loses: S1 sees a subsidy to the oil-production chain and doubts dissolved-plume MRV. S11 Permian residents already face overpressure-driven surface water flows and seismicity, and CO2-laden brine reaching the surface would degas. S10 bears liability for wells and casing exposed to carbonic acid (the ADM monitoring-well corrosion failure mode applies). Disposal operators face Class VI compliance costs.
closest_known_work: (a) Eyitayo & Watson, SPE 224197 (Texas Tech; JPT summary March 2026; not peer reviewed): supercritical CO2 and brine co-injection or water-alternating-gas coupled with disposal wells. (b) Burton & Bryant, SPE 2009: surface dissolution removes buoyant migration, at +60% capex and 3-9% power when brine has to be lifted for the purpose. (c) Carbfix and Coda Terminal.
why_different: Eyitayo & Watson co-inject a free CO2 phase. Burton & Bryant lift brine specially for dissolution, which drives their cost penalty. Here the brine is already being lifted and paid for, and CO2 is fully dissolved, so neither the buoyancy risk nor the water-lifting cost is incurred. The scale is quantified for the Permian.
cheapest_falsifying_test: Desk work, about 3 weeks: (1) PHREEQC (Pitzer) solubility and scaling or corrosion runs on 50-100 Permian produced-water analyses from the USGS Produced Waters Database, at realistic disposal-well mixing pressures. (2) Overlay Texas RRC data on disposal zones with legacy-well density and documented surface breakouts or seismic response areas. The idea is falsified if median solubility at achievable pressure is under 10 kg/m3, or if more than about 70% of disposal volume goes to zones where a pressure drop or a legacy well could exsolve CO2. Bench follow-up: a 50 bar flow loop with real produced water to measure dissolution and precipitation.

title: Two-tank solvent storage with off-peak electric regeneration for cycling gas plants with capture
one_line: Let a cycling gas plant's absorber run whenever the turbine runs. Store the CO2-rich solvent and regenerate it with a heat pump on cheap, low-carbon off-peak power, so the plant sells full output at peak and the costly regeneration train runs nearly all the time.
conventional_core: Gas-fired combined-cycle plant with amine capture (UK NZT Power, Calpine Baytown; NETL Rev 4A F-class 90% at $60.7/t, 85% capacity factor, 2018$).
graft: Two-tank hot/cold thermal storage from concentrating solar power (e.g. Andasol molten-salt plants, operating since about 2009), which decouples collection from conversion. Here the tanks hold rich and lean solvent. Regeneration uses electric heat (a high-temperature heat pump or vapour recompression), so it can run while the turbine is off.
mechanism: Capture cost is dominated by fixed costs divided by capture hours. Gas plants that follow renewables run 25-60% of the time, so capture cost rises from $61/t to about $105/t at 40% capacity factor. Storing rich solvent lets the stripper, reboiler, CO2 compressor and dehydration be sized for the daily average rather than the peak, roughly 45-60% of peak, and run continuously. Regenerating in midday solar hours with a heat pump removes the steam-extraction penalty, 0.25-0.30 MWh/t, from the most valuable peak hours. The absorber stays full-size.
target: New US and UK gas plants with capture (gas is the fastest-growing US interconnection queue entrant, +86% to 253 GW) and utilities running them on 45Q ($85/t) or contracts for difference. The bottleneck it removes is capacity factor, as named in the map.
quantitative_claims: (1) NETL-anchored split (my decomposition): variable $21/t plus fixed $39/t at 85% capacity factor. That gives $77/t at 60%, $105/t at 40% and $155/t at 25%. (2) NZT scale: 2 Mt/yr design, peak 254 t CO2/h. With the turbine on 10-14 h/day, about 1,400 t CO2 must be stored, 21-28k m3 per tank (15-20 m3 solvent per t, assumption). Tanks plus extra solvent cost $27-74M, i.e. $2-8/t. (3) A regeneration train sized at 45-60% of peak saves $9-17/t of fixed cost at 40% capacity factor. The heat pump (82-110 MW_th at $500-1,000/kW_th, assumption) costs $3-12/t. (4) Energy arbitrage: heat-pump regeneration uses 0.18-0.36 MWh_e/t (COP 2-4; Carnot COP 3.98 from 25 to 125 C, 13 for stripper-overhead recompression) at $10-30/MWh, i.e. $2-11/t. The peak steam penalty it replaces is $20-45/t at $80-150/MWh. (5) Net at 40% capacity factor: about $80/t central, range $50-117/t, against $105/t. The idea fails if the peak to off-peak price spread is below about $50/MWh. (6) Verifier floors (separation 0.22 GJ/t for 4% CO2 + compression to 150 bar 0.28 GJ/t) against 1.2-1.65 GJ_e/t of electricity use give 30-41% second-law efficiency. (7) The regeneration power must be under about 0.1 t CO2/MWh; at 0.4 t/MWh it would emit 0.14 t per t captured.
who_gains: S5: full peak output, lower capture cost, and flexible load that soaks up midday solar surplus. S3 keeps gas demand. S7 gets firm low-carbon capacity. S9 sees lower contract-for-difference or firm-power costs. Solar owners (within S5) gain an off-peak buyer for curtailed power. S10: lower technology risk, since every component is mature.
who_loses: S1 objects to gas lock-in (CAN opposes fossil-power CCS). Battery and long-duration storage developers lose part of the firming market. S11: large amine tanks raise local nitrosamine and spill concerns. Solvent suppliers face degradation risk during storage.
closest_known_work: (a) Cheng, Patankar, Chakrabarti & Jenkins, IJGGC 2022: gas plant flexibility with flexible CCS via solvent storage and flexible regeneration. (b) Cohen, Rochelle & Webber, around 2012, and Oates et al. 2014 on solvent storage and price response (from memory). (c) The map's open problem proposing exactly this graft.
why_different: Prior solvent-storage work mostly regenerates with the plant's own steam, so the turbine must be running. This variant regenerates with grid-powered heat pumps while the turbine is off, sizes the regeneration train to the daily average, and is tested explicitly against NETL Rev 4A at 25-60% capacity factor with real 2025 hourly prices. Novelty is modest and should be checked against Cheng et al. before investing.
cheapest_falsifying_test: (1) An hourly dispatch and cost model (about 2-3 weeks): NETL Rev 4A F-class cost structure plus 2025 ERCOT West and CAISO hourly prices and grid carbon intensity, comparing the plant with and without tanks and heat pump. The idea is falsified if net cost at 40% capacity factor is not at least $10/t below baseline. (2) A bench test, about 30 days: hold rich commercial-type amine at 40 C under an N2 blanket and measure heat-stable salts and capacity loss. The idea is falsified if storage-induced degradation adds more than $5/t.

title: Results contract for China's adipic-acid N2O with EU-ETS-grade stack monitoring and production-capped baselines
one_line: Pay Chinese adipic-acid (nylon precursor) producers a reverse-auction price near cost, about $1-2/t CO2e, for N2O destroyed. Verify it with continuous stack monitoring and a baseline capped at historical output, so the cheapest large tonnes left are bought without repeating the CDM's perverse incentives.
conventional_core: Results-based payments, purchase agreements and reverse auctions for verified reductions (German climate contracts-for-difference style; Frontier-style buyer clubs; Article 6.2 buyers).
graft: The EU ETS monitoring regime for industrial N2O: continuous emission measurement at adipic and nitric acid stacks, combined with production-indexed benchmarks. EU coverage since 2013 is from memory and unverified this run. Fenceline or plume measurement provides the independent cross-check that the CDM lacked.
mechanism: Abatement technology (thermal or catalytic decomposition, above 90%) costs only $0.25-4/t CO2e, and the barrier is the lack of any revenue. The CDM failed because credits per tonne of adipic acid exceeded product margins, which rewarded overproduction (17-22% non-real credits). A creditable volume capped at pre-contract historical output removes that incentive. Stack monitoring plus cheap downwind plume surveys that independently separate abated from unabated plants remove the measurement-gaming route. Reverse auctions keep the price near cost.
target: China's 11+ adipic acid plants (about 94% of global adipic N2O, abatement status unknown per the map), then nitric acid plants not reached by NACAG.
quantitative_claims: (1) China adipic N2O is about 76 Mt CO2e (AR5), i.e. about 287 kt N2O, or 78 Mt CO2e at the AR6 GWP of 273. (2) Unabated emissions are about 0.3 t N2O per t adipic acid (IPCC default, assumption), i.e. 82 t CO2e per t. (3) At a cleared $1-2/t CO2e with 95% abatement, the payment is $78-156 per t adipic acid and $74-149M/yr for all of China. At $5/t it would be $389 per t adipic acid, about 25% of its price (assumed $1,400-1,800/t). This is the CDM perverse-incentive regime, and it is why the production cap is required. (4) Detectability: an unabated plant of about 26 kt N2O/yr gives about 1.5 ppm above the 337 ppb background some 2 km downwind (Gaussian plume, u = 5 m/s). At 90% abatement it is about 150 ppb, so a vehicle-mounted laser analyser separates abated from unabated plants in a day. (5) The same tonnes by DAC at $400/t would cost about $31bn/yr. (6) No energy penalty: decomposition is exothermic.
who_gains: S1/S2 get the cheapest verifiable large tonnes, which also protect the ozone layer. S4: nylon producers are paid cost plus, with no output restriction below historical levels. S7 China gets cheap progress on its non-CO2 NDC, plus ozone co-benefits. S10: buyers get high-integrity, cheaply audited reductions. S8: finance flows to developing-country industry in a NACAG-style model.
who_loses: S7 China may see stack data sharing as a sovereignty issue, and the corresponding-adjustment choice stays with China. Sellers of low-integrity offsets face a cheaper, higher-integrity competitor. Buyers pay $74-149M/yr. Plants already abating lose nothing but gain nothing, which is the additionality test.
closest_known_work: (a) CDM adipic and nitric projects (2005-2012) and their documented gaming. (b) The Nitric Acid Climate Action Group (Germany-funded grants for nitric-acid N2O abatement in developing countries). (c) Kanter et al. (PNAS 2013, Montreal Protocol route; Climate Policy 2026, US regulation: 90-190 Mt CO2 over 20 years for $25-221M). (d) The map's open problem on production-capped baselines with inversion verification.
why_different: NACAG covers nitric acid with grants, Kanter covers regulation, and the CDM had no production cap and no independent measurement. This design combines a production-capped baseline, EU-ETS-standard stack monitoring, a plume cross-check (inversions are too coarse at plant scale) and auction pricing near cost, and targets the adipic gap.
cheapest_falsifying_test: (1) A desk check (1 week): establish the current abatement status of China's adipic plants from company disclosures, Chinese standards and policy, and published inversions. The idea is moot if more than about 90% of capacity already abates. (2) A field test (about $20-40k; rent a laser N2O analyser plus a vehicle, 1-2 weeks): downwind transects at 2-3 plants to confirm that emission rates can be estimated within +/-50%. The idea is falsified if plumes cannot be attributed. (3) Outreach to 3 producers or industry associations. The idea is falsified for multi-party purposes if none will share stack monitoring data at any price.

title: Refinery-style fenceline monitoring network at every HCFC-22 plant to close the HFC-23 gap
one_line: Adapt the US refinery benzene fenceline rule to HFC-23. Run a continuous canister network with public action levels around each HCFC-22 plant, so plant-level non-destruction is visible within weeks. Destruction is already required under Kigali and costs under $1/t CO2e.
conventional_core: HFC-23 thermal destruction at HCFC-22 plants. It is TRL 9, and Kigali requires it 'to the extent practicable' from 2020.
graft: From refining: the US EPA Refinery Sector Rule fenceline programme (40 CFR 63.658, 2015, from my own knowledge; not re-fetched). It uses time-integrated samplers on the perimeter, a numerical action level, a mandatory root-cause analysis when the level is exceeded, and public data. Here the benzene tubes are replaced by time-integrated whole-air canisters, because HFC-23 is too volatile for passive sorbent tubes. Analysis uses preconcentration GC-MS, the same method AGAGE uses for flasks.
mechanism: Place 8-12 perimeter canister samplers around each HCFC-22 plant (weekly or two-weekly integration), plus a short annual tracer-release calibration as in Rust et al. 2024. A plant at the practicable abated emission factor gives a small downwind signal; a plant venting its HFC-23 gives a signal 5-15x larger. An exceedance triggers root-cause analysis and incinerator inspection under the national regulator, with data shared to the Montreal Protocol bodies. This replaces regional inversions, which cannot name a plant, with plant-level attribution.
target: HFC-23 by-product from HCFC-22 production (F-gases). The binding constraint is MRV and compliance, not technology.
quantitative_claims: (a) Gap size, my calculation from map figures: measured global HFC-23 was 14.0 Gg/yr in 2023, against about 2.8 Gg implied by reports. The 11.2 Gg gap is about 163 Mt CO2e/yr at GWP100 14,600. Rust et al. (Nature 2024, measured at one facility with regional observations and a tracer) found an abated emission factor of 0.19% (0.13-0.24%) of HCFC-22 produced. They extrapolate that proper destruction could cut global emissions by at least 84%. (b) Detectability, my Gaussian plume calculation (Briggs rural class D, u = 4 m/s, ground release, 100 kt/yr HCFC-22 plant). At EF 0.19% the centreline is about 19,000 ppt at 2 km. At EF 1% it is about 100,000 ppt. A two-week mean at 15% of the time downwind is about 2,900 ppt versus about 15,000 ppt, against a background of about 37 ppt (assumed). Detection is therefore not the limit; quantification needs the tracer calibration. (c) Cost: assumed $0.15-0.4M per plant per year across an assumed 25-40 plants comes to $4-16M/yr, or $0.02-0.10 per t CO2e of the gap. Destruction itself is assessed at well under $1/t CO2e; that is my recollection of CDM-era literature, not verified this run. No energy claim, because thermal destruction is a small fuel load.
who_gains: S1 and S2: a verifiable cut of up to about 160 Mt CO2e/yr at the lowest cost per tonne in this map. S4: compliant fluorochemical producers that already destroy HFC-23 (Rust et al. measured one such plant) get a level playing field against non-compliant competitors. S7: Montreal Protocol parties and national regulators get evidence that holds up in enforcement. S8: no cost burden; Multilateral Fund support is possible.
who_loses: S4: non-compliant HCFC-22 plants must run incinerators they may be bypassing, at a small cost. S7, specifically China: a sovereignty concern. The design must therefore be operated nationally, with data shared, not imposed from outside. S11: near-zero effect.
closest_known_work: Rust et al., Nature 2024 (doi 10.1038/s41586-024-07833-y). This was a one-off, research-grade facility-level quantification with regional stations and a deliberately released tracer at one European HCFC-22/fluoropolymer plant. Regional inversions such as Communications Earth & Environment 2024 cannot attribute emissions to a plant.
why_different: This idea turns that one-off research measurement into a routine compliance instrument with action levels, modelled on the refinery fenceline rule that already survives in the US regulatory system. The novelty is the institutional graft, not the measurement physics.
cheapest_falsifying_test: For 3 months, run 6-8 weekly canisters around one HCFC-22 plant with a known emission factor, ideally the Rust et al. facility or a cooperating Western plant, plus one tracer release. Then blind-test whether the fenceline-only inference separates EF 0.2% from 1% and recovers the emission rate within ±50%. The idea fails if the weekly inference uncertainty exceeds about ±50%, or if site geometry (stack heights, neighbouring HFC sources in chemical parks) causes misattribution. Cost is about tens of thousands of dollars.

title: Close the adipic-acid N2O loop: N2O oxidises benzene to phenol, which becomes the plant's own KA-oil feed
one_line: Turn the N2O by-product of China's adipic-acid plants into the oxidant for a Fe-zeolite benzene-to-phenol step. The phenol is hydrogenated to cyclohexanone/ol, the plant's own feedstock, so abatement pays for itself and is never switched off when credit prices fall.
conventional_core: N2O abatement at adipic-acid plants. Thermal or catalytic decomposition is TRL 9, with more than 90% abatement since the late 1990s.
graft: From petrochemicals: N2O as a selective oxygen-atom donor. BASF's commercial cyclododecanone process uses N2O (documented in 'Catalysis from A to Z' 2020, details unverified here). Fe-zeolite benzene hydroxylation with N2O ran at pilot-plant scale (AlphOx/Solutia) and failed on catalyst deactivation (Snyder et al., PNAS 2018).
mechanism: Adipic-acid off-gas is 30-50% N2O. It goes to a fixed-bed Fe-ZSM-5 reactor with benzene, which the plant already holds because it makes cyclohexane from benzene. Phenol is hydrogenated to cyclohexanone/ol (KA oil) and oxidised with nitric acid to adipic acid, which regenerates the N2O. Thermal destruction remains as the backup. The incentive differs from credits: the N2O displaces a production step, so turning abatement off costs the plant money.
target: Industrial N2O from adipic acid. China has about 76 Mt CO2e/yr unabated (map; about 0.28 Mt N2O at GWP 273), which the map flags as about 94% of global adipic-acid N2O.
quantitative_claims: All figures are my stoichiometry and calculations; prices are assumed. (a) The loop closes chemically. Per t of adipic acid (6.84 kmol), 0.30 t N2O (IPCC default) is 6.82 kmol, a molar ratio of 1.00. That makes 0.641 t phenol and then 0.683 t cyclohexanol, against a KA-oil need of about 0.685 t. So the by-product N2O can in principle supply the plant's whole KA-oil oxidant step. (b) Per t of phenol the reaction uses 0.468 t N2O and 0.830 t benzene. China's unabated N2O could make up to 0.60 Mt/yr of phenol-equivalent. (c) Merchant-phenol gross margin at assumed prices (phenol $1,000-1,300/t, benzene $750-1,000/t) is $170-678 per t phenol. That is $364-1,449 per t N2O, or $1.3-5.3 per t CO2e, about the same as thermal destruction cost ($0.25-4/t CO2e, NRDC 2026). Net of capex for a 55 kt/yr phenol unit at a 100 kt/yr adipic plant ($60-150M assumed, 10%/15 yr), the result is -$2.0 to +$1.7 per t CO2e. The claim is therefore roughly cost-neutral abatement that cannot be switched off profitably, not a profit centre. (d) Perverse-incentive check: the gross value is at most about $109-435 per t of adipic acid, against about $1,395/t under CDM-era credits (0.30 x GWP 310 x $15). That is too small to drive overproduction, and N2O output is capped by adipic-acid demand. (e) Energy: the floor to enrich 35% N2O to 99%, if needed at all, is 3.9 kJ/mol, or 0.32 MJ per t CO2e. That is negligible.
who_gains: S4: Chinese adipic-acid and nylon producers gain a feedstock credit instead of a cost line. S7 China: abatement that needs neither foreign credits nor foreign MRV, though verification is still advisable. S1 and S2: durable abatement that removes the CDM switch-off failure mode. S8 and S9: no price impact.
who_loses: S4: cumene-phenol and acetone producers lose marginally, since 0.6 Mt is a small share of the phenol market. Cyclohexane-oxidation catalyst and licence vendors lose some business. Carbon-credit developers lose a project type. S10: catalyst technical risk falls on the first adopter.
closest_known_work: Solutia/Boreskov AlphOx: pilot-scale benzene to phenol with N2O on Fe-zeolite, conceived around adipic-acid N2O (my recollection of the motivation). PNAS 2018 confirms the pilot and the deactivation by Fe(III)-phenolate poisoning. BASF commercially uses N2O as an oxidant for cyclododecanone. The NRDC 2026 report treats adipic N2O as pure cost with no revenue.
why_different: The idea uses N2O oxidation as an abatement-financing and anti-gaming mechanism inside the adipic loop, not as a phenol venture. Abatement becomes durable because it is integrated into production, at a time when the cheapest large non-CO2 tonnes lack any revenue.
cheapest_falsifying_test: Bench test: Fe-ZSM-5 microreactor run for 500-1,000 h on synthetic adipic off-gas (35% N2O plus realistic O2, CO2, H2O and NOx traces) with benzene. Measure phenol selectivity, N2O conversion, the deactivation rate and the regeneration interval, and compare against the pilot literature. Add a desk techno-economic analysis of the in-loop configuration. The idea fails if the regeneration interval is under about 1-2 days or selectivity is under about 90%, which makes the net result below -$2 per t CO2e. Cost is about $50-100k and 3 months.

title: Fermentation CO2 by liquid-CO2 unit train: no pipeline, no eminent domain
one_line: Ship liquefied ethanol-plant CO2 in DOT-105 pressure cars, aggregated into 100-car unit trains like LPG and NGL, to existing Class VI hubs. This uses rights of way the rail network already owns, avoiding the landowner and state-law fight that stalled Summit.
conventional_core: Fermentation CO2 capture and geological storage. It is TRL 9 at about 1 Mt/yr (ADM Decatur, Red Trail), with near-zero separation work.
graft: From midstream gas processing: NGL/LPG pressurised rail logistics. This means a dedicated pressure-car fleet, a gathering train calling at several plants on one line, and a hub unloading terminal. The CO2 is handled in the medium-pressure, refrigerated liquid state Northern Lights uses for ships.
mechanism: Each rail-served ethanol plant gets a small liquefaction skid (about 20 bar, -20 C) and buffer storage. The plant loads about 10 cars a day. A unit train gathers along one corridor and runs to a storage site with an unloading pump and an injection well. Most Midwest ethanol plants already ship by rail, so no new right of way is needed.
target: US fermentation CO2 pool (BECCS): 44.2 Mt/yr. That is my calculation from 15.5 bn gal/yr, consistent with the map's 43-46 Mt. This pool is blocked by pipeline politics, not physics.
quantitative_claims: (a) Energy: ideal liquefaction (isothermal compression from 1 to 20 bar, 0.168 GJ/t, plus refrigeration of the latent heat at 50% of Carnot, 0.123 GJ/t) is about 0.29 GJ/t. The verifier's pipeline compression floor to 150 bar is 0.28 GJ/t, so liquefaction carries no energy penalty against a pipeline. Real liquefaction is about 0.36-0.47 GJ/t (100-130 kWh/t, assumed). (b) Logistics: a 100 Mgal/yr plant produces 0.285 Mt/yr, or 781 t/d. That is about 10 cars a day at about 80 t per car (assumed), or 36 unit trains a year. (c) Cost, from Frontiers 2024 competitive unit-train rates of $0.039-0.115 per t-mile, plus my assumptions of $10-20/t for liquefaction, $10-20/t for storage and car ownership at $212k per car and 8%/30 yr. Delivered and stored cost is $35-78/t at 300 mi, $44-102/t at 500 mi and $53-126/t at 700 mi, against $85/t under 45Q. The idea works up to about 500 rail-miles at competitive rates. Small historic CO2 rail shipments (5-6 cars) earned about $85/t over 684 mi (Frontiers 2024), so manifest-rate shipping fails and unit-train aggregation is essential. (d) Transport emissions, assuming 0.020-0.045 kg CO2 per payload t-mile including empty return: 0.6-1.4% of the CO2 moved at 300 mi and 1.0-2.2% at 500 mi. (e) Fleet for the whole pool at 500 mi: about 10,600 cars, about $2.2bn.
who_gains: S11: landowners avoid eminent domain, the main reason South Dakota banned it in 2025. S4: ethanol plants get 45Q ($85/t) and a lower carbon intensity score for LCFS and 45Z. S6: rail and terminal jobs; Frontiers 2024 frames CO2 as a replacement for lost coal freight. S7: Midwest states keep corn-ethanol viable. S3: storage operators (Illinois Basin, Gulf Coast) get feedstock. S1: partial support (biogenic CO2, no new pipelines).
who_loses: S10: investors in CO2 trunk pipelines (Summit-type projects) lose volume. S11: communities along rail corridors face hazmat-car risk perception (CO2 is an asphyxiant; Satartia 2020 was a pipeline event, but the fear transfers). S1 groups opposed to corn ethanol or BECCS on land-use grounds. S9: neutral.
closest_known_work: 'Opportunities for rail in the transport of carbon dioxide in the United States', Frontiers in Energy Research 2024 (doi 10.3389/fenrg.2023.1343085). It finds rail is least cost below about 2 Mt/yr and names Midwest ethanol plants (4-6 cars/day). Related: Northern Lights ship-based medium-pressure liquid CO2. Merchant CO2 already moves by rail in small lots. I found no commercial ethanol-CCS-by-rail project in this run, but could not search the news.
why_different: Frontiers 2024 is a feasibility screen. This idea specifies the operating model (gathering unit trains to existing Class VI hubs), sets the distance at which cost crosses 45Q (about 500 mi), checks liquefaction energy against the pipeline floor, and frames it as the way to unlock the 44 Mt pool blocked by property-rights politics.
cheapest_falsifying_test: Desk study, about 4 weeks. (1) Pull realised revenue per t-mile for pressurised-gas tank-car moves (unit train versus manifest) from the public STB Carload Waybill Sample. (2) In GIS, map rail-served ethanol plants within 300-500 rail-miles of permitted or pending Class VI wells. (3) Ask BNSF, UP and CPKC for indicative unit-train quotes. The idea fails if unit-train rates exceed about $0.10 per t-mile, which puts it above $85/t at 500 mi, or if fewer than about 10 Mt/yr of plant capacity lies within 500 mi of permitted storage.

title: Heat-pump (MVR) top-up to lift waste-heat-capped cement capture from ~50% to 90%
one_line: At Brevik-type cement plants whose capture is limited to the share low-grade waste heat can regenerate, add a mechanical vapour recompression heat pump on the stripper overhead and other low-grade heat sources. It supplies only the extra reboiler duty, taking capture to 90% without a new fossil boiler.
conventional_core: Amine capture on cement-kiln flue gas with waste-heat-integrated regeneration (Brevik, operating since June 2025, 400 kt/yr, about 50% of plant CO2).
graft: From refining and petrochemicals: heat-pumped distillation. Mechanical vapour recompression of column overhead vapour to drive the reboiler, as in propane/propylene (C3) splitters and in evaporators.
mechanism: The stripper overhead (about 95-105 C) and low-grade capture-plant heat (CO2 compressor intercoolers at about 60-90 C) are recompressed or heat-pumped to about 125-130 C. That supplies the incremental reboiler duty beyond what kiln waste heat covers. Absorber and stripper capacity are extended in a parallel train, and the heat pump replaces a gas boiler for the marginal tonnes.
target: Cement process CO2 (about 60% of cement emissions, with no fuel-switch alternative). The binding constraint is the waste-heat ceiling on capture fraction.
quantitative_claims: (a) Verifier floors at 25% CO2: 0.089 GJ/t at 50% capture and 0.110 at 90%. The marginal tonne from 50% to 90% has a floor of 0.137 GJ/t. Compression floor to 150 bar is 0.281 GJ/t. (b) For an 0.8 Mt/yr plant the increment is 0.32 Mt/yr. At an assumed 2.6-3.5 GJ/t reboiler duty that needs 29-39 MWth extra (8,000 h). (c) Heat-pump performance: Carnot COP for 95 to 130 C is 11.5, or 5.2-6.3 at 45-55% of Carnot. For 60 to 130 C it is 5.8 Carnot, or 2.6-3.2 real. The modelled effective COP in the literature (CCST 2025, MVR plus lean vapour compression plus high-temperature heat pump) is 3.72, from 100 MWth replaced by 26.9 MWe. (d) At COP 3.72 the marginal tonne uses 0.81 GJe/t (224 kWh/t), costing $9-18/t at $40-80/MWh. Separation second-law efficiency against the marginal floor is 17%, the same order as steam-driven amine. The gain is a heat source with no new fuel, not efficiency. (e) A gas boiler for the same increment burns 3.33 GJ gas/t, costs $27-40/t at $8-12/GJ and emits 0.187 t CO2 per t captured unless it is also scrubbed. (f) Heat-pump capex at an assumed 400-900 $/kWth is $13-30M, or $4-10 per incremental t (8%/20 yr). (g) Indirect emissions are 0.7% of captured CO2 on a 30 g/kWh grid (Norway), 5.6% at 250 and 10% at 450, so the idea is grid-sensitive. (h) Sector scale: lifting 1 Gt/yr of treated cement CO2 from 50% to 90% adds 0.4 Gt/yr captured for 0.32 EJ of electricity, 0.30% of world electricity.
who_gains: S4: cement producers sell more net-zero cement (evoZero-type) from the same kiln and the same storage contract. S1: process-CO2 capture is CAN's narrowest opening, and 90% with no new fossil boiler removes the 'half-measure' critique. S5: about 9 MWe of new firm load per plant. S6: kiln jobs are kept. S11: no new combustion stack.
who_loses: S3: loses a small gas sale for the boiler. S9: cement price rises by the marginal capture cost. S7: possibly more subsidy per plant, because the extra stripper and absorber capacity, not the heat pump, likely dominates marginal capex (unquantified here). Grid-intensive regions get a weaker climate case.
closest_known_work: 'Techno-economic assessment of high temperature heat pumps integrated in MEA-based post-combustion CO2 capture for cement plant', Carbon Capture Science & Technology 2025 (doi 10.1016/j.ccst.2025.100446). It is modelled: the best case is MVR plus high-temperature heat pump plus lean vapour compression, at €125.9/t CO2 avoided against €149.6 for the gas-boiler case. Lean and rich vapour compression stripper configurations go back to the 2011 literature. I recall that Capsol's hot-carbonate process with vapour recompression is used at Stockholm Exergi; that is unverified.
why_different: The prior work designs a new full-capture plant. This idea is a retrofit top-up for plants already capped by waste heat (Brevik and the other GCCA flagships), sized for the marginal 40 percentage points and judged on marginal cost per tonne against a gas boiler. It also requires measured COP on real amine-laden overhead vapour, which the modelling lacks.
cheapest_falsifying_test: Two steps. (1) Desk check, about 2 weeks: from a cement capture plant's published or partner heat-and-mass balance, check whether low-grade sources at 60 C or above (stripper condenser, compressor intercoolers) have enough duty to supply about 33 MWth through a heat pump. It fails if that is under about 60%. (2) Pilot: run a skid-scale MVR on a stripper-overhead slipstream at a solvent test centre (e.g. Technology Centre Mongstad) for 1,000 h, measuring COP, amine carry-over and compressor fouling or corrosion. It fails if the sustained COP is under 2.5, which means more than 1.2 GJe/t. That puts the marginal cost above a gas boiler at power prices over about $80/MWh.

title: Forced-aeration of ultramafic tailings with the mine's own power-station exhaust (heap-leach practice)
one_line: Build brucite-bearing nickel tailings into agglomerated, aerated heaps, as copper bioleach heaps are built, and blow the mine's gas-engine or turbine exhaust (about 5% CO2) through them. This removes the CO2-supply limit that holds passive carbonation at Mt Keith to about 11% of mine emissions.
conventional_core: Passive carbonation of ultramafic tailings (Mt Keith: about 39.8 kt CO2/yr, 11% of the mine's emissions; measured by Wilson et al. 2014).
graft: From mining hydrometallurgy: heap-leach construction. Fines are agglomerated for permeability, stacked in lifts, aerated from below with low-pressure blowers through perforated pipe (an ASTM F2987 heap-leach aeration specification exists), and drip-irrigated to control moisture.
mechanism: Fresh tailings with brucite (Mg(OH)2) are agglomerated and stacked 6-10 m high over aeration pipe. Exhaust from the mine power station (about 5% CO2, cooled) is blown through the stack, and drip irrigation keeps the pores moist without flooding them. CO2 reacts with brucite to form hydromagnesite and nesquehonite. Passive tests show the reaction is limited by CO2 supply (Energy Procedia 2017: CO2 diffusion slower than reaction). Treated exhaust leaves through the top of the heap. The result is a permanent mineral store of the mine's own fossil CO2. This is an emissions reduction, not a removal.
target: Mine-site Scope 1 CO2, through mineral storage in tailings at nickel, chrysotile, diamond and PGM mines.
quantitative_claims: (a) Capacity, my stoichiometry with an assumed 11 Mt/yr of tailings and 0.5-3 wt% brucite: full brucite carbonation stores 33-199 kt CO2/yr. That is 9-55% of an approximately 360 kt/yr mine, against the 11% achieved passively. (b) Gas-phase delivery is necessary, because dissolved delivery fails on water. Carbonated water at pCO2 0.05 atm holds 0.07 g/L, which needs 1,337 Mm3 of water per 100 kt CO2. At 1 atm pure CO2 it still needs 67 Mm3. (c) Blower work, my Darcy calculation for 100 kt/yr over a 2 km2 pad 8 m high with 5% CO2 and 30-60% uptake. Permeability of 1e-11 m2 gives 0.013-0.05 GJ/t. 1e-12 m2 gives 0.13-0.52 GJ/t. 1e-13 m2 (silty, unagglomerated) gives 1.3-5.2 GJ/t, which is unworkable, so agglomeration is required. Air-fed aeration (420 ppm) would cost 27-27,000 GJ/t, far above the DAC fan figure of 0.29 GJ/t at 100 Pa. The graft only works with a concentrated source. (d) Removal versus reduction: the CO2 is fossil from the power station, so it is reduction. Background atmospheric carbonation continues on the heap surfaces.
who_gains: S4: miners (BHP Nickel West-type, Anglo, chrysotile and diamond operators) cut Scope 1 by tens of percent with equipment they already know. S11: carbonate cementation stabilises tailings and reduces dust, and possibly lowers the risk of tailings-dam failure. S1: permanent mineral storage with no pipeline or injection well. S7: Western Australia and Canada can claim a 'carbon-neutral mine' story.
who_loses: Few. S10 and S4 take on blower and agglomeration opex (binder cost is unquantified here). S6: neutral. MRV across heterogeneous tailings is hard, which is a risk for S1/S2 trust if the tonnes are sold as credits. Projects should claim Scope 1 reduction, not credits, until this is resolved.
closest_known_work: Harrison, Power & Dipple, 'Accelerated carbonation of brucite in mine tailings for carbon sequestration', ES&T 2013 (doi 10.1021/es3012854). This was a bench study with CO2-enriched gas; I did not retrieve the rate numbers this run. Wilson et al. 2014 (Mt Keith, passive). Energy Procedia 2017 (supply-limited, watering frequency matters). The map mentions BHP and Anglo American accelerated-carbonation trials with Isometric, and Arca's tailings-tilling approach (my recollection, unverified).
why_different: The prior work shows the chemistry at bench scale and the supply limit in the field. This idea imports a proven field-scale gas-delivery and stacking practice from heap leaching to feed concentrated CO2 at depth. The calculation shows permeability, not CO2 chemistry, is the go/no-go variable.
cheapest_falsifying_test: Column test, about 3 months: 1-2 m columns of real brucite-bearing tailings, agglomerated and not, fed humidified 5% CO2 against an air control. Measure gas permeability, inlet and outlet CO2 (uptake), and total inorganic carbon by depth over time. It fails if agglomerated permeability is under about 1e-12 m2, or if brucite conversion stalls below about 30% from surface passivation.

title: Rich/lean amine tankage plus off-peak electric regeneration for cycling gas plants
one_line: Borrow refinery intermediate tankage to decouple absorption from regeneration at an NGCC with capture running 25-40% of the time. Store rich amine while the turbine runs, keeping full output at peak prices. Regenerate around the clock in a stripper sized for average flow, using an electric boiler or heat pump in the cheap, renewable-surplus hours when the gas plant is off.
conventional_core: NGCC post-combustion amine capture (NZT Power, Calpine Baytown; NETL Rev 4A cost basis).
graft: From refining: intermediate tankage that decouples units with different run schedules, in this case between absorber and stripper. The off-peak electric reboiler is a sub-element of the same decoupling, not a second mechanism.
mechanism: The absorber is sized for full flue-gas flow and runs only with the turbine. Rich solvent goes to a nitrogen-blanketed tank, and lean solvent is drawn from a second tank. The stripper, reboiler and CO2 compressor are sized for the daily average CO2 rate and run 24 h. When the turbine is off, regeneration heat comes from an electric boiler or heat pump on low-price power. The turbine therefore sells its full output at peak prices with no steam extraction, and expensive regeneration equipment runs at a high capacity factor.
target: The capacity-factor penalty on gas-plant capture. NETL's $61/t at 85% CF rises to about $99-110/t at 40% CF (map). This is the map's first open problem.
quantitative_claims: My calculation, all assumptions labelled in the script. Basis: 742 MW NGCC with 270 t/h captured at full load; capture capex of $717M from NETL Rev 4A H-class ($970 to $1,936/kW, 2018$); 35% of it in regeneration and compression (assumed); scaling exponent 0.65. (a) Verifier floor at 4% CO2 and 90% capture: 0.219 GJ/t. (b) At 40% CF and one daily block, the buffer is 1,555 t CO2/day. That needs 71 kt of 30 wt% MEA (cyclic capacity 0.5 mol/kg) or 41 kt of 5 m PZ (0.86 mol/kg), i.e. 39-67k m3 per tank. Added capex (amine $38-49M, two tanks at $150-300/m3, 90 MWth e-boiler) is $69-97M, against a regeneration-train capex saving of $113M. At 25% CF it is $52-73M against $149M. At 60% CF it is $75-106M against $71M, so the sign flips near 50-60% CF. That is consistent with Cohen et al. 2011, who found only 15-30 min of storage optimal at high capacity factor. (c) Energy arbitrage: lost peak output of about 0.30 MWh/t at $100-150/MWh against e-boiler regeneration of 0.93 MWh/t at $0-20/MWh saves $11-45 per t. Over 0.95 Mt/yr at 40% CF that is $11-43M/yr. Combined with annualised capex savings of $1.6-4.3/t, the reduction is about $13-49/t against an approximately $100/t CF-adjusted baseline. (d) Climate guard: off-peak electric regeneration at 0.93 MWh/t adds 0.09 t CO2 per t captured if marginal grid emissions are 100 g/kWh, 0.37 at 400 and 0.84 at 900. It must run only in hours under about 100 g/kWh, or with a heat pump (0.43 MWh/t at COP 2.5).
who_gains: S5: capture no longer costs peak-hour output, and the plant becomes a flexible load-shifter. S3: gas-plant capture remains bankable as capacity factors fall, which preserves gas demand. S7: firm low-carbon capacity at lower cost per tonne. S6: jobs in industrial clusters such as Teesside. S10: lower stranded-capex risk.
who_loses: S1: may see this as entrenching gas (lock-in), and it does nothing about upstream methane. S11: very large solvent tanks (two tanks of 40-70k m3) add a perceived chemical-storage hazard. S9: capacity-payment pass-through. Solvent vendors could gain or lose depending on inventory.
closest_known_work: Cohen, Rochelle & Webber, Energy Procedia 2011 (doi 10.1016/j.egypro.2011.02.159). For a 500 MW coal plant, solvent storage gave a 9-29% profit advantage at $30-100/t CO2, and only 15-30 min of storage was optimal. Aburime et al., CCST 2022 (doi 10.1016/j.ccst.2021.100024), modelled AMP capture with solvent storage at an NGCC; I could not retrieve the details. Energy 2025 covers predictive control of solvent storage. The map lists this as an open problem.
why_different: The prior work assumed high-capacity-factor plants that shift a little stripping into peak hours. This idea targets 25-40% capacity factor, sizes for a full daily cycle, downsizes the regeneration train to average flow, and moves regeneration energy to an electric source in the gas plant's off-hours. The calculation shows it pays only below about 50-60% CF and only on low-carbon off-peak power.
cheapest_falsifying_test: Computation, about 3-4 weeks: an hourly dispatch-and-storage optimisation for a real cycling CCGT using 2024-25 GB or ERCOT hourly prices and marginal emission factors, plus a vendor-checked regeneration capex share. The idea fails if net present value is not positive at a 40% capacity factor, or if fewer than about 1,500 h/yr fall below 100 g/kWh (the climate guard). Parallel bench test: oxidative and thermal degradation of rich MEA and PZ held 24-72 h at 40-50 C under a nitrogen blanket. It fails if hold-up adds more than about 0.5 kg amine per t CO2 of make-up.

title: Flameless methanotroph biofilters for lean coal-mine ventilation air (0.05-0.25% CH4)
one_line: Packed methanotroph biofilters treat the ventilation-air methane (VAM) that is too lean for regenerative thermal oxidisers (RTOs) to run on without extra fuel. Mines get a flame-free way to cut fossil methane at the shafts they already ventilate.
conventional_core: Packed-bed biofiltration (TRL 9 for odour and VOC control; landfill biocovers are its methane analogue), mounted on the existing mine ventilation fans and evasés, which already move 100-600 m3/s per shaft.
graft: Particulate methane monooxygenase (pMMO) in type I/II methanotroph biofilms, which oxidise CH4 to CO2 and biomass at 20-30 C with no flame.
mechanism: The mine fans already move the air, so the bed adds only its own pressure drop. CH4 dissolves into a moist biofilm, where methanotrophs oxidise it. Henry's law (kH 1.4e-3 mol/L/atm) puts the physics in a sweet spot. At 0.1-0.5% CH4, dissolved CH4 is 1.4-7 uM, around the Km of low-affinity pMMO (assumed 1-10 uM). At ambient 1.93 ppm it is 0.0027 uM, roughly 1,000x below that Km. Biology therefore suits lean VAM and not atmospheric methane. The bed complements RTOs instead of competing with them: it takes the shafts and periods below the autothermal threshold, plus RTO turndown and bypass, where a 1,000 C oxidiser on methane-laden mine air is least welcome.
target: VAM below the RTO autothermal threshold, and VAM vented during RTO outages. Demand drivers are the EU Methane Regulation's VAM venting ban for gassy mines from 2031, China's coal-mine methane standards and the Global Methane Pledge. Fossil CH4.
quantitative_claims:
All by my calculation (climate/runs/2026-10-05/scripts/bio_graft_calcs.py and bio_graft_extra.py) unless noted.
(1) RTO autothermal threshold, from an energy balance (1,000 C bed, 27.6 K adiabatic rise per 0.1% CH4): 0.18% CH4 at 95% regenerator effectiveness and 0.11% at 97%. This matches the map's field minimum of about 0.2%. At 0.10% CH4 an RTO must burn supplementary fuel equal to about 77% of the CH4 it destroys.
(2) Bed sizing for one 300 m3/s shaft at 0.2% CH4 and 50% removal. Assumption: first-order kinetics scaled from an elimination capacity (EC) of 5-15 g/m3/h at 0.5% CH4. The lab range is about 3-20 g/m3/h at low concentration (Gonzalez et al. 2026, ChemRxiv preprint, not peer reviewed). Result: EC 2-6 g/m3/h; bed 118,000-354,000 m3 (7.9-23.6 ha at 1.5 m depth); empty-bed residence time 6.5-20 min. It removes 5,665 t CH4/yr, which is 153 kt CO2e/yr net (GWP100 fossil 29.8, minus 2.74 t CO2 from oxidation).
(3) Required apparent first-order rate constant: at least 0.0018 1/s (half-life 6.5 min) for 50% removal at a 393 s residence time.
(4) Modelled cost. Assumptions: capex $100-400 per m3 of bed, 10% over 15 years, 4%/yr O&M, 400 Pa extra pressure drop, power at $80/MWh. At 0.2% CH4 the cost is $14-54/t CO2e if EC at 0.5% is 15, and $40-159/t if it is 5. At 0.3% it is $9-36/t. For comparison, the MATEC RTO design case (0.326%) gives EUR 9.8/t CO2e gross. So the biofilter wins only below the autothermal threshold or where flameless operation is required. It does not beat RTOs at 0.3% or above.
(5) Fan work (verifier fan_work_gj_per_tonne; 0.3% CH4, 50% removal, 400 Pa, 60% fan efficiency): 0.68 GJ/t CH4, or 0.023 GJ/t CO2e. The same bed on ambient air (1.93 ppm) needs 1,054 GJ/t CH4 (35 GJ/t CO2e), and first-order extrapolation needs about 1,300 m3 of bed per t CO2e/yr. This rules it out as atmospheric methane removal.
(6) Global scale, assumption-driven. Take the ~9.5 Mt CH4/yr of VAM that the IEA, via the map, says oxidation could abate. If 20-40% of it lies below the autothermal threshold and the beds remove 50%, the result is 0.95-1.9 Mt CH4/yr, or 26-51 Mt CO2e/yr net (GWP100). The share below the threshold was not verified.
who_gains: S4/S5 coal-mine owners and operators: a compliance route for the EU 2031 VAM rule and China's coal-mine methane standards with no ignition source on the fan outlet, the main reason operators hesitate over RTOs. S6 miners: a safety gain, plus local construction and media-handling work. S7 China, Poland and Australia: low-cost fossil-methane cuts toward the Methane Pledge. S2: inlet and outlet CH4 can be measured directly, so MRV is simple. S1 and S8: a real cut in fossil methane at mines that will run for years anyway.
who_loses: RTO and catalytic-oxidiser vendors lose the lean band but keep shafts at 0.3% and above. S11 neighbours give up 8-24 ha per shaft at 1.5 m depth (deeper beds halve this). S1 groups that oppose anything easing coal's licence to operate. Mine operators take on biological process risk: cold winters, since activity peaks near 28-30 C; dust fouling; and the bed drying out.
closest_known_work: Limbri, Gunawan, Rosche and Scott (2013), a review of methane biofiltration for VAM (Water Air Soil Pollut, 10.1007/s11270-013-1566-5), and their 2011 lab work with Methylosinus sporium. Nikiema and Heitz's methane biofilters (Sherbrooke): EC 39 g/m3/h at 28-30 C at much higher loading; without irrigation, performance fell 45% in a week. Gonzalez et al. 2026 (ChemRxiv): replicated low-concentration columns with EC about 3-20 g/m3/h and 89% removal at 0.5%. Landfill biocovers, and Windfall Bio's farm methanotroph systems (from memory, unverified).
why_different: It positions the biofilter only in the sub-autothermal band and as RTO turndown backup, with a computed rate-constant threshold (k of at least 0.0018 1/s) at which it beats supplementary-fuel RTOs. It also states plainly that the same biology fails on ambient air. I found no published multi-month field pilot on a live VAM shaft, but my search was limited, so one may exist.
cheapest_falsifying_test: Run a 1-5 m3 containerised biofilter on a slipstream from a live ventilation shaft for 3 months, or on synthetic humid air with mine dust at 0.1-0.25% CH4, logging CH4 at inlet and outlet with laser analysers. It is falsified if (a) the apparent first-order k stays below about 0.0006 1/s (half-life over 20 min), meaning more than 1,200 s residence time and over $40/t CO2e at 0.2%, or (b) dust and biomass clogging pushes the pressure drop above about 1,000 Pa within 3 months. Cost is about $50-150k with a mine partner. A zero-cost desk version comes first: get bed volumes from the 2026 preprint authors and fit k to their data.

title: N2O-respiring bacteria grown in livestock slurry before it is spread
one_line: Use the slurry tankers farmers already run to deliver N2O-reducing (NosZ) bacteria to soil. This extends a method already shown in Nature with biogas digestate to the much larger livestock-slurry stream.
conventional_core: Spreading manure slurry and digestate: a routine, regulated practice on livestock and biogas farms. In terms of N2O management, it is the conventional fertiliser channel.
graft: NosZ, nitrous oxide reductase, the only known biological sink for N2O. It is carried by N2O-respiring bacteria (e.g. Cloacibacterium sp. CB-01) enriched in the slurry before spreading.
mechanism: Wet soils leak N2O from denitrification when NosZ activity is weak. An organism that respires N2O to N2 without producing it shifts the end product toward N2. Hiis et al. showed that organic waste can serve as both growth substrate and vector, and that the effect lasts because the bacterium persists in soil. The graft extends the vector from biogas digestate, whose supply is capped by biogas capacity, to raw livestock slurry enriched on the farm or by contractors.
target: Direct soil N2O from synthetic fertiliser and manure on denitrification-dominated soils (wet, fine-textured), starting where slurry is already spread.
quantitative_claims:
(1) Measured (Hiis et al., Nature 630, 2024): digestate carrying about 6e9 cells/mL cut N2O by 50-95% depending on soil type. Scaled up in a model, national anthropogenic N2O in Europe could fall 5-20%.
(2) Per hectare (my calculation; verifier GWP100 for N2O = 273). At 150 kg N/ha and an emission factor of 1%, emissions are 2.36 kg N2O = 0.64 t CO2e/ha/yr; across emission factors of 0.5-1.6% the range is 0.32-1.03 t. A realised field cut of 30-60% (assumed, below the measured 50-95%) saves 0.10-0.62 t CO2e/ha/yr.
(3) Cost: assuming $10-30/ha for enrichment, it is $26-155/t CO2e at an emission factor of 1%, and $16-311/t across 0.5-1.6%. That is comparable to 3-NOP ($44-117/t, map) and far above industrial N2O abatement ($0.25-4/t, map), so adipic and nitric acid plants should be done first.
(4) Global direct soil N2O, assuming about 140 Mt N/yr applied and emission factors of 0.8-1.2%, is about 0.48-0.72 Gt CO2e/yr. Realistic reach is 14-86 Mt CO2e/yr: 50-60% of soils denitrification-dominated, times 20-40% adoption, times a 30-50% cut.
(5) Energy penalty is negligible; the aeration energy for enrichment was not quantified.
who_gains: Farmers (S9/S6-like rural producers) keep their spreading routine and gain a sellable climate attribute. S4 fertiliser makers and biogas operators gain a premium low-N2O product without selling less nitrogen. S7 (EU, Denmark, New Zealand) gain an agricultural N2O lever that does not cut output. S1 and S2 support it as a pure emissions cut with no offsetting logic. S8 gains if it is adapted to smallholder manure in the tropics.
who_loses: Nitrification-inhibitor vendors (DMPP, DCD) face a competitor. Farmers carry the cost unless payment schemes (CAP eco-schemes, livestock-tax credits) cover it. Only denitrification N2O is addressed; nitrifier-derived N2O is untouched. MRV payers (S10) therefore risk paying for unproven cuts on soils where nitrification dominates.
closest_known_work: Hiis, Vick, Molstad, Rosdal, Jonassen, Winiwarter and Bakken, 'Unlocking bacterial potential to reduce farmland N2O emissions', Nature 630 (2024), doi 10.1038/s41586-024-07464-3. It uses the same mechanism and organism class with biogas digestate as the vector. Also Li et al. 2026 (Life 16:635): a Bacillus subtilis biofertiliser cut cumulative N2O by 39% in a field trial on Chinese saline-alkali soil, by a different mechanism (less amoA, i.e. less nitrification).
why_different: The change is honestly incremental. It moves the vector from digestate to raw livestock slurry and sells through the slurry-contractor and fertiliser channel. The open scientific question is whether slurry's labile carbon still selects for N2O respirers rather than for N2O-producing denitrifiers.
cheapest_falsifying_test: A 2-4 week bench test. Try to grow CB-01-type N2O-respiring bacteria to at least 1e9 cells/mL in raw cattle and pig slurry under Hiis-style O2- and N2O-limited enrichment. Then incubate soil microcosms on 2-3 soils with automated gas kinetics. Falsified if other denitrifiers outgrow the target organism in slurry, or if inoculated slurry cuts N2O by less than 20% versus plain slurry. Cost under $20k at any soil-microbiology lab.

title: Sulfate-recharged AWD: gypsum plus alternate wetting and drying in rice
one_line: Add a small dose of gypsum (clean FGD gypsum, or phosphogypsum within a contaminant cap) to alternate-wetting-and-drying rice. Sulfate-reducing bacteria then outcompete methanogens, and each drying cycle should re-oxidise sulfide back to sulfate, so the small dose keeps working.
conventional_core: Alternate wetting and drying (AWD): TRL 9 agronomy, credited under Verra VM0051, cutting rice CH4 by 30-50% and saving about 30% of water (map).
graft: Thermodynamic competitive exclusion, as in marine sediments: when sulfate is present, sulfate reducers outcompete methanogens for H2 and acetate.
mechanism: Each mole of sulfate diverts the electrons of about one mole of CH4 (acetate + SO4 to 2 HCO3- + HS-; or 4 H2 + SO4). Under continuous flooding the sulfate is consumed once. Under AWD the drying phase lets O2 in, re-oxidising FeS and H2S to sulfate, so the same sulfur can suppress methanogenesis again in the next flood. This is the hypothesis under test. Many South Asian rice soils are short of sulfur, so the dose may also raise yields.
target: Paddy rice CH4, assumed about 30 Mt CH4/yr: 0.81 Gt CO2e at GWP100 or 2.4 Gt at GWP20, using the verifier's biogenic GWPs. Starting point: irrigated systems where AWD is feasible, in India, Bangladesh, Vietnam and China.
quantitative_claims:
(1) Measured (Malyan et al. 2021, Agric. Ecosyst. Environ., irrigated rice in India, lab plus field). Four amendments cut cumulative CH4 by 9.3-27.5%. Phosphogypsum had the largest GWP reduction (23.6%), so I infer it was near the top of that range. Grain yield rose 3.1-11.2%, and GHG intensity fell from 0.309 to 0.212 kg CO2e/kg grain.
(2) Stoichiometry (my calculation). Assume 100-250 kg CH4/ha/season emitted, with emissions equal to 30-60% of production. Diverting 20-40% of production then needs 0.4-3.6 t gypsum/ha/season without recycling, or 0.1-1.2 t if AWD drying recycles sulfate 3x (assumed).
(3) Savings: 0.54-2.7 t CO2e/ha/season (GWP100 biogenic 27.0). Gypsum at 0.7-2 t/ha, $15-40/t plus $10/ha spreading (assumed), costs $20-90/ha, or about $7-170/t CO2e before any yield credit. A 5% yield gain on 5 t/ha at $300/t is worth about $75/ha and would pay for the gypsum. Confound: the yield gain may come from sulfur nutrition, not from methane suppression.
(4) Scale: 10-30% adoption times an extra 10-25% cut beyond AWD alone gives 8-61 Mt CO2e/yr (GWP100), or about 3x that at GWP20.
(5) Energy: negligible; there is no separation step.
who_gains: S8 smallholders: yield and sulfur nutrition, plus a credit stacked on AWD's water saving. S4 phosphate-fertiliser industry: phosphogypsum is a large stacked waste and liability that becomes a product, and FGD gypsum sellers also benefit. S7 India, Bangladesh and Vietnam: methane cuts using an input their extension systems already handle (India supports gypsum for sodic soils; from memory, unverified). S2: a clear mechanism that is easy to test. S1: supportive if contaminant limits hold.
who_loses: S11 and S9 consumers carry a food-safety risk. Sulfate reducers methylate mercury, and rice accumulates MeHg. Phosphogypsum carries Ra-226, fluoride and cadmium. Iron-poor soils risk H2S toxicity, and sulfate can leach to groundwater. S10 credit buyers distrust rice MRV after Verra suspended its CDM rice methodology (4.56M credits). Natural-gypsum suppliers may face competition from subsidised waste gypsum.
closest_known_work: Malyan et al. 2021 (doi 10.1016/j.agee.2021.107545) on phosphogypsum and other CH4-mitigating chemicals in rice. Kumar et al. 2020, Chemosphere (doi 10.1016/j.chemosphere.2019.124824), a review of fly ash, steel slag and phosphogypsum for paddy GHG mitigation. Many sulfate-in-paddy studies. AWD under Verra VM0051 (map).
why_different: Prior work treats gypsum and AWD as separate options. This idea sizes the gypsum dose around sulfate recycling during drying cycles, so a fraction of the stoichiometric dose lasts the season. It also routes industrial gypsum through fertiliser channels under an explicit contaminant and MeHg cap.
cheapest_falsifying_test: A 10-week pot or microcosm trial with four arms: continuous flood, AWD, flood plus gypsum, and AWD plus gypsum, at 0.3-1 t/ha equivalent. Measure CH4 flux by chamber, porewater sulfate after each drying, and soil and grain MeHg. Falsified if any of these holds: (a) AWD plus gypsum beats AWD alone by less than 10 percentage points of CH4; (b) porewater sulfate does not rebound after drying; (c) MeHg rises more than 50% above control. Cost about $15-30k at a university greenhouse.

title: Repair-cycle DAC sorbent: wash out and reload the oxidised amine in place
one_line: Photosystem II repairs itself by swapping out only its damaged D1 protein. Copy that: build solid-amine DAC contactors so the oxidised amine is flushed and re-impregnated in place, while the costly support and structure stay.
conventional_core: Solid-amine temperature-vacuum swing DAC (Climeworks type; PEI-class amines on silica or laminate supports), regenerated at about 80-100 C.
graft: The photosystem II D1 repair cycle. The FtsH protease degrades photodamaged D1, and a new D1 is made and reassembled into the PSII complex, whose other parts are kept (Zhang et al. 2026, New Phytologist).
mechanism: Oxidative degradation attacks the amine, not the inorganic support. Physically impregnated amine (rather than covalently grafted) can be washed out with a solvent, and fresh amine solution can re-coat the same structured support inside the contactor. The sorbent becomes a permanent scaffold plus a consumable amine, and the design goal shifts from 'make the amine last' to 'make the amine cheap to replace'.
target: Sorbent lifetime and replacement cost. The map flags this as the main materials lever at gigatonne scale: no public field-lifetime data exist, and TEA needs 1e4 to 1e5 cycles. The target plants are Mammoth-class and later solid-sorbent plants.
quantitative_claims:
(1) Parametric (my calculation): sorbent replacement costs $69-1,038/t CO2. Inputs are a working capacity of 1-1.5 mol/kg, 3-6 cycles/day, 1-2 yr life and $20-50/kg for structured sorbent, which gives 48-289 kg CO2 per kg of sorbent over its life. In-place reload cuts this by 46-54%, or $33-560/t depending on the case. Reload assumptions: amine is 20-30% of sorbent cost, the support is reused 5-10 times, and process overhead is 10-15%.
(2) Material flow: replacement mass falls from 3.5-21 Mt/yr of sorbent per Gt CO2 to mostly amine, at 1.4-8.3 Mt/yr per Gt (40 wt%). Amine supply, the Deutz and Bardow concern, is not solved.
(3) Reload energy, assuming 2 kg methanol evaporated per kg sorbent per reload, is 0.008-0.046 GJ/t CO2. That is under 1% of real DAC energy (5-10 GJ/t) and at most 10% of the 0.465 GJ/t floor (verifier).
(4) Degradation is fast enough to test in days. In an accelerated test (Thakkar et al. 2024, ACS Omega), PEI-silica lost about 94% of its capacity within 24 h at 120 C in air with 21% O2.
who_gains: S10 DAC buyers and investors get a lower, more predictable cost per delivered tonne. Solid-sorbent DAC operators gain, including S3/S4-backed ones such as Shell- and Mitsubishi-backed Avnos. S4 amine and chemical makers sell a recurring consumable. S1 and S8 gain cheaper durable removal, reserved for residual emissions.
who_loses: Sorbent and contactor suppliers whose revenue comes from replacing whole modules. S1 critics who see cheaper DAC as moral hazard. S11, if the solvent handling during reload (methanol VOCs, spent amine waste) is poorly contained.
closest_known_work: Climeworks' sorbent and filter upgrades at Mammoth (map). Thakkar et al. 2024 accelerated PEI-silica testing (doi 10.1021/acsomega.4c05639). Zhao et al. 2025 PEI on layered double hydroxide, which resists oxidation (doi 10.1002/advs.202507756). Han et al. 2026, epoxide-functionalised amines stable in O2 and humidity (Adv. Sci.). The antioxidant-additive literature.
why_different: Existing work tries to make the amine last longer. This idea accepts degradation and makes the amine cheap to replace in place without dismantling the contactor. I found no published wash-and-reload study for DAC laminates, but my literature search was cut short by the search budget, so prior art may exist.
cheapest_falsifying_test: A 4-6 week bench loop needing only a TGA and an oven. Age PEI/silica powder and a PEI-coated laminate coupon at 100-120 C in air to about 50% capacity loss. Wash with water and methanol, re-impregnate, then re-measure CO2 capacity at 400 ppm and BET surface area. Repeat 5 times. Falsified if recovered capacity is below 80% of fresh after the second reload, or if BET area falls more than 10% per cycle (oxidation products bonding to silica or blocking pores). Cost under $10k.

title: CAM-style capture for cycling gas plants: absorb while generating, regenerate on surplus power
one_line: CAM plants fix CO2 into a stored acid at night and release it by day. Copy that for gas plants with carbon capture: store rich amine while the plant runs, and strip it with electric heat, imported through the plant's own grid connection, when the plant is off and power is cheap and clean.
conventional_core: Post-combustion amine capture on a combined-cycle gas plant (NETL Rev 4A reference; NZT Power and Calpine Baytown under construction).
graft: Crassulacean acid metabolism (CAM): CO2 uptake by PEP carboxylase into a malate store is separated in time from decarboxylation, a carbon-concentrating mechanism in biology.
mechanism: The absorber is sized for full flue-gas flow and runs only while the plant generates. Rich and lean solvent tanks buffer one day's CO2. The stripper, compressor and an electric boiler or heat pump are sized for the daily average and run in off-hours, importing power through the plant's existing connection. Peak output is no longer derated by steam extraction, and regeneration becomes a flexible load that absorbs surplus renewable power.
target: Gas plants with capture running at 30-60% capacity factor. Per the map, NETL's $61/t at 85% capacity factor rises to about $95-109/t at 40%.
quantitative_claims:
All modelled, by my calculation.
(1) Storage for a 742 MW-class plant capturing 270 t/h in 10-h generation blocks: 2,700 t CO2/day, needing 51,000-77,000 t of solvent per tank at 0.8-1.2 mol/kg cyclic capacity. Tanks plus amine cost $38-104M (assumed $150-300/m3 for tanks, $1.5-2.5/kg for amine).
