(2) Capex: regeneration sized at 42% of the peak rate (cost exponent 0.65). Of an assumed $628M capture capex, with regeneration and compression at 45-60%, this saves $123-164M. After about $14M for the electric boiler and the storage cost, the net capex saving is $27-103M, or $2.6-10/t at 946 kt/yr.
(3) Energy: steam extraction loses about 0.37 MWh/t at peak (Boundary Dam 3 derate), while electric-boiler regeneration uses 0.94 MWh/t off-peak. The saving is $1/t at $80/MWh peak against $30/MWh off-peak, and $37/t at $150 against $20. The total benefit is about $4-47/t against the $95-109/t baseline at 40% capacity factor.
(4) Thermodynamics (verifier): the floor is 0.219 GJ/t (4% CO2, 90% capture) plus 0.282 GJ/t compression, 0.50 GJ/t in all. Second-law efficiency falls from about 38% (steam extraction) to 15% (electric boiler) or 30% (heat pump, COP 2.4). The gain is economic, not thermodynamic.
(5) Climate break-even: worse than steam extraction if the off-peak marginal grid exceeds 0.18 t CO2/MWh (electric boiler) or 0.36 t/MWh (heat pump). On a 0.4 t/MWh grid an electric boiler emits 0.38 t per t captured.
who_gains: S5 utilities get capture without a peak derate, and regeneration becomes a flexible load that soaks up curtailment. S3 keeps gas demand and a storage business. S7 gets firm low-carbon capacity plus balancing. S9 gets cheaper firm power through contracts for difference. S6 keeps plant and cluster jobs.
who_loses: S1 opposes gas lock-in. Battery storage and other flexible loads compete for cheap off-peak power. S11 near a tank farm holding 50-80 kt of amine solvent faces spill and amine-emission risk. If off-peak power is fossil-marginal, the climate case reverses.
closest_known_work: Solvent storage for flexible post-combustion capture by Cohen, Rochelle and Webber (UT Austin, about 2011-12), and later flexible-CCS optimisation such as Mac Dowell and Shah (2015). I cite these from memory; my fetch to re-verify them failed. NETL Rev 4A provides the cost basis.
why_different: Earlier solvent-storage work shifted stripping to low-price hours using the plant's own steam. Here regeneration moves entirely to hours when the plant is off, is electrified through the existing interconnection, and is sized to the average rather than the peak rate. A grid-intensity condition is attached as an explicit go/no-go.
cheapest_falsifying_test: A 2-4 week desk test: an hourly dispatch model using one year of real prices and marginal emissions (for example GB or ERCOT 2025) for a combined-cycle plant at 30-60% capacity factor, with NETL Rev 4A capex shares. Falsified if the net saving is below $5/t, or if off-peak marginal intensity exceeds 0.18 t/MWh in more than 30% of regeneration hours. A side bench test checks rich-solvent hold-up stability (degradation and CO2 off-gassing) over 14 h at 40 C.

title: Enzyme-promoted carbonate capture so cement kilns can capture beyond Brevik's 50% on low-grade heat
one_line: Swap the amine for potassium carbonate promoted by carbonic anhydrase and regenerated under vacuum at about 75 C. Kiln-shell hot water, deeper exhaust cooling and low-lift heat pumps could then push capture from about 50% toward 90%, with no new fuel and no amine emissions.
conventional_core: Brevik-type post-combustion capture on a cement kiln, regenerated with waste heat, with ship-to-Northern-Lights storage (400 kt/yr, about 50% of plant CO2, capped by available waste heat).
graft: Carbonic anhydrase, which catalyses CO2 hydration with kcat about 1e6/s (textbook value). It makes slow, inorganic K2CO3 absorb fast enough to be practical.
mechanism: K2CO3 binds CO2 weakly, so it can be stripped under vacuum at 70-80 C, but on its own it absorbs CO2 slowly; carbonic anhydrase closes that rate gap. Heat at 75 C can come from kiln-shell heat exchangers (shell surfaces run at about 250-315 C), from cooling the preheater and cooler exhausts below 100 C, and from heat pumps or mechanical vapour recompression with a small lift (45 to 80 C). The solvent is inorganic, so there is no oxidative degradation and no nitrosamine emission. The enzyme becomes the consumable.
target: Process and fuel CO2 at cement kilns where capture is limited by waste heat. Within the cement CCUS wedge (GCCA roadmap: about 1.37 Gt by 2050), it raises the capture fraction per kiln.
quantitative_claims:
(1) Verifier floors: separation 0.110 GJ/t (25% CO2, 90% capture) and 0.115 at 95%. Compression 0.282 GJ/t from 1 bar and 0.350 from 0.3 bar; the vacuum stripper adds 0.068.
(2) Exergy of regeneration heat: 0.68-0.80 GJ/t for amine at 125 C (2.7-3.2 GJ/t), against 0.36-0.50 for CA-K2CO3 at 75 C (assumed 2.5-3.5 GJ/t). Second-law efficiency is about 33-36% against about 43-52%.
(3) Heat-pump COP (50% of Carnot) from a 45 C source: 5.0 to 80 C, against 2.4 to 130 C.
(4) Heat inventory per tonne of clinker. Assumptions: 0.85 t CO2/t clinker; heat above 130 C calibrated to Brevik's 50%, giving 1.15 GJ/t clinker; kiln-shell loss 0.15-0.4 GJ/t clinker (11.7% of input in one audit), half of it recoverable; deeper exhaust cooling 0.15-0.25 GJ/t. Result: free heat covers 46-75% capture. Reaching 90% needs 17-72 kWh/t clinker of heat-pump power.
(5) Average energy cost to reach 90% capture, at $60/MWh and $10/GJ gas: about $3-4/t CO2 for CA-K2CO3 with a low-lift heat pump; about $8/t for amine with a high-lift heat pump; about $13/t for amine with a gas boiler, which also emits 0.075 t CO2 per t captured. The energy saving of about $4-5/t is small, as the map predicts. The case rests instead on capture with no amine and no new fuel.
(6) Enzyme make-up, for an inventory of 0.4-3.4 t of carbonic anhydrase: $0.03-34/t CO2 across half-lives of 7-90 days and prices of $20-200/kg. It stays under $1/t if the half-life is at least 30 days at $50/kg or less and the dose is 1 g/L or less.
(7) Per kiln: moving from 50% to 90% capture at a 0.8 Mt/yr kiln adds about 0.32 Mt/yr stored.
who_gains: S4 cement makers can sell genuinely net-zero cement per plant, rather than through mass-balance allocation, without buying new fuel. S11 avoids amine and nitrosamine emissions, since K2CO3 is non-volatile and non-toxic. S3 storage operators get about 80% more tonnes per kiln. S6 keeps kiln jobs. S1 accepts it for process CO2, where CAN's objection to industrial CCS is evidential rather than categorical.
who_loses: Amine licensors (SLB Capturi, Shell Cansolv) lose these sites. Gas suppliers sell no boiler fuel. S10 returns suffer if the larger absorber and vacuum stripper raise capex more than the savings. The enzyme supply chain becomes a new single point of failure.
closest_known_work: Lu et al. 2011, IVCAP (integrated vacuum carbonate absorption with carbonic anhydrase; Energy Procedia, doi 10.1016/j.egypro.2011.01.185). Gladis et al. 2017, 10-m pilot absorber with carbonic-anhydrase-enhanced MDEA (doi 10.1016/j.egypro.2017.03.1278). Shen, Yuan and Salmon 2022, carbonic anhydrase immobilised on textile packing (100% retained after 71 days). Saipem's CO2 Solutions enzyme process (from memory, unverified). The EST 2025 mass-transfer study in the map, which found that only carriers smaller than 0.35 um beat MEA.
why_different: Earlier enzyme-carbonate work targeted power plants and lower regeneration energy. Here the regeneration temperature is matched to the actual low-grade heat at a cement kiln (shell heat, deep exhaust cooling, low-lift heat pumps) to break the waste-heat cap on capture fraction, the map's open problem. Energy savings are explicitly not the selling point.
cheapest_falsifying_test: A 4-8 week wetted-wall column test. Measure the overall gas-side mass-transfer coefficient (K_G) of 20-30 wt% K2CO3 with carbonic anhydrase at 40-50 C, using simulated kiln flue gas (25% CO2, about 10% O2, 50-200 ppm SO2, NOx, dust), with the solvent cycled through 75 C. Falsified if K_G is below about one third of 30 wt% MEA's, which means an absorber 3x taller whose capex outweighs the solvent and energy savings, or if enzyme half-life in contaminated solvent is under 30 days at an affordable dose. Pair it with a desk heat-inventory audit of 3 real kilns (shell temperatures, exhaust flows) to check the 46-75% free-heat estimate. Cost about $30-60k.

title: Tool-down-if-abatement-down: semiconductor-fab abatement interlocks plus signed analyser telemetry for HFC-23 by-product destruction
one_line: Wire each HCFC-22/HFC reactor's feed permissive to a verified-running HFC-23 destructor, the way fabs interlock hazardous-gas tools to their scrubbers. This could close an inversion-measured gap of about 160 Mt CO2e/yr at a few cents per tonne.
conventional_core: HFC-23 by-product destruction (thermal oxidation or plasma) at HCFC-22 and HFC plants. It is TRL 9, CDM-era destructors exist at most plants, and Kigali Art. 2J(6) has required by-product destruction since 2020.
graft: Semiconductor-fab abatement practice. Hazardous-gas delivery is hard-interlocked to point-of-use abatement status (SEMI S2-style), and abatement uptime is logged so that gas flowed during downtime counts as unabated (the US EPA 40 CFR 98 Subpart I logic; recalled). Telemetry is signed with a hardware root of trust, also borrowed from semiconductor security.
mechanism: The reactor's HF and chloroform feed valves get a permissive that needs three things: (a) the destructor at temperature; (b) in-situ FTIR or QCL inlet and outlet analysers showing destruction efficiency of at least 99.9-99.99%; (c) analyser health checks passing. Each record is hashed and signed on a tamper-evident module. Raw data stays in-country (custody by China's environment ministry). Only signed uptime and destruction summaries go to the Ozone Secretariat or Multilateral Fund. Venting while producing then needs physical tampering that leaves a signed gap. The scheme pays no credits, which avoids the CDM perverse incentive (credits worth more than the product).
target: The HFC-23 compliance gap: the map's 'MRV is the binding constraint' bottleneck for F-gases, and the cheapest large non-CO2 tonnes.
quantitative_claims: Measured: Adam et al. 2024 (Commun Earth Environ, 10.1038/s43247-024-01946-y) put global HFC-23 emissions at 14.0±0.9 Gg/yr in 2023, about 5x reported, with excess emissions from eastern China. Non-HCFC-22 sources explain only 'a minor, albeit highly uncertain, fraction', and the authors conclude HFC-23 has 'not been destroyed to the extent reported by the Parties'. My calc (GWP100 14,600): 204 Mt CO2e/yr in total, a gap of about 163 Mt CO2e/yr against the ~41 Mt implied by reports. That is about 2.5x today's 64 Mt/yr of global operating CCS capacity. Destruction cost (ASSUMED $5-10M capex, $0.5-2M/yr opex, 200-1,000 t HFC-23/yr per plant, 8%/15 yr) is $1,100-15,800 per t HFC-23, or $0.07-1.1/t CO2e. Interlock plus analyser retrofit (ASSUMED $0.3-1M per plant x 30-40 plants) is $9-40M one-off, or $0.005-0.025/t CO2e over 10 years of the gap. Energy is negligible against the abated mass: no separation, and the by-product stream is already concentrated. For HCFC-22 buyers the impact is about 1% of price at large plants (ASSUMED 3% by-product ratio), and up to ~15% at small plants if destructors must be built new.
who_gains: S1/S2: the cheapest verifiable tonnes available, checkable by independent atmospheric inversions. S7: China can show Kigali compliance while keeping data custody, and other parties gain treaty credibility. S4: compliant fluorochemical producers (Chemours, Honeywell, Arkema, compliant Chinese firms) stop being undercut by venters. S8: Article 5 parties keep Multilateral Fund standing at no consumer cost. S9: negligible price effect. S3, S5, S6 and S11 are unaffected.
who_loses: Plant operators who currently vent lose an illicit saving of about $0.5-2M/yr each in destructor opex. S7 bodies wary of foreign MRV need the domestic-custody design, or they will refuse. Analyser vendors win; there is no major loser industry.
closest_known_work: CDM HFC-23 projects (2005-2013: monitored destruction, but credits created perverse production incentives). US EPA AIM Act by-product rule requiring 99.99% destruction (recalled) and 40 CFR 98 Subpart O monitoring. EU F-gas Regulation. Inversion studies: Stanley et al. 2020 (Nat Commun) and Adam et al. 2024. Semiconductor point-of-use abatement with Subpart I uptime accounting.
why_different: Existing regimes rely on self-reported destruction. Here production is physically conditional on verified destruction, and the verification is cryptographically signed yet stays in domestic custody. No credits are paid, so there is no incentive to overproduce, and nothing new has to be invented; it is a transfer of practice from fabs.
cheapest_falsifying_test: Desk study, about 2-4 weeks. Overlay the published eastern-China inversion emission fields (Adam et al. 2024 and regional Gosan/Hateruma inversions) on a geolocated list of HCFC-22 and HFC plants with their reported production and destruction. The idea is falsified if the excess is not co-located with plants that have destructors, for example if it is diffuse, sits at unlisted facilities, or implies unreported production lines that an interlock at known plants would not reach. A bench check runs alongside: confirm that a commercial QCL or FTIR CEMS resolves HFC-23 at 0.01% of inlet concentration in HF/HCl-laden destructor exhaust, using calibration gas. If it cannot, destruction efficiency cannot be verified to 99.99% and the interlock logic fails.

title: Capture-ready power from negative-price associated gas: SOFCs whose anode exhaust is nitrogen-free CO2
one_line: Burn stranded Permian associated gas electrochemically in solid-oxide fuel cells, where nitrogen never mixes with the fuel. Inject the near-pure anode CO2 under 45Q, and sell firm low-NOx power. The producer's negative gas price plus 45Q pay for most of the stack.
conventional_core: Associated-gas utilisation, flare elimination and Class VI geological CO2 storage (all TRL 9).
graft: Solid-oxide fuel cell (electrochemistry). The oxide-ion-conducting electrolyte passes only O2- ions, so the anode exhaust is CO2 + H2O + residual H2/CO, with no N2. A second high-utilisation 'scavenger' cell stage, or a small O2 stream, oxidises the residual fuel.
mechanism: At a wellpad or gathering hub where gas is stranded or negatively priced (Waha), the gas goes through sulfur clean-up and a pre-reformer for C2+ components, then into SOFC stacks. Power serves field electrification, a co-located data centre or the grid. Anode exhaust is cooled, the water knocked out, and the residual fuel oxidised; the CO2 is then compressed for dedicated saline storage, not EOR, to stay within S1 red lines. The solvent capture plant and the post-combustion separation step disappear.
target: The map's 'stranded-gas sink' open problem and the Waha negative-price bottleneck. Also point-source capture capex, because no absorber is needed.
quantitative_claims:
My calculations (scratchpad electrochem_grafts.py) use the OptiLex verifier for separation and compression floors. All inputs marked ASSUMED are mine.
- **Emissions and 45Q value:** SOFC efficiency of 55-60% (LHV) gives 0.33-0.36 t CO2/MWh. 45Q at $85/t is worth $28-31/MWh.
- **Anode-gas purification:** dry anode gas is 56-71% CO2 at 80-90% fuel utilisation. Purifying it costs a separation floor of only 0.04-0.06 GJ/t. Oxidising the residual fuel instead takes 0.15-0.29 t O2 per t CO2, or 0.12-0.24 GJe/t at an ASSUMED 225 kWh/t O2.
- **Compression:** the floor to 150 bar is 0.28 GJ/t, or 0.40 GJ/t at 70% efficiency. That is 3.7-4.0% of gross output.
- **Route total vs amine:** the whole route needs about 0.5-0.65 GJe/t. Amine capture on 4% NGCC flue gas, derived from real plants in the map, needs 1.0-1.4 GJe/t.
- **Gas price:** at the 2026 year-to-date Waha average of -$2.38/MMBtu, the plant is paid $15-16/MWh to take the gas. At +$2/MMBtu the gas costs $13-14/MWh.
- **Cost before fuel:** $47-87/MWh. This ASSUMES capex of $2,500-4,500/kW, a 10% capital recovery factor, a 90% capacity factor, and $15-30/MWh for O&M and stack replacement. After the 45Q and negative-gas offsets, the net cost is about $0-44/MWh before power sales.
- **Firm-power comparison:** Fervo-type firm-power PPAs in the map are around $100-130/MWh (Rystad range, not Fervo's contracted price).
- **Scale:** 1 bcf/d of constrained gas is about 10.3 bcm/yr. That would give about 6.6 GW of average output (58 TWh/yr) and about 20 Mt CO2/yr captured (ASSUMED 1.9 kg CO2/m3), about 31% of today's global operating CCS capacity.
who_gains: S3: Permian producers get an outlet for gas they currently pay to dispose of, plus 45Q income. S5/S10: firm, near-zero-NOx power for data centres and oilfield electrification. S6: Permian service jobs. S7: relief for the congested ERCOT grid and use of the durable 45Q credit. S11: less flaring smoke and NOx. S2: a large concentrated point source with near-zero separation work.
who_loses: S1: will see this as extending fossil life. A gas outlet also enables marginally more oil production (a rebound confound that must be quantified), and EOR use would breach CAN red lines, hence dedicated storage only. Midstream pipeline owners lose takeaway demand. Gas-engine and genset vendors lose the market. Taxpayers pay about $1.7bn/yr of 45Q per 20 Mt.
closest_known_work: NETL natural-gas fuel cell (NGFC) with CCS system studies (Iyengar et al. 2020, ASME J Electrochem Energy Convers Storage, 10.1115/1.4048247). These are utility-scale and oxy-combust the anode off-gas with an air separation unit. FuelCell Energy/ExxonMobil carbonate fuel cells concentrate CO2 from flue gas. Crusoe flare-to-compute uses gensets without capture, and the map gives its cumulative impact as about 0.05% of one year of flaring. SOFC vendors sell on-site power to data centres. I could not verify any deployed SOFC-with-anode-capture at a wellpad; the web search budget was exhausted.
why_different: Separation is moved into the energy converter itself (an ion-selective electrolyte), and the plant is sited where the fuel has negative value. The revenue stack is therefore negative fuel cost plus 45Q plus firm power, rather than a capture plant bolted onto a turbine. A scavenger-cell stage removes the need for an air separation unit.
cheapest_falsifying_test: Desk netback model, about 1-2 weeks, using daily Waha prices for 2024-2026, 45Q, an SOFC capex/O&M range and stack-degradation scenarios. It is falsified if the median-year net cost exceeds about $60/MWh, the price of competing firm-power alternatives for a data-centre offtaker. Bench test, about 2-3 months, on a 1-5 kW SOFC stack running sulfur-cleaned simulated rich associated gas with a second high-utilisation stage. It is falsified if dry CO2 purity stays below 95% (H2 + CO above about 4%) without an air separation unit, or if degradation exceeds 1% per 1,000 h.

title: Absorber-decoupled electrochemical regeneration at chlor-alkali current density, with a mass-transfer gate on electrode-contact DAC
one_line: Keep the cheap plastic-packing hydroxide air contactor. Replace the 900°C calciner with zero-gap bipolar-membrane cells run at hundreds to thousands of A/m2 and built by the chlor-alkali supply chain. Treat any design where the electrode itself touches air as capex-limited by gas-side mass transfer.
conventional_core: Liquid KOH/K2CO3 air contactor (Carbon Engineering/Stratos design, TRL 7-8) or hot-potassium-carbonate absorbers (Benfield, TRL 9).
graft: Chlor-alkali zero-gap membrane-cell engineering: low area resistance, 4-6 kA/m2-class operation, multi-year membranes and an existing industrial manufacturing base. It is applied to bipolar-membrane or electrolytic acidification of the loaded carbonate solution, which releases CO2.
mechanism:
Two separate design facts drive this.
- **Electrode area:** electrode area per t/yr of capacity equals nF/(j x operating seconds). Electrode capital therefore falls as 1/j, while ohmic energy rises with j x area resistance (ASR). That trade-off has an optimum current density.
- **Mass transfer:** an electrode that contacts air directly cannot draw more current than the gas-side CO2 flux allows, whatever the chemistry.

The consequence is to put mass transfer on cheap packing (about $/m2 of plastic) and electrochemistry in compact, high-current-density cells. This removes the calciner's 4.04 GJ/t heat floor and its 25% share of exergy destruction (Long-Innes & Struchtrup 2022).
target: DAC regeneration energy and capex, and electrochemical capture on dilute streams (DAC; aluminium smelters at ~1%). These are the map's claims that energy and capex dominate, and that electrochemical DAC is not yet proven at scale.
quantitative_claims:
My calculations, using the verifier and the scratchpad script:
- **Electrode area:** at 100 A/m2 (typical lab 10 mA/cm2), area is 0.77 m2 per t/yr for 1 electron per CO2 and 1.54 m2 for 2 electrons. A 1 Mt/yr plant needs 0.77 km2. At 1,000 A/m2 it needs 0.077 m2 per t/yr.
- **Gas-side limit:** for an electrode contacting 420 ppm air with a gas-side mass-transfer coefficient of 0.01-0.05 m/s, CO2 flux limits current to 17-83 A/m2. That forces at least 0.9-4.7 m2 of electrode per t/yr; at $200-2,000/m2 that is $19-930/t of capital charge at a 10% capital recovery factor. At 1% CO2 (smelter gas) the limit is 390-1,970 A/m2, so it binds far less.
- **Optimum current density:** with stack cost of $500-2,000/m2, ASR of 1-10 ohm.cm2, V0 = 0.8 V, power at $40/MWh and a 10% capital recovery factor, the optimum is 400-1,300 A/m2. There, electrode capital is $3-19/t and energy is 90-155 kJ/mol (2.0-3.5 GJe/t, second-law efficiency 13-23%). At 100 A/m2, electrode capital is $39-154/t.
- **Gigatonne scale:** 1 Gt/yr at 1,000 A/m2 needs about 77 km2 of cell area. That is about 47x today's global chlor-alkali membrane area (about 1.6 km2 at 5 kA/m2, from an ASSUMED 95 Mt Cl2/yr), or 16x at 3,000 A/m2. At 130 kJ/mol, 1 Gt/yr needs 2.95 EJe, which is 2.7% of world electricity.
- **Caveat:** my cell model is optimistic. Sabatino et al. 2022 (IECR, 10.1021/acs.iecr.2c00889), a system model of BPMED-based DAC, gives 24 GJ/t (about 1,056 kJ/mol) in its base case and identifies membrane cost and performance as the binding limits. It reaches below $250/t only with better membranes. Lab BPMED for direct ocean capture measured 155 kJ/mol (Digdaya 2020).
who_gains: S4: chlor-alkali and electrolyser makers with idle capacity after the hydrogen slump get a new market (thyssenkrupp nucera, Asahi Kasei and Chinese makers are examples; their capacity status is unverified). S5: large flexible DC loads. S1: DAC without fossil heat or a gas calciner. S3: Oxy/1PointFive could retrofit regeneration. S6: chemical-plant workforce skills transfer.
who_loses: Calciner and gas suppliers for KOH-loop DAC. Developers of electrode-contact electro-swing DAC architectures face a hard capex gate. Thermal Ca-looping DAC (Heirloom-type) gains a competitor.
closest_known_work: Eisaman et al. 2011 (PARC; BPMED regeneration of carbonate). Sabatino et al. 2020 and 2022 (IECR; techno-economics of BPMED-based DAC). Digdaya et al. 2020 (Nat Commun; BPMED direct ocean capture, 155 kJ/mol). Commercial pH-swing electrochemical DAC: Mission Zero and Phlair (Frontier offtake about $651/t). Electrode-contact electro-swing: Verdox and Harvard phenazine (104 kJ/mol at 10 mA/cm2, 4 cm2).
why_different: It turns the field's figure of merit from kJ/mol at 10 mA/cm2 into $/t at the optimal current density, under an explicit gas-side mass-transfer ceiling. It also sources cells from the chlor-alkali industry's manufacturing and zero-gap know-how instead of from battery-style low-current flow cells, and states the gigatonne-scale manufacturing gate as 16-94x the global chlor-alkali membrane area.
cheapest_falsifying_test: Bench, about 3 months and under about $100k. Run a commercial 10-100 cm2 zero-gap electrodialysis/chlor-alkali test cell with commercial bipolar membranes on 1 M K2CO3/KHCO3 loaded in a small packed-column air contactor. Measure kJ/mol of CO2 released, current efficiency and voltage decay at 100, 300 and 1,000 A/m2 over 500 h. The idea is falsified if energy exceeds 200 kJ/mol at 500 A/m2 or more, current efficiency falls below 70%, or performance decays more than 10% in 500 h. Desk companion: rerun the Sabatino 2022 model with the measured ASR and current density.

title: Steam-free flexible gas CCS: rich-solvent tanks plus a grid-dispatched electrified stripper sized for average, not peak
one_line: Decouple amine regeneration from the turbine's steam cycle. Store rich solvent while a cycling CCGT runs, and regenerate it continuously with a VFD heat pump or electrode boiler on off-peak power. The stripper and compressor shrink to the plant's average output, and the plant sells full output at peak.
conventional_core: Amine post-combustion capture on a CCGT (Shell Cansolv; NZT Power, TRL 7-8 for gas).
graft: Power-to-heat demand response from power electronics. Medium-voltage electrode boilers or variable-speed high-temperature heat pumps (mechanical vapour recompression) run as a dispatchable load that soaks up cheap or curtailed power, replacing steam extraction.
mechanism: The absorber runs whenever the gas turbine runs, filling a rich-solvent tank. The stripper runs about 24 h/day on electric heat, mostly off-peak, from a lean tank. With no steam taken from the turbine, the peak derate disappears, so the plant earns more capacity and energy value. The stripper and CO2 compressor are sized to the plant's average output rather than its peak, which is the capex lever the map identifies for low capacity factors.
target: The map's capacity-factor bottleneck: NETL $61/t at 85% capacity factor, rising to about $95-110/t at 40%. This addresses its 'flexible, low-capex capture for cycling gas plants' open problem.
quantitative_claims:
My calculations; inputs marked ASSUMED.
- **Plant basis:** an NZT-like 742 MW CCGT at an ASSUMED 0.35 t/MWh with 90% capture produces 234 t CO2/h at full load.
- **Stripper sizing:** running 10-14 h/day (42-58% capacity factor), the stripper can be 42-58% of peak size.
- **Buffer:** the tanks must hold 1,363 t CO2, which is 18,000-25,000 t of 30 wt% MEA per tank at a loading swing of 0.25-0.35 mol/mol (54-76 g CO2/kg).
- **Net capex:** the saving is $146-209M. This ASSUMES stripper plus compression are 35-50% of the NETL H-class capture adder of about $966/kW, and costs storage at $25-60M. At 42% capacity factor (0.85 Mt/yr), 8% and 25 yr, that nets $9-20/t.
- **Energy:** at an ASSUMED 2.7 GJth/t reboiler duty, a heat pump at COP about 1.9-3.3 (45% of Carnot for 30->125°C or 70->125°C) uses 375 kWh/t at COP 2. That costs $9-15/t at $25-40/MWh off-peak. An electrode boiler uses 750 kWh/t ($19-30/t). Steam extraction costs 0.68 GJ/t of exergy, about 209 kWh lost at peak, or about $19/t at $90/MWh.
- **Peak derate avoided:** about 111 MW. At an ASSUMED £60k/MW-yr capacity value that is £6.7M/yr, about £8/t.
- **Total:** about $20-45/t lower than the NETL-derived $95-110/t at 40% capacity factor, before any ancillary-service revenue.
who_gains: S5: utilities get capture that tolerates cycling and full peak output. S3: gas demand is kept. S7: firm low-carbon power, plus a sink for curtailed renewables. S6: cluster jobs (e.g. Teesside). S9: cheaper firm low-carbon electricity than inflexible CCS. S10: lower capex risk. The design can also be retrofitted to gas plants with no spare steam.
who_loses: S1: gas lock-in objection, and electricity used for capture rather than to displace fossil generation. S11: large amine inventories and tanks raise spill, odour and amine-emission concerns. Steam-integration EPC packages lose scope.
closest_known_work: Cohen, Rochelle & Webber 2012 (solvent storage for flexible CCS, ERCOT, modelled). Mac Dowell & Shah 2015 (IJGGC, flexible capture optimisation). Chalmers & Gibbins 2009. Review: 'Flexible CCU technologies in future energy systems' (RSER 2019, 10.1016/j.rser.2019.109338). The heat-pump-for-capture literature (e.g. CET 2025). The verified map already lists solvent storage with an electric reboiler as an open problem. None is deployed.
why_different: Prior solvent-storage work keeps steam extraction and uses storage to time-shift the derate. Here regeneration is fully electric and runs all day, so the stripper and compressor are sized to the average, not the peak. That turns a capacity-factor penalty into a capex saving, while the regeneration load becomes a dispatchable grid asset.
cheapest_falsifying_test: Desk study, about 3-4 weeks. Build a capacity-factor-aware cost model from NETL Rev 4A H-class account-level capex (absorber, stripper/reboiler and compression line items) and real 2025 hourly CCGT dispatch and prices (GB Elexon or ERCOT). The idea is falsified if net $/t is not at least $10/t below the steam-integrated base case across 30-60% capacity factors. Bench, 1-2 months: hold rich CESAR1 or MEA for 12-24 h at 40-50°C with dissolved O2. It is falsified if storage more than doubles oxidative degradation rates.

title: An AEC-Q100 for carbon removal: semiconductor-style mechanism-matched accelerated qualification of DAC sorbents, gating offtake contracts
one_line: Before any DAC plant is bought from, require a sorbent and contactor qualification report built the way carmakers qualify chips: mechanism-specific highly accelerated stress tests calibrated against field data. Sorbent lifetime alone swings cost by $10-1,100/t, and no field-lifetime data are public.
conventional_core: Solid-amine temperature-vacuum-swing DAC (Climeworks Gen2/Gen3 class, TRL 7-8).
graft: Semiconductor reliability engineering. JEDEC-style stress-test-driven qualification (HAST, temperature-humidity bias, Arrhenius-Peck acceleration models; failure-mechanism-specific per JESD47/JEP122) with a buyer council setting the gate, as the Automotive Electronics Council's AEC-Q100 does for chips (founded by US carmakers in the 1990s; recalled).
mechanism: Stress matrix: temperature 80-120°C, O2 21-100%, RH 0-80%, plus ozone at 100 ppb and SO2/NO2 spikes. Capacity fade is fitted to Arrhenius-Peck models. Acceleration factors are accepted only when the stress degradation-product fingerprint (FTIR carbonyl, imine and urea bands; N loss) matches field-aged samples, the semiconductor 'same failure mechanism' rule. The dominant buyers (Frontier and Microsoft, about 80-90% of DAC demand) then require a qualified lifetime of at least N cycles before prepaying. This prices delivery risk, which the map shows is the binding constraint (Mammoth at 3.75% of nameplate).
target: DAC utilisation and delivery risk, sorbent oxidative degradation, and the map's finding that no public field-lifetime data exist for any commercial DAC sorbent.
quantitative_claims:
My calculations:
- **Sorbent cost per tonne:** C/(0.044 x q x N), where C is sorbent price, q working capacity and N cycles. At q = 1-2 mmol/g and $20-50/kg:
  - N = 1,000: $227-1,136/t
  - N = 5,000: $45-227/t
  - N = 20,000: $11-57/t
  - N = 100,000: $2-11/t
- **Acceleration:** 100->120°C gives 2.7-4.4x at an ASSUMED activation energy of 60-90 kJ/mol. Adding pure O2, if degradation is first-order in O2, gives 13-21x. One week of stress then equals about 3-5 months of 100°C regeneration exposure, so a full qualification fits in 4-8 weeks.
- **Utilisation lever:** capital charge per tonne scales with 0.9/utilisation, which is 24x at Mammoth's 3.75% and 3.3x at Orca's ~27%.
- **Energy:** none. This is a test protocol.
who_gains: S10: buyers and insurers can price and underwrite delivery risk. S1/S2: removal claims become more credible. Robust-sorbent suppliers and DAC developers can differentiate on qualified lifetime. S7: DOE and the EU CRCF can reference a standard. S3: Oxy, Shell/Avnos and others selling DAC get a credible quality signal.
who_loses: Vendors with fragile sorbents are exposed earlier. Startups face 1-2 months of extra qualification time and about $0.1-0.3M of cost. No major industry loses.
closest_known_work: NETL 'Amine Degradation Experiments on a Polymer Supported Molecular Amine DAC Sorbent' (2024, OSTI 2429563). Jones group, ACS AMI 2023 (contributions of CO2/O2/H2O to oxidative stability of solid amine DAC sorbents). Jamdade, Cai & Sholl 2024 (J Phys Chem C, ozonolysis degradation, DFT-based with no field validation). Sayari group oxidation studies. Open DAC 2025 (screening, no lifetime). Climeworks' internal upgrades (unpublished).
why_different: Existing work is per-paper degradation chemistry with no agreed acceleration model and no field calibration. The graft adds two things: a mechanism-matched, field-calibrated acceleration standard, and a buyer-council gate that ties it to money, which is the way semiconductors turned reliability into a purchasing condition.
cheapest_falsifying_test: About 6 months for about $50-150k. Take two commercial sorbents (Lewatit VP OC 1065 and a PEI/silica). Run 4-6 stress cells for 1-4 weeks, plus an outdoor real-air TVSA cycling rig for 6 months. The idea is falsified if the fitted Arrhenius-Peck model mispredicts 6-month field capacity fade by more than ±30%, or if the stress-aged FTIR or N-loss fingerprint differs from field-aged material (a mechanism change, so no valid acceleration exists).

title: CO2 as voidage replacement for lithium brine: let direct lithium extraction pay for storage pressure management
one_line: Where saline storage formations carry lithium-rich brine, produce brine for pressure relief, strip the lithium with battery-industry direct lithium extraction (DLE), and let injected CO2 take the vacated pore space instead of spent-brine reinjection. In Smackover-class brines this is worth about $8-54/t CO2, and it is negligible elsewhere.
conventional_core: Saline-aquifer CO2 storage with active pressure management by brine production (Gorgon practice; DOE brine-extraction storage tests).
graft: Battery-materials electrochemistry: direct lithium extraction, either electrochemical intercalation (lambda-MnO2 or LiFePO4 electrode ion pumping) or ion-exchange sorbents, applied to the produced pressure-management brine.
mechanism: Brine production wells relieve formation pressure, raising injectivity and dynamic capacity; Gorgon's failure mode was pressure and produced water. A DLE unit recovers lithium and sells it as lithium carbonate. The Li-depleted brine is disposed of in a separate zone or desalinated rather than fully reinjected, so CO2 is the pressure-support fluid. Lithium revenue offsets well and water-handling costs. The USGS found these costs usually make brine extraction uneconomic.
target: The map's storage-side bottleneck (Gorgon injected 25% vs an 80% requirement because of pressure and brine handling; the USGS found the cheapest option is usually no brine extraction) and its 'pressure management + brine co-products' open problem.
quantitative_claims:
My calculations:
- **Brine volume:** CO2 at 600-750 kg/m3 occupies 1.33-1.67 m3 per t. I take brine:CO2 volume ratios R = 0.3-1.0 and 85% lithium recovery.
- **Lithium value per t CO2:** lithium carbonate (LCE) is ASSUMED at $10-20/kg; margin is after an ASSUMED DLE cost of $4-7/kg.
  - 20 mg/L Li: $0-3 gross
  - 50 mg/L: $1-7
  - 100 mg/L: $2-14
  - 200 mg/L: $4-27
  - 400 mg/L: $8-54 gross ($3-35 margin)
- **Smackover:** 200-600 mg/L in SW Arkansas (recalled company and USGS-2024 figures, unverified this session).
- **Pumping energy:** about 0.02 GJ/t CO2 (ASSUMED 20 MPa, 70% pump efficiency), small against the 0.28 GJ/t compression floor.
- **Scale check:** a Gorgon-scale 4 Mt/yr site at R = 0.5 would yield only 271 t LCE/yr at 20 mg/L and 1,357 t at 100 mg/L. The idea only works in lithium-rich formations.
who_gains: S3: Exxon and Equinor reportedly hold both Smackover lithium and Gulf Coast CCS positions (recalled). S7: domestic critical-mineral supply plus 45Q. S6: jobs in Arkansas and East Texas. S11: lithium royalties to landowners (Arkansas set a royalty in 2025; recalled). S10: lower-risk storage. S4: battery supply chain.
who_loses: S8: Lithium-Triangle brine exporters face mild competition. S11: concerns about induced seismicity, brine disposal and the CO2 plume. There is an operational conflict: CO2 breakthrough at lithium production wells would end brine production, so well spacing caps how much CO2 can go in. S1: still opposes CCS that extends fossil use, unless it is restricted to process emissions and removals.
closest_known_work: Anderson & Jahediesfanjani 2020 (USGS, IJGGC 10.1016/j.ijggc.2020.103161): net costs of brine production for Mt. Simon storage, where the cheapest option was injection into high-injectivity sweet spots without brine extraction. 'Integrated CO2 Storage and Brine Extraction' (Energy Procedia 2017). DOE Brine Extraction Storage Tests. Smackover DLE projects (Standard Lithium/Equinor SWA; ExxonMobil). OpenAlex returned no paper combining DLE revenue with CO2 voidage replacement, but prior-art search was incomplete (search budget exhausted).
why_different: Brine extraction is studied as a pure cost and DLE as a standalone mine. The graft makes each pay for the other: lithium revenue funds pressure management, and CO2 replaces the spent-brine reinjection that DLE needs for pressure support. It is also self-limiting by geology, which the arithmetic makes explicit, so it should be pursued only where lithium is at least 100-200 mg/L.
cheapest_falsifying_test: Desk screen, about 2 weeks. Join the USGS National Produced Waters Geochemical Database (Li concentrations) to the formations and locations of US Class VI permits and applications and planned storage hubs, then compute the $/t CO2 distribution. The idea is falsified if under about 10% of planned saline storage capacity (Mt) sits in brines of at least 100 mg/L Li. Next step, about 1 month: a 2D/3D simulation in OPM Flow or MRST-CO2lab of a Smackover-like pattern. It is falsified if CO2 reaches the lithium production wells within 20 years at injection rates of at least 0.5 Mt/yr per well pair.

title: Carbonated disposal water: dissolve CO2 into existing produced-water disposal wells
one_line: Use the roughly 1.9 km3/yr of US oilfield wastewater already being pumped into Class II disposal wells (2021) to carry dissolved CO2 into the subsurface. The CO2 is stored as dense, non-buoyant carbonated brine, with no new wells, no free-phase plume and about 2% added volume.
conventional_core: Class II saltwater disposal (SWD): TRL 9. In 2021, 11.8 bn bbl/yr of US produced water was disposal-injected; Texas disposed 5.5 bn bbl and New Mexico about 0.7 bn bbl.
graft: Carbfix dissolved-CO2 injection, imported from basalt mineralization. CO2 is sparged into the down-flowing water at depth (or at a surface mixer), so it enters the formation already dissolved.
mechanism:
Stream: concentrated CO2 from Permian gas-processing amine units (verifier separation floor about 0.007 GJ/t), ammonia plants, or later DAC. It is compressed only to about 55 bar and dissolved to about 85% of saturation in high-TDS produced water already flowing into SWD wells.

Why it stays down: CO2-laden brine is slightly denser than formation brine, so it sinks. Solubility rises with depth, so the CO2 stays dissolved in the receiving formation. Examples: Delaware Mountain Group at about 1.3 km has 34 kg/m3 solubility against a 24 kg/m3 load; Ellenburger at about 4.5 km has 43 kg/m3.

What the operator gains: the pore space, wells, pumps and permits already exist. The operator adds a compressor, a sparger, corrosion-resistant tubing and Subpart-RR MRV.
target: Cheap, small, concentrated CO2 sources in oil basins that are too small for a pipeline-plus-dedicated-Class-VI hub (20-200 kt/yr). Start with Permian gas-processing acid gas. Later, DAC CO2 near Stratos.
quantitative_claims:
All computed in climate/runs/2026-10-05/scripts/subsurface_ideas.py and co2_brine.py, using a Spycher 2003 plus Duan-Sun salting-out model. The model was checked at 50 C and 100 bar: 1.14 mol/kg against about 1.09 in the literature.

Solubility and loading:
- Saturation in 130 g/L TDS brine is 24.5-31.6 kg CO2/m3 at 30-40 C and 40-80 bar (17-22 kg/m3 at 200 g/L; 31-40 at 80 g/L).
- Design loading is 23.8 kg/m3, which means 42 m3 (265 bbl) of brine per t CO2.

Scale:
- Ceiling if every barrel carried CO2: 24 Mt/yr for Texas plus New Mexico disposal, 45 Mt/yr for all US disposal (2021 volumes, GWPC).
- Realistic case, 10-25% of Texas plus New Mexico disposal volume: 2-6 Mt/yr.
- One 20,000 bbl/d SWD well carries about 28 kt/yr, so about 36 wells per Mt/yr. A dedicated injector carries about 0.7 Mt/yr.

Volume, energy and cost:
- Added volume is about 1.9% of the disposal stream, so the pressure and seismicity increment is small.
- Energy is 0.31 GJ/t for CO2 compression from 1.5 to 55 bar (real, 65% isothermal efficiency), plus up to 0.28 GJ/t if brine must be pumped up for surface mixing. Total is 0.31-0.59 GJ/t, against about 0.43 GJ/t real for dense-phase compression to 150 bar. Energy cost is $5-10/t at $60/MWh.
- Modelled marginal cost is $12-21/t, covering compressor capex, a $0.5-1M workover per well, energy and $3-8/t MRV (all assumptions). That is well below 45Q at $85/t.

Risk check: the loaded brine has a bubble point of about 34 bar at 25 C. It degasses only if it rises above about 315 m depth, for example through a leaking orphan well.
who_gains: S3 (Permian operators and midstream): monetize vented gas-plant CO2 at about $85/t 45Q with no new Class VI wells. S6 (Permian water-handling workforce). S7 (Texas and New Mexico): Mt-scale storage without pipeline or eminent-domain fights. S1 and S2: a non-buoyant phase lowers leak risk compared with supercritical injection, and there is no EOR. S10 (lower permitting risk).
who_loses: S11 Permian residents if legacy-well integrity is poor. Townsend-Small and Hoschouer (2021) measured orphaned Permian wells flowing produced water to surface at thousands of L/min, and carbonated brine there would degas. Dedicated-storage hub developers lose some small-source customers. Part of S1 may reject anything that 'greens' oilfield wastewater. Regulators face a Class II vs Class VI question: acid-gas injection from gas processing is Class II today, but external DAC CO2 likely needs Class VI (unverified).
closest_known_work: Carbfix: dissolved injection in basalt, more than 95% mineralized in under 2 years (pilot of a few hundred t, 2012). Burton and Bryant (2008-2009): surface dissolution of CO2 into brine for aquifer storage. Eke et al. (SPE 124711, 2011): CO2/brine surface dissolution and injection. BRGM 'CO2-DISSOLVED' (2014): dissolved storage plus geothermal doublet. Energies 2021: micro-CT study of carbonate precipitation from CO2 plus produced-water co-injection into sandstone (lab). Liu, Wang and Zhang (Chem Eng J 2026): surface CO2 mineralization plus Li/REE from produced water. Permian acid-gas injection wells.
why_different: Prior dissolved-CO2 schemes must produce or pump about 25-40 t of water per t CO2, which the verified map flags as Carbfix's binding constraint at 25 km3/yr per Gt. This idea rides on water the oil industry already pays $0.5-1/bbl to dispose of. The water cost is therefore sunk, and the wells, pore space and permits already exist. I found no deployment or proposal that uses the SWD network itself as the CO2 carrier. Caveat: web search was exhausted, so this rests on OpenAlex title searches only.
cheapest_falsifying_test:
Desk test (1 week): run the solubility model on RRC/NMOCD data for 50 large Permian SWD wells (TDS, injection P and T, rate) to get site-specific loading and capacity. Also count unplugged penetrations within the area of review of each candidate deep zone.

Bench test (6-8 weeks, about $50-100k at a university core lab):
- Core-flood Ellenburger and Delaware Mountain Group cores with real produced water plus CO2 at 55 bar, measuring the injectivity change.
- Run carbon-steel vs lined-tubing corrosion coupons.

Kill criteria: more than 30% injectivity loss from scaling or fines; a regulator ruling that gas-plant CO2 co-injection needs full Class VI; or legacy-well density in the target zones that implies brine reaching shallower than 315 m.

title: Lithium voidage swap: CO2 replaces spent-brine reinjection in Smackover lithium/bromine fields
one_line: Gulf Coast lithium and bromine brine producers must create pore-space voidage, and CO2 storage needs pressure relief, the failure that limited Gorgon. Matching the two lets each tonne of CO2 replace 1.74 m3 of withdrawn brine worth $9-59 of lithium, and turns a lithium plant into a Mt-scale storage site.
conventional_core: Saline-aquifer CO2 storage with active brine extraction for pressure management: Buscheck et al. 2012 ACRM; the DOE Brine Extraction Storage Test; Gorgon's produced-water handling.
graft: Direct lithium extraction (DLE) from oilfield and bromine brines (Smackover; Standard Lithium/Equinor, ExxonMobil, Albemarle). The brine that storage must remove becomes a mineral feedstock.
mechanism:
Smackover brines in southern Arkansas exceed 400 mg/L Li (USGS, Knierim 2024). DLE projects plan to produce brine, strip the Li, and reinject the spent brine into the Smackover for pressure support. Bromine producers already do the same.

The swap: CO2 from Gulf Coast ammonia, gas-processing and hydrogen plants (separation floor about 0.002-0.007 GJ/t) is injected into the Smackover down-dip, below the Buckner anhydrite seal, as the pressure-support fluid. The spent brine goes to a shallower disposal zone or to treatment.

The result: storage gets continuous pressure relief, and the lithium operation gets pressure maintenance plus a storage-fee revenue line. Injection must stay out of hydrocarbon-bearing compartments, with no EOR.
target: The approximately 25 Mt/yr of Gulf Coast concentrated industrial CO2 within reach of the Smackover trend (Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, East Texas). Also the profitability gap of first-wave Arkansas DLE projects, which Malone et al. (2026) find unprofitable at 2025 lithium prices.
quantitative_claims:
Computed with CoolProp in subsurface_ideas.py.

Per tonne of CO2:
- CO2 density at Smackover conditions (100-130 C, 250-320 bar) is 575-588 kg/m3, so the voidage is 1.70-1.74 m3/t.
- Lithium in that voidage, at 80% DLE recovery (assumption): 0.21-0.56 kg Li, or 1.1-3.0 kg LCE, worth $9-59/t CO2 at $8-20k/t LCE (150-400 mg/L).
- Equivalently, 337-900 t of CO2 storage per t of LCE.

System scale:
- The three initial Arkansas DLE projects (about 53,100 t/yr LCE, Malone 2026) imply about 42 Mm3/yr of brine (about 716 kbbl/d) at 300 mg/L. That is voidage for about 24 Mt CO2/yr.
- One 25 kt/yr LCE plant at 400 mg/L gives about 8.4 Mt/yr.
- Brine already handled in 2022 (5,000 t Li brought to surface, USGS) gives 8-14 Mt/yr of voidage at 200-350 mg/L.

Costs and energy:
- Disposing spent brine elsewhere costs $5.5-11/t CO2 at $0.5-1/bbl.
- Added energy is only CO2 compression (floor 0.28 GJ/t to 150 bar). Brine lift is already paid by the DLE plant.

Side check (negative result for the map's 'storage plus produced-brine geothermal' open problem): the heat in the voidage brine is 0.33 GJ_th/t, about 9 kWh_e/t at 10% binary efficiency, against about 120 kWh/t of compression.
who_gains: S3 and S4 (ExxonMobil, Equinor/Standard Lithium, Albemarle, Lanxess; Gulf Coast ammonia and hydrogen emitters needing storage). S7 (US critical minerals plus CCS; Arkansas and Louisiana revenue). S6 (south Arkansas oilfield workforce as legacy production declines). S10 (de-risks DLE economics). S1, cautiously: dedicated storage with no oil EOR, plus battery minerals.
who_loses: Hard-rock and evaporite lithium producers (Australia, Chile and Argentina, which matters for S8) and Chinese processors, through added competition. S11 in south Arkansas, from brine-spill, CO2-pipeline (Satartia-type) and water concerns. Part of S1 may see 'CO2 injected to push out brine' as EOR-like. Fossil CO2 sources benefit, which is S1's subsidy concern. Bromine operators bear CO2-breakthrough risk to their brine supply.
closest_known_work: Buscheck et al. 2012 (Int J GHG Control, 214 citations): active CO2 reservoir management with brine extraction, desalination and geothermal. Rock Springs Uplift pressure-management field demonstration (2017). DOE BEST brine extraction test (2022). Huang et al. 2026: review of lithium plus geothermal co-production in the Smackover. Malone et al. 2026: scoping review of Arkansas oilfield-brine DLE, which finds the first projects greenfield and unprofitable at 2025 prices. Liu et al. 2026 (Chem Eng J): surface CO2 mineralization plus Li from produced water.
why_different: ACRM-type schemes treat extracted brine as a cost (desalination or disposal), and DLE schemes treat reinjection as a cost. This idea makes the two flows each other's solution, a two-way pore-space swap in which lithium pays for pressure relief and CO2 provides pressure support. I found no paper coupling DLE voidage to CO2 storage capacity (OpenAlex title searches only; absence of evidence in a quick search is weak).
cheapest_falsifying_test:
Simulation (2-4 weeks, open-source OPM Flow or MRST): a line-drive or 5-spot Smackover sector model using published porosity, permeability and Li data. Compute the time to CO2 breakthrough at brine producers against well spacing, the pressure-relief fraction, and the cumulative Li value per t stored. Kill if breakthrough comes in under 10 years at economic spacing, or if under 50% of injected volume is offset by production.

Bench (4 weeks): Li uptake of a commercial Li-Al-LDH or ion-sieve sorbent from synthetic Smackover brine pre-equilibrated with CO2 (lower pH). Kill if uptake falls more than 30% and pH correction costs more than about $10/t CO2.

title: Fracture-stimulated mineralization doublets in hot olivine-rich rock
one_line: Apply Fervo-style horizontal, multistage-stimulated well pairs to hot peridotite or ultramafic rock. CO2-charged water circulates in a closed loop and turns CO2 into carbonate permanently. Kinetics put the viable window at rock of 90 C or hotter, at roughly 3 km or deeper on a normal gradient.
conventional_core: In-situ CO2 mineralization in reactive rock: Carbfix (basalt) and 44.01 (Oman peridotite, about 88% mineralized in 45 days in a 2025 pilot).
graft: Shale/EGS completion technology: long horizontal laterals, 40-stage stimulation, and an injector-producer doublet as at Fervo Project Red/Cape. It is used to create reactive surface area and to recirculate the carrier water.
mechanism:
Natural fractures limit the area current mineralization pilots can reach, and freshwater supply limits scale (Carbfix uses about 25 t water per t CO2).

A stimulated horizontal doublet in hot olivine-rich rock creates about 8x10^5 m2 of fracture face per well. Water is carbonated at about 60 bar, pumped through the fracture network, produced, re-carbonated and reinjected, so freshwater use is about zero. Heat can be co-produced.

The chemistry: forsterite dissolution consumes CO2 to make magnesite. The reaction's volume increase can either clog the rock or propagate cracks (Kelemen's 'reaction-driven cracking'). Whether permeability survives is the central uncertainty.
target: Large ophiolite and ultramafic bodies near CO2 sources or DAC: Oman/UAE (Samail; ADNOC/44.01), plus US and other ultramafic and basalt provinces. Durable storage that needs no caprock, about 1.6 Gt olivine per Gt CO2.
quantitative_claims:
Computed with Palandri and Kharaka (2004) forsterite kinetics in subsurface_ideas.py.

Stoichiometry: 1.60 t forsterite per t CO2 at most.

Reaction rate and surface area needed:
- For 0.1 Mt CO2/yr per doublet, reactive area needs are:
  - 1.5x10^10 m2 at 40 C, pH 5 (about 18,600x the geometric fracture face; the wall rock would need to react to 1.9 m depth at 10^4 m2/m3 grain area)
  - 3.1x10^9 m2 at 60 C (39 cm)
  - 4.1x10^8 m2 at 90 C, pH 5 (5 cm)
  - 1.5x10^8 m2 at 90 C, pH 4 (1.8 cm)
  - 1.7x10^7 m2 at 150 C (0.2 cm)
- Conclusion: shallow, cool peridotite cannot reach 0.1 Mt/yr per well, while rock at 90 C or hotter plausibly can.
- The reaction front advances about 8.6 cm/yr into each fracture face (about 69,000 m3 of rock per year at 70% olivine).

Water and energy:
- Carrier water is 25-38 t per t CO2 (0.6-0.9 mol/kg), about 44-65 kbbl/d per doublet, recirculated.
- Circulation pumping takes 0.19-0.38 GJ/t (5-10 MPa loop pressure drop). CO2 compression to about 60 bar adds 0.35 GJ/t. The total of about 0.55-0.73 GJ/t is about 1-2% of world electricity per Gt/yr.
who_gains: S3 and S7 in Gulf states with ophiolites (Oman, UAE): a storage business using frac and EGS skills. S6 (frac crews during shale downturns). S4 Gulf industry (ammonia, steel, cement) needing storage. S1 and S2: mineral permanence over more than 10,000 yr, no caprock dependence and no EOR. S8 host countries, if benefit-sharing is designed in.
who_loses: S11 near sites: induced seismicity from stimulation and water handling. The anti-fracking part of S1, which may reject 'fracking for carbon' framing despite the climate benefit. Basalt and saline-aquifer storage competitors lose some share. Clogging risk falls on S10 investors.
closest_known_work: Kelemen and Matter 2008 (PNAS): in-situ carbonation of peridotite, explicitly proposing hydraulic fracturing plus heating. Kelemen et al. 2011 (Annu Rev): recipes for enhanced in-situ storage. 44.01 Oman pilot (Nature 2025, about 88% in 45 days). Carbfix (Matter 2016). Nguyen et al. (ARMA 2026, LANL): induced shear fractures raise peridotite permeability up to 5 orders of magnitude and sustain carbonation. Dai et al. 2026: thermo-hydro-chemical model of fractured peridotite for H2 plus heat. Fervo Cape and Project Red horizontal EGS (drilling time down about 75%, S-1/A 2026).
why_different: Kelemen proposed fracturing in 2008, before horizontal multistage EGS was demonstrated (Fervo, 2023-26). This idea is an engineering realization: closed-loop doublets that remove the freshwater bottleneck. It comes with an explicit kinetic design rule (rock at 90 C or hotter) that rejects shallow, cool targets. It is not a new concept, and the novelty is modest.
cheapest_falsifying_test:
Bench (2-3 months, LANL-type triaxial rig or a university lab): flow CO2-charged water (60 bar pCO2) through a saw-cut or shear-fractured dunite core at 90 C and at 150 C for 60-90 days. Track permeability, carbonate yield (TGA/XRD) and reacted-rim thickness. Kill if permeability falls more than 10x within 30 days at both temperatures, or if the reacted rim grows under about 0.5 cm/yr equivalent at 90 C.

Desk: fit the 44.01 Oman pilot mass balance to the same kinetic model to calibrate the reactive area per fracture.

title: EGS heat, not power: sell horizontal-geothermal doublets as industrial steam and capture-plant reboiler heat
one_line: A Fervo-type doublet yields about 30 MWth of heat but only about 3.6 MWe of power. Selling the heat to chemical, food and paper plants, or to CCS and DAC sorbent regeneration, gives about 8x the energy and 1-3.7x the revenue per well, at about $3-7/GJ against $3.9 (US) to $12.3 (EU/Asia) per GJ for gas-boiler steam.
conventional_core: Industrial steam and low-temperature process heat (under 150-200 C), today supplied by gas boilers and cogeneration (CHP).
graft: Horizontal multistage-stimulated EGS doublets from shale technology (Fervo; drilling time down about 75% and cost per foot down about 70% from 2022 to 2025, per the company-reported S-1/A).
mechanism:
The power cycle is skipped: 10-12% conversion efficiency throws away about 88% of the produced heat.

The doublet is sited inside an industrial cluster, with 120-190 C water feeding steam generators and process heat exchangers. The same heat can supply amine reboilers at 120-135 C, which removes Brevik's 'waste-heat cap' that limits capture to 50%, or solid-sorbent DAC at 80-100 C, without burning fuel.

Oilfield bottom-hole temperature data locate the resource. Oilfield crews drill it.
target: Industrial heat below about 200 C (a large share of industrial heat; the size was not verified here) in clusters on sedimentary basins with oil and gas well data: Gulf Coast, Upper Rhine/Ruhr, Rotterdam, Po Valley. Also heat for point-source capture and DAC.
quantitative_claims:
Computed in subsurface_ideas.py.

Cost of heat:
- At a high-gradient site using Fervo-like capex (company estimate of $7,000/kWe for 50 MWe; 55-70% wellfield share assumed; plus $100/kWth surface equipment; 8%, 25 yr; 8,000 h; $1/GJ O&M): $562-688/kWth, giving heat at about $2.8-3.2/GJ.
- At a normal-gradient site with 2-3x drilling cost: about $4.9-6.7/GJ.
- Gas-boiler steam costs $3.9/GJ at $3.5/MMBtu and $12.3/GJ at $11/MMBtu, emitting 66 kg CO2 per GJ of steam.
- In the US the implied abatement cost is about $0-42/t CO2. In the EU and Asia it is negative.

Per doublet: 60 kg/s cooled from 190 to 70 C gives 30 MWth vs about 3.6 MWe. A 100 MWth heat field (8,000 h) supplies 2.9 PJ/yr and avoids 0.19 Mt CO2/yr.

Capture regeneration: an amine reboiler duty of 2.5-3.5 GJ/t at $3-8/GJ means $8-28/t CO2 of regeneration heat with no fuel CO2.

Exergy factors: 0.30 at 150 C, 0.24 at 120 C, 0.20 at 100 C.
who_gains: S4 (chemicals, food, pulp and paper, refineries; cement CCS): fixed-price, carbon-free heat, and capture beyond the 50% waste-heat limit. S3 and S6 (drilling contractors and service crews; Fervo/SUU-style retraining). S10 (utility-like heat contracts). S1 and S2 (renewable heat; geothermal is broadly accepted). S7 (energy security in Europe, where gas steam is expensive).
who_loses: S3 gas producers and S5 utilities selling gas or CHP steam to industrial sites (lost load). S11 (induced seismicity from stimulation; Rittershoffen-type stimulation seismicity is documented). Heat cannot travel more than a few km, so sites without a resource gain nothing.
closest_known_work: Rittershoffen/ECOGI (Alsace): a geothermal doublet supplying heat to the Roquette biorefinery since about 2016; an LCA was published in Energies (2021); the capacity of about 24 MWth is from memory and unverified. Kawerau, NZ: the Tasman pulp and paper mill has used geothermal steam for decades (Geothermics 1992). Paris Basin Dogger and Munich district heat; Dutch greenhouse doublets; Orca/Mammoth DAC on Hellisheidi geothermal heat. Fervo Cape (power) for the drilling learning curve.
why_different: Existing industrial geothermal heat depends on rare natural hydrothermal sites. EGS developers (Fervo) sell electricity because PPAs are bankable. This idea pairs the new horizontal-EGS cost curve with direct-heat offtake at industrial clusters and at capture reboilers. That route gives about 8x more useful energy and 1.2-3.7x more revenue per well, which shortens the path to the $3,000/kW-equivalent target.
cheapest_falsifying_test:
Desk TEA (3-4 weeks): use oil and gas bottom-hole-temperature databases (e.g. SMU) within 5 km of the 20 largest steam users in the US Gulf Coast and in the Upper Rhine/Rotterdam. Compute the depth to 150 C, and the heat cost from Fervo's per-foot cost curve with a depth multiplier. Kill if no cluster reaches $8/GJ or less (Europe) or $5/GJ or less (US) at 150 C within 5 km depth.

Next step: an offtake letter of intent from one chemical plant for a single-doublet pilot.

title: Reverse-auction buyout and plugging of high-emitting low-production well sites
one_line: Pay small operators, through a reverse auction ranked by measured methane, to permanently plug the worst-emitting of the US's 565,000 low-production sites. Those sites emit about 4 Tg CH4/yr while producing about 6% of output. Retiring the top 10% could cut about 48-72 Mt CO2e/yr at about $4-18/t, roughly 100x cheaper per tonne than plugging orphan wells.
conventional_core: Well plugging and abandonment by oilfield service crews, plus methane measurement (aerial and satellite surveys, site-level measurement).
graft: A vehicle-scrappage / 'cash-for-clunkers' reverse auction applied to active marginal wells. Operators bid $ per verified tonne of CO2e permanently retired, and payment is released on plugging and post-plug measurement.
mechanism:
Omara et al. (2022) found that low-production sites (15 boe/d or less) emit more than 10% of their gas and roughly half of all US well-site methane. That rate is more than 10x the emission rate of unplugged abandoned wellheads. Many are run by small operators (52% of operators own 5 or fewer such sites) who lack capital for LDAR or repairs and whose wells will eventually become public orphan liabilities.

How the auction works:
- A state agency or philanthropic or federal fund runs repeated reverse auctions.
- Eligibility requires a site measured above about 1 kg/h on two or more overpasses.
- Bids clear lowest $/t first.
- The winning operator plugs the well with oilfield P&A crews and removes the surface equipment (tanks and pneumatics, the emission sources).
- A post-plug measurement verifies the result.

The operator may instead repair the site and keep producing, but repair earns no payment.
target: US low-production well sites, 565,000 in 2019 at about 2.8 boe/d each. The design transfers to Canada and to other mature basins.
quantitative_claims:
Computed in subsurface_ideas.py from Omara 2022 (modelled from n=240 measurements, 2019).

Baseline:
- Mean emissions are 7.1 t CH4 per site per year (0.81 kg/h), or 211 t CO2e/yr at GWP100.
- 90% of sites emit under 1 kg/h, which implies the top 10% of sites hold about 40-65% of emissions (my inference from the paper's mean and its 90th-percentile statement).

Retiring the top 10% (56,500 sites), assuming they hold 40-60% of emissions:
- 1.6-2.4 Tg CH4/yr avoided, or 48-72 Mt CO2e/yr at GWP100.
- At $50-150k per site (buyout plus plugging, assumed) with 10 years of credit: $4-18/t CO2e at GWP100, or $1-6/t at GWP20.
- Programme cost $2.8-8.5bn; forgone output about 156 kboe/d (about 0.56% of US output).

Retiring all low-production sites: $24-71/t at GWP100, 119 Mt CO2e/yr, about 1.56 Mboe/d forgone.

Comparison with orphan wells: Townsend-Small (2021) measured a mean of 6.2 g/h across 37 Permian shut-in and abandoned wells. Plugging such wells at $30-76k costs $618-1,565/t CO2e counting methane alone, ignoring their real brine and groundwater benefits.
who_gains: S1 and S2 (large, verifiable methane cuts; oil kept in the ground). S6 (P&A crews and union jobs in oil regions during downturns). S11 (air quality, fewer brine surface flows, fewer future orphans). S7 (lower state orphan-well liability; a cheap methane lever now that the US fee is delayed to 2034). Small S3 operators (a paid exit from liabilities). Large S3 operators (lower basin-level intensity, which helps EU import MRV). S10 (surety and bond exposure falls).
who_loses: Royalty and mineral owners of retired wells (small income, which can be compensated in the bid price). Producing states lose small severance taxes. The stripper-well lobby (National Stripper Well Association) may object to 'retirement' framing. S9 is unaffected at about 0.5% supply. Funders carry a moral-hazard risk if operators inflate baselines, so the auction needs a pre-announcement measurement baseline.
closest_known_work: US IIJA orphan-well plugging programme ($4.7bn, about $76k/well, from memory). ACR's orphan-well methane methodology and the Well Done Foundation. Canada's 2020-22 Site Rehabilitation Program, a downturn jobs programme for oilfield services (from memory). EPA OOOOb/c LDAR rules for existing sources (delayed). Omara 2022 and Cusworth's persistent Permian super-emitters (62 low-production sites linked). The reverse-auction design follows Germany's Klimaschutzverträge and vehicle scrappage schemes.
why_different: Current public plugging money targets orphaned wells. Per Omara those emit more than 10x less per well than active low-production sites, and per my calculation they cost about $600-1,600/t CO2e on methane alone. LDAR rules ask cash-poor marginal operators to repair sites repeatedly. A measured, auctioned buyout targets the heavy tail of active marginal sites. It pays once and leaves a permanent, verifiable zero, and it pre-empts the next generation of orphans.
cheapest_falsifying_test:
Desk (2-3 weeks): reanalyse public site-level measurements (Omara's compiled n=240 and the Carbon Mapper/Cusworth Permian plume revisits) to get the share of low-production-site emissions held by the top decile and their persistence across overpasses. Pair this with state P&A cost records (Texas RRC, PA DEP).

Kill if the top 10% of sites hold less than 30% of emissions, or if more than half of top emitters are intermittent and fixable for less than $10k (repair then dominates retirement).

Pilot: a 100-site reverse auction with one state and a philanthropic funder, with before and after aerial measurement.

title: Retire-and-store: dedicated CO2 storage in depleted oil fields whose hydrocarbon rights are permanently extinguished
one_line: A conservation-easement-style covenant permanently extinguishes production rights in a depleted oil field that becomes a dedicated CO2 store. That gives S1 an enforceable no-EOR, keep-it-in-the-ground guarantee, gives S3 payment for marginal residual reserves, and costs about 6-15% of a $500/t carbon-removal credit.
conventional_core: Dedicated geological CO2 storage in depleted oil reservoirs, which have the best-characterized traps, seals and data (TRL 9).
graft: Conservation easements and land-trust reserve retirement (permanent, recorded restrictions that run with the property), applied to the subsurface hydrocarbon estate of the storage complex.
mechanism:
Under OBBBA (2025), 45Q pays the same for EOR as for dedicated storage, so an operator storing CO2 in a depleted oil field will rationally choose EOR. That is S1's sharpest red line (Climate Action Network position 7) and a source of CDR-buyer distrust.

The covenant has four parts:
- Storage operator, mineral owners and a land trust record a perpetual extinguishment of hydrocarbon production rights within the storage complex.
- Owners are compensated from a buyer premium.
- The field is plugged for production and converted to Class VI dedicated storage, run with the same reservoir-engineering team.
- CO2 comes preferentially from DAC or BECCS, where the premium is affordable.
target: Permian and Gulf Coast depleted oil fields near DAC hubs (e.g. Stratos) and BECCS sources. The aim is high-integrity carbon removal that S1 and Frontier-type buyers will accept.
quantitative_claims:
Computed in subsurface_ideas.py.

Cost to the operator: forgone EOR margin of 2-3 bbl per t CO2 × $15-25/bbl netback (assumptions) = $30-75/t CO2. That equals 35-88% of the $85/t point-source 45Q credit, which makes it unaffordable for point-source CO2 without a premium. It equals only 6-15% of a $500/t DAC credit, which makes it affordable for removal.

Climate benefit of not producing the EOR oil: 0.86-1.29 t CO2 gross per t stored (0.43 t CO2/bbl assumed), or 0.17-0.65 t net after 50-80% market replacement.

Energy: compression only (floor 0.28 GJ/t to 150 bar; separation 0.47 GJ/t floor for the DAC source, per the verifier).
who_gains: S1 (an enforceable no-EOR guarantee, plus barrels kept in the ground). S10 CDR buyers (Microsoft, Frontier): a removal quality tier. S3 depleted-field owners (paid for marginal residual reserves plus storage fees and pore-space lease). S11 mineral and pore-space owners (compensation). S6 (storage operations jobs). S2 (cleaner removal accounting).
who_loses: EOR operators and CO2-for-EOR pipeline owners (lost CO2 supply). S7 producing states (forgone severance tax on retired barrels). Point-source capture projects, for which the premium is unaffordable. Some S3 groups, which may resist setting a 'stranded reserves' precedent.
closest_known_work: Frontier and Microsoft CDR procurement rules that exclude EOR storage. 1PointFive Stratos dedicated Class VI wells. Lease buyouts and 'keep it in the ground' instruments (Ecuador's 2023 Yasuni Block 43 referendum; Arctic lease cancellations), from memory. Pore-space ownership statutes (North Dakota, Wyoming). Carbon takeback obligation (Allen, Jenkins et al. 2021). Supply-side leakage literature (replacement 50-80%, from memory and unverified).
why_different: Today's 'no-EOR' assurances are contractual promises by the storage operator that apply only to the CO2 sold. This idea attaches a perpetual, recorded property restriction to the hydrocarbon estate itself, so the field cannot be produced later by anyone. It prices that restriction explicitly as a $30-75/t premium. It is mainly a socio-technical idea, and its physics is conventional.
cheapest_falsifying_test:
Three steps (about 6 weeks in total):
1. A cash-flow model for 3 depleted Permian San Andres units, comparing EOR plus 45Q with dedicated storage plus the covenant, to get the required premium in $/t.
2. A structured interview or survey experiment with about 20 S1 organisations (CAN members) and 5 CDR buyers, asking whether the covenant changes their acceptance and their willingness to pay.
3. A legal memo on whether Texas law allows perpetual extinguishment of a mineral estate.

Kill if most S1 respondents still reject storage in oil fields, or if the required premium exceeds about $100/t.

title: Solar collector-adsorber DAC: one passive capture-release cycle per day
one_line: A glazed solar panel packed with sorbent sheets loads CO2 from night air with a ~10 Pa breeze. By day it is sealed and steam-swept at 1 atm by its own solar heat, so all regeneration heat is free, there is no vacuum pump and no large contactor, and purchased electricity falls to compression only (~130 kWh/t, against the 650 kWh/t Climeworks states).
conventional_core: Mass-manufactured glazed and evacuated-tube solar-thermal collectors (the solar-water-heater supply chain), plus existing DAC sorbents: supported amine on silica, or K2CO3 on carbon.
graft: The sorption cycle used in atmospheric-water harvesters and solar adsorption ice makers: the sorbent adsorbs at night and is desorbed by sunlight inside the same enclosure (Pons & Guilleminot zeolite/carbon ice makers, 1980s; Kim et al. 2017 Science, MOF-801 water harvester).
mechanism:
Night: louvres open, and air passes at 1.2-2.5 cm/s through a 3-5 cm layer of sorbent sheets. Each m2 must process 529-1,059 m3 of air per night for 0.3-0.6 kg CO2 at 75% capture (verifier air volume). Wind or a ~10 Pa fan is enough: 0.03 GJ/t by the verifier fan formula. Cool, humid night air raises sorbent capacity.

Day: louvres close and residual air is purged. The panel heats to ~105 C (amine variant). Co-adsorbed and injected water flashes to steam, which sweeps CO2 out at 1 atm to a condenser, and the water is recycled. A glazed flat box cannot hold process vacuum (1 atm is ~10 t of force per m2), so the design is atmospheric steam sweep by construction.

K2CO3 variant: thermochemistry (NBS data) gives a night equilibrium pCO2 of 3.5e-6 bar at 25 C and pH2O 0.01 bar, far below the 4.2e-4 bar in air, so loading is strongly favoured. Release needs >=110 C at 0.2 bar total or >=141 C to self-pressurise to 1 atm, so this variant needs evacuated-tube-class collectors.

What the panel replaces: purchased regeneration heat, the fan and contactor ductwork, vacuum pumps, and the separate heat plant. Heating happens after O2 has been purged, which should slow oxidative degradation.

With one cycle per day, the binding parameter becomes sorbent inventory and calendar life. That is why the cheap strong sorbent can win here: K2CO3's 140 kJ/mol is 7x the floor, but when heat is free and ample per m2, enthalpy costs only collector area.
target: DAC regeneration heat source, fan/contactor work, vacuum-pump electricity and separate contactor capex, using free diurnal temperature, humidity and solar gradients.
quantitative_claims:
All figures are modelled; assumptions are labelled; scripts are climate/runs/2026-10-05/scripts/thermo_ideas.py and thermo_ideas2.py.

- **Solar heat delivered:** 6.9-12.6 MJ/m2/day, from 5.5-7 kWh/m2/day on the tilted aperture at 35-50% daily collector efficiency (assumed).
- **Heat demand, all solar:** amine variant (1.2 mmol/g, 75 kJ/mol, 1.5+1.5 mol H2O/mol, dT 80 K) 314 kJ/mol = 7.1 GJ_th/t. K2CO3 variant (0.8 mmol/g, 140 kJ/mol, dT 120 K) 424 kJ/mol = 9.6 GJ_th/t.
- **Heat-limited ceiling:** 1.25 and 0.97 kg CO2/m2/day. The design target of 0.3-0.6 kg/m2/day uses 24-62% of the solar heat.
- **Purchased electricity:** 0.46 GJe/t (129 kWh/t): compression 1 to 150 bar at 65% efficiency (floor 0.28 GJ/t) plus a 10 Pa fan. That is 20% of the 2.34 GJe/t Climeworks Gen2 states, and 0.4% of world electricity per Gt/yr.
- **Productivity:** 90-180 kg CO2/m2/yr over an assumed 300 sunny days, i.e. 5.6-11 m2 of aperture per t/yr. Land is 11,000-22,000 km2 per Gt/yr at twice the aperture area.
- **Sorbent inventory:** 63 kg (amine) or 95 kg (K2CO3) per t/yr of capacity.
- **Sorbent cost per tonne over 3,000 daily cycles (10 yr):** $126/t for amine at an assumed $20/kg, and $28/t for K2CO3 at an assumed $3/kg.
- **Capex:** $840-3,500 per t/yr, assuming panels at $100-200/m2 installed. Stratos is ~$2,600 per t/yr.
- **Rough levelised cost of removal (CRF 0.10, O&M 4%/yr, electricity at $60/MWh, transport and storage $25/t):** $150-230/t for the K2CO3 variant at 0.6 kg/m2/day, and $290-520/t for the amine variant. For comparison, Fan & Xu 2026 model $160-200/t core and $300-350/t deployment-adjusted for CSP plus sand storage.
who_gains:
- **S7 and S8 in sunny regions with storage** (Oman/UAE peridotite, Saudi Arabia, US Southwest, India): local manufacture of glass-and-steel hardware, and removal that does not compete for grid power.
- **S3 NOCs and majors:** land host and storage operator role.
- **S10:** modular, factory-built, low grid exposure.
- **S5:** neutral to slightly positive (small load).
- **S1 and S2:** no fossil energy input and a transparent energy budget. S1's general DAC moral-hazard concern remains.
who_loses:
- **S11 desert land users and ecology:** 11-22 km2 per Mt/yr.
- **Grid-powered DAC developers:** compete for the same offtake buyers.
- **Water:** none on net, since condensate is recycled. In the K2CO3 variant, night humidity is a reactant.
closest_known_work:
- **Kar et al. 2025, Nature Energy (Reisner lab):** a lab dual-bed reactor that captures at night and uses concentrated light by day to release CO2 and convert it to syngas.
- **Fan & Xu 2026, ES&T:** CSP plus sand storage feeding a conventional sorbent DAC. Above 80% capacity factor, $160-200/t core cost (modelled), 6,000 t/yr in <1 km2.
- **Kim et al. 2017, Science:** MOF water harvester, the source of the graft.
- **Heirloom:** fan-free passive trays, but an electric kiln for release.
- **Qi et al. 2026, ACS Sust Chem Eng:** solar-driven regenerative sorbent from wood waste (abstract not read).
- **Search limit:** prior-art search was cut short because the web search budget was exhausted, so an unseen close match is possible.
why_different:
- The panel is non-concentrating and at atmospheric pressure, and it is contactor, regenerator and heat source in one.
- It is steam-swept, with no vacuum and no fans.
- The CO2 product goes to storage rather than conversion.
- It deliberately picks a cheap strong sorbent because heat is free and plentiful per m2, while sorbent inventory is the cost driver at one cycle per day.

title: Heat-pump-lifted capture fraction at waste-heat-limited cement plants (50% to 90-95%)
one_line: Brevik captures 50% of its CO2 because the capture plant was sized to the waste heat available. Industrial heat pumps can recycle the capture plant's own rejected heat to supply the missing reboiler duty at ~0.97 GJe/t (about $11-22/t), so whole-plant capture fraction becomes a capex decision rather than a heat decision.
conventional_core: Amine post-combustion capture on cement kiln gas with waste-heat integration (Brevik, SLB Capturi), with liquefaction and ship transport to Northern Lights.
graft: High-temperature steam-generating industrial heat pumps and vapour recompression, from the food, paper and evaporator industries. They recycle heat from the stripper overhead, the absorber intercooling and the lean-amine cooler.
mechanism:
- **Why capture stops at 50%:** GCCSI's 2026 Brevik profile says 'waste heat availability was chosen as the basis for the capture capacity specified', which caps capture at ~50%.
- **Heat needed:** the reboiler needs ~2.6-3.2 GJ/t at ~120-135 C.
- **Heat available:** the capture plant itself rejects most of this. About a third comes from stripper overhead vapour at ~90 C, and most of the rest is lower-grade heat from absorber and lean-amine cooling at ~55 C.
- **Heat pump performance:** at 50% of Carnot to a 135 C sink, the coefficient of performance is 4.5 from the 90 C overhead and 2.6 from the 55 C coolers. Blended, that is 0.97 GJe/t (270 kWh/t).
- **Efficiency:** this delivers the 0.76 GJ/t of regeneration exergy at ~78% exergetic efficiency.
- **Implication:** separation thermodynamics is not the barrier (see claims), so the residual 40-45% is a capex and finance question.
target: The cap that regeneration-heat availability puts on point-source capture fraction. This is a capacity limit, not a separation-efficiency problem.
quantitative_claims:
All figures are modelled; scripts are thermo_ideas.py §4 and thermo_ideas2.py §4'.

- **Verifier floors for 25% CO2 kiln gas:** 0.089 GJ/t at 50% capture, 0.110 at 90%, 0.115 at 95%, 0.121 at 99%. Going from 50% to 90% adds only 0.021 GJ/t of minimum work.
- **Extra capture at a Brevik-size plant:** 400 kt/yr is 50%, so the plant emits ~800 kt/yr. Reaching 90-95% adds 320-360 kt/yr, which needs 0.83-1.15 PJ/yr of reboiler heat (29-41 MW_th).
- **Heat-pump energy cost:** $11, $16 and $22/t at $40, $60 and $80/MWh. An electric boiler costs $32-64/t. A gas boiler costs $32/t at $10/GJ and adds 0.18 t CO2 per t captured.
- **Heat-pump capex:** $600-1,200/kW_th gives $6-12/t.
- **Marginal capture-plant capex:** at 60-80% of Brevik's EUR1,052 per t/yr (EUR421M for 400 kt/yr), the capital charge is EUR63-84/t at CRF 0.10. All-in marginal cost is ~EUR100-160/t (modelled). Offsetting the same residual with DAC removals at $400-1,000/t would cost far more.
- **New electric load:** ~10 MW (86 GWh/yr) per Brevik-size plant.
who_gains:
- **S4:** plant-level 90%+ capture supports net-zero-cement claims without book-and-claim allocation, and cuts ETS/CBAM exposure as free allocation phases out over 2026-2034.
- **S6:** keeps cement jobs.
- **S1:** capture of cement process CO2 is the narrowest S1-S4 bridge. CAN's objection there is partly evidential, and a whole-facility capture fraction removes Quest-style accounting fights.
- **S7:** more tonnes per krone of Longship subsidy.
- **S5:** a new, flexible ~10 MW load.
- **S2:** consistent with the finding that the point-source constraint is not thermodynamic.
who_loses:
- **S3 gas suppliers:** no gas boiler is needed.
- **S10:** more capex at risk per plant.
- **Sellers of DAC removals and offsets:** a smaller residual market.
- **S9:** a marginal rise in cement price, negligible per building.
closest_known_work:
- **Brevik CCS:** waste heat only, sized to that heat, 400 kt/yr, opened June 2025 (GCCSI 2026 profile).
- **Heat-pump-assisted amine regeneration and lean or overhead vapour recompression:** established in amine-process modelling and design studies.
- **Stockholm Exergi and Ørsted Kalundborg BECCS:** recover capture heat into district heating, the opposite direction.
- **Commercial steam-generating heat pumps:** available up to ~150-165 C (from memory, not re-verified).
