- EU (assumed cushion/working ratio 0.6-1.0 on about 103 bcm working gas): 40-204 Mt one-off, freeing 19-52 bcm (5-16% of one year of EU demand; €6.6-19bn at €35/MWh).
- Over 10 years, 4-20 Mt/yr in the EU, i.e. 8-40% of the NZIA 50 Mt/yr injection objective.

Cost claim: incremental cost below $30/t, because wells, compression and monitoring already exist. This is an assumption to test.
who_gains:
S3/S5 storage owners (NAM, TAQA, Uniper, SEFE, Snam/Stogit, US utilities): a one-off gas asset release plus a new storage tariff.
S4 inland cement and lime plants: a storage outlet without waiting for offshore hubs.
S7: energy security from the freed strategic reserve and possibly about 30% more working gas (Oldenburg, one model).
S6: keeps storage workforces employed.
S2: process CO2 is stored.
who_loses:
S11 communities above onshore fields. The precedent is Shell's Barendrecht onshore CO2 storage in a depleted gas field, cancelled in 2010 after local opposition, and that mechanism still applies.
S1, if the freed gas is sold and burned (net 15-39%).
Gas traders, through a small loss of storage optionality if CO2 contaminates working gas.
Possible regulatory friction from holding both a UGS licence and an EU CCS-Directive storage permit.
closest_known_work:
- Oldenburg (2003, Energy & Fuels, LBNL): reservoir simulation found about 30% more methane storable with a CO2 cushion, and that mixing control is critical.
- Nitrogen cushion gas used in European storage (Laille et al. 1986/88).
- Mirzaei-Paiaman et al. (2026, Energy & Fuels): a facility-level analysis of CO2 cushion replacement in US UGS. I could not retrieve its results.
- Lab and simulation papers on CO2/CH4 mixing in cushion cores (2023-2026).
- No commercial CO2-cushion deployment found.
why_different: This frames the swap as a European process-CO2 storage product run by the incumbent storage owners, rather than a gas-storage efficiency trick. Sites are selected by distance to cement and lime clusters. Credit counts only net-of-burn tonnes, or the freed gas goes to a strategic reserve, which addresses S1's objection directly. The 2026 US facility study means the concept is not new; the European cluster pairing and the accounting design are the contribution.
cheapest_falsifying_test:
1. Build a 2D compositional simulation in open-source MRST or OPM Flow of a representative depleted-field UGS (dipping anticline, real cycling schedule) with a 30% and a 50% CO2 cushion swap.
2. Kill criterion: withdrawn-gas CO2 exceeds 2.5 mol% within 10 seasonal cycles, or working-gas deliverability falls more than 10%.
3. In parallel, compile an EU UGS list (GIE storage database) with distance to cement and lime plants. Kill criterion: fewer than about 10 depleted-field sites within 100 km of 0.3 Mt/yr or larger process-CO2 sources.

Effort: 2-3 months for 1-2 reservoir engineers.

title: Enhanced lithium recovery: CO2 as the voidage-replacement fluid in lithium-brine fields (Smackover)
one_line: Use CO2 instead of spent brine to hold reservoir pressure in Smackover lithium-brine fields. The brine extraction a saline storage site needs for pressure relief then becomes lithium revenue instead of a cost, giving storage an oil-free co-product that replaces EOR.
conventional_core: Saline-formation CO2 storage with active pressure management by brine extraction (the Gorgon failure mode; the DOE/EERC BEST project). Oil majors own the pieces: ExxonMobil holds Smackover lithium acreage and the former Denbury Gulf Coast CO2 pipeline network; Chevron holds Smackover acreage; Equinor partners Standard Lithium.
graft: Direct lithium extraction (DLE) from the extracted brine, borrowed from the brine-lithium industry. The produced pressure-relief water becomes the feedstock.
mechanism:
1. Inject CO2 (45Q $85/t) into a lithium-rich saline formation in a line-drive pattern.
2. Produce brine from wells ahead of the plume, which relieves pressure.
3. Run the brine through a DLE plant. Dispose of the spent brine in a separate, shallower non-lithium zone, or dissolve CO2 into it before disposal (see the produced-water idea).
4. Because CO2 rather than lithium-depleted brine fills the void, the lean-brine dilution that limits brine-recirculation lithium projects is avoided until CO2 breaks through. Breakthrough is handled like EOR recycle: degas, recompress, reinject.
target: CO2 storage economics without EOR in US Gulf Coast lithium-brine provinces (Smackover in Arkansas, East Texas and North Louisiana). The pattern transfers to other lithium-brine-plus-storage basins (Alberta Leduc, Paradox).
quantitative_claims:
All figures are my calculations from the same script.

Brine and lithium per tonne of CO2:
- CO2 density at Smackover-like conditions (110-125C, 280-320 bar): 570-580 kg/m3 by Peng-Robinson. PR runs about 5-10% low, so the realistic range is about 600-750.
- So 1.33-1.74 m3 of brine is displaced per t CO2.
- At 200-550 mg/L Li (assumed range; SW Arkansas company resource reports cite roughly 400-500 mg/L, not re-verified here) and 90% DLE recovery, that is 1.3-4.4 kg LCE per t CO2.

Revenue per tonne of CO2 (lithium price is an assumption; 2026 price not verified):
- Gross: $13-88/t at $10-20k/t LCE.
- Net of an assumed $7k/t all-in DLE cost: $4-57/t, with a central case of $8-42/t at 400 mg/L. This is on top of 45Q $85/t.

Scale and energy:
- One 22.5 ktpa LCE plant at 450 mg/L circulates 10.4 Mm3/yr of brine (about 180k bbl/d). Full voidage replacement equals 6.3-7.8 Mt CO2/yr per plant, roughly 4-5x Northern Lights phase 1.
- Brine lift work: 0.03-0.10 GJ/t CO2 (1-2.5 km lift, 50% pump efficiency, assumed).
- Compression floor 0.28 GJ/t (1 to 150 bar).
- Separation floor: about 0 for AGRU, ammonia or fermentation sources; 0.11-0.16 GJ/t for kiln or coal flue (verifier).
who_gains:
S3 majors (Exxon, Chevron, Equinor, Oxy): a lithium plus 45Q business that reuses CO2 pipelines, subsurface teams and the brine-handling skills of waterflooding.
S1: a storage co-revenue that produces battery lithium, not oil. This removes the EOR objection that CAN states explicitly.
S7 (US): domestic critical minerals.
S6/S11 in South Arkansas: jobs and severance taxes.
S4 Gulf emitters (ammonia, steel): a storage outlet.
who_loses:
Pure-play DLE developers, who may lose pore-space control to storage operators.
S11, if spent-brine disposal raises pressure in shallow zones; the Permian shallow-disposal over-pressure problem is the cautionary analogue.
Foreign lithium refiners at the margin.
CO2-EOR operators, who lose a captive CO2 supply.
closest_known_work:
- DOE/EERC Brine Extraction and Storage Test (BEST, about 2017-2022): pressure management by brine extraction for CO2 storage.
- The CO2-enhanced water recovery (CO2-EWR) literature (China): brine and mineral co-production with storage.
- Geological Survey of Canada (2024): DLE on raw and CO2-mineralization-treated Montney flowback brine. It found no clear lithium-recovery gain but less Ca/Mg precipitation.
- Smackover DLE projects (Standard Lithium/Equinor SWA; ExxonMobil; Chevron), which plan to reinject spent brine.
why_different: Prior work treats brine extraction as a pressure-management cost or as a water source. Here the voidage-replacement fluid of a lithium field is CO2 that earns 45Q, and the lithium field and the storage site are the same reservoir under one operator who already owns the CO2 pipelines. It is the EOR business model with lithium in place of oil, which is the specific substitution S1 needs.
cheapest_falsifying_test:
1. Bench test (about 4-6 weeks, a university lab): run a commercial DLE sorbent (LDH-type or LMO) on synthetic Smackover brine (about 4-5 M chloride, Ca-rich, 400 mg/L Li) with and without CO2 saturation at 100C.
   - Kill criterion: lithium capacity or selectivity drops more than 30% in CO2-bearing brine, and there is no cheap degassing fix.
2. Two-phase CO2-brine simulation of a 5-spot or line drive with public Smackover porosity and permeability.
   - Kill criterion: CO2 breakthrough before about 0.3 pore volumes injected, so that degassing and recycle cost exceeds about $15/t.
mechanism_note: Energy and lithium numbers depend on reservoir temperature, pressure and lithium grade; all assumptions are labelled.

title: Dissolve AGRU vent CO2 into produced water already going down saltwater-disposal wells (Permian)
one_line: The Permian already pumps roughly a cubic kilometre of brine underground each year. Dissolving the basin's vented gas-processing CO2 into that stream, Carbfix-style, stores CO2 as dense, non-buoyant dissolved carbon without new water, new wells or a buoyant plume.
conventional_core: Oilfield produced-water gathering and Class II saltwater disposal (SWD) wells, operated by majors and water midstream firms. Gas-plant amine units (AGRU) already separate near-pure CO2 that is often vented.
graft: Carbfix's in-well dissolution: CO2 is released down a dip-tube below about 350-1,000 m, where hydrostatic pressure dissolves it in the down-flowing water before it reaches the formation. Burton & Bryant's 2009 surface-dissolution concept is the related method.
mechanism:
1. Dehydrate and compress AGRU off-gas (more than 95% CO2) to about 35-100 bar.
2. Release it into the tubing of selected deep SWD wells at a depth where it dissolves fully. Water velocity of about 6 m/s in 3.5-inch tubing at 20k bbl/d far exceeds the bubble rise speed of about 0.2-0.3 m/s.
3. The CO2-charged brine is denser than formation brine and sinks. No free-phase plume forms, so no perfect caprock is needed.
4. Limit design loading to about 70-80% of saturation at the dissolution point, so no free gas can exsolve downstream where pressure only rises.
5. Use only deep disposal zones with verified containment (not over-pressured shallow zones).
target: The 5-15 Mt/yr of processing-plant CO2 in the Permian and other shale basins, plus any basin where disposal water and concentrated CO2 are co-located.
quantitative_claims:
All figures are my calculations from the same script.

CO2 solubility (Spycher 2003 equilibrium constant, PR fugacity, Sechenov salting-out 0.10-0.12 kg/mol):
- Check against pure water: 1.17 mol/kg at 25C and 50 bar (literature about 1.25); 1.10 at 50C and 100 bar (literature about 1.05-1.1).
- In 1.5-4 molal NaCl brines: 12-26 kg CO2 per t water at 30C and 35 bar; 14-31 at 40C and 60 bar; 17-36 at 45C and 100 bar.
- Design loading is therefore 10-25 kg/m3, depending on salinity and dissolution depth: 40-100 t of carrier water per t CO2 (Carbfix uses about 25 t/t).
- Added volume from dissolved CO2 is only about 0.8 m3 per t, so disposal pressure is essentially unchanged.

Scale and source match:
- Permian disposal of 12-20 MMbbl/d (assumed; industry estimates put total Permian produced water above 20 MMbbl/d, not re-verified) is 0.70-1.16 km3/yr. That supports 7-29 Mt CO2/yr.
- That matches the basin's gas-processing CO2 of 8-16 Mt/yr (my estimate: 27 Bcf/d raw gas at an assumed 1.5-3% CO2; part already goes to EOR or acid-gas injection).

Energy:
- Compression floor 0.20 GJ/t to 35 bar and 0.26 to 100 bar, against 0.28 for supercritical injection at 150 bar. Separation is about 0 for AGRU off-gas.
- Scale check: 25 Mt/yr at 0.25 GJ/t is 6 PJ/yr (0.001% of world primary energy).

Cost claim: below $35/t (compression about $10-15/t, plus dip-tube, corrosion-resistant tubing and monitoring retrofits), against 45Q $85/t. This is an assumption to test.
who_gains:
S3 Permian operators and gas processors (Oxy, Exxon, Chevron, and water midstream such as Aris and WaterBridge): 45Q income on CO2 they now vent, using wells and water they already handle.
S6 Permian workers.
S7: no new water use in an arid basin.
S1/S2: storage without EOR, no added oil, and a non-buoyant storage form.
S11: CO2 vents near gas plants are eliminated.
who_loses:
S11 if containment fails. Texas regulators have curtailed deep disposal in seismic response areas, and shallow disposal zones have over-pressured, with brine breakouts at the surface. CO2-charged brine reaching the surface would degas (a CO2 hazard), so only proven-containment deep zones qualify.
SWD operators bear corrosion and retrofit cost.
Regulatory risk: Class II wells would need Class VI permitting or an equivalent ruling to earn 45Q.
closest_known_work:
- Carbfix (Iceland): in-well dissolution into basalt, measured more than 95% mineralised within 2 years (Matter et al. 2016).
- Burton & Bryant (2009, SPE): surface dissolution of CO2 into extracted aquifer brine, with a cost assessment.
- 'Dissolved-water CO2 injection' studies (Energy & Fuels, about 2024-25).
- Permian acid-gas injection (AGI) wells: free-phase, not dissolved.
- A Crossref search found no deployment that dissolves CO2 into oilfield disposal water.
why_different: Carbfix's binding constraint is water: about 25 t per t, or 25 km3/yr per Gt. This idea uses water that is already being lifted, treated and pumped underground for disposal, in wells that already exist, next to concentrated CO2 that is already separated and vented. The carrier water's marginal cost is zero, and the storage form is dissolved and sinking rather than a buoyant plume.
cheapest_falsifying_test:
1. Desk study (about 1 month): pull Texas RRC disposal-well volumes and injection pressures, plus produced-water chemistry from the USGS Produced Waters Database. Compute well by well the deliverable dissolved CO2 at 80% saturation with PHREEQC or the script above.
   - Kill criterion: fewer than 3 Mt/yr of CO2 can be carried by deep wells that have verified containment and lie outside seismic response areas.
2. Bench test (about 2 months): corrosion coupons in CO2-saturated Permian brine.
   - Kill criterion: the retrofit cost per well exceeds about $5/t over 10 years.

title: Measure-first buy-and-plug of high-emitting low-production wells ('cash for clunkers' for stripper wells)
one_line: Majors use their service crews and cash flow to buy out and plug the worst-emitting low-production US well sites. Sites are picked by measured emissions, with acquisition priced per tonne of CO2e avoided, and the forgone production is replaced with low-intensity supply.
conventional_core: Well plugging and abandonment by oilfield service crews, the same workforce used by the IIJA orphan-well programme.
graft: Vehicle-scrappage ('cash for clunkers') design: a voluntary, measurement-gated buy-out that retires the dirtiest units first. This reverses the observed pattern of majors selling aging wells to small operators.
mechanism:
1. Screen low-production sites (15 boe/d or less) by mobile or aerial survey at about 1 kg/h detection.
2. Re-measure to confirm the emissions are persistent, not a one-off malfunction. If a cheap repair (a hatch, a controller) fixes the site, repair it instead.
3. For persistent high emitters, offer the operator the present value of remaining cash flow, plus plug and reclamation.
4. Finance with measured-baseline methane credits, methane-intensity premia in the major's gas offtakes, and residual state or federal plugging funds.
5. Release payment only after post-plug verification.
target: US onshore methane from about 565,000 low-production well sites. These emit about 4 Tg CH4/yr (95% CI 3-6), 50% more than the whole Permian Basin, from 5.6% of US oil and gas output (Omara et al. 2022, measurement-integrated estimate).
quantitative_claims:
Context (Omara 2022): 565,000 sites, average 0.8 kg/h (7.1 t CH4/yr) per site, a loss rate above 10%, and average output of about 2.9 boe/d (my calculation).

Cost per tonne avoided (my calculation, GWP100 29.8; plug plus buy-out $75-200k assumed):
- Site at 0.8 kg/h: $18-96/t CO2e.
- Site at 2 kg/h, 10-20 years of avoided emissions: $7-38/t.
- Site at 5 kg/h: $3-15/t.
- On GWP20 the figures fall to about one-third.

Programme scale, IF the top 10% of sites emit 50% (an assumption to test):
- 56,500 sites at about $150k each = $8.5bn.
- Avoids about 2 Tg CH4/yr = 60 Mt CO2e/yr (GWP100). That is about $9/t over 15 years, roughly the scale of all US operating CCS.

Energy: net positive, since plugging uses negligible rig diesel against 7-35 t CH4/yr avoided per site.

Compared with removing methane from air: verifier fan work alone is about 263 GJ/t CH4.
who_gains:
S1/S2: the methane cuts with the highest certainty.
S11 rural communities: VOC and benzene air-quality gains.
S6 service crews: plugging work during shale downturns.
S3 majors: credible methane-intensity claims and no 'transferred emissions' criticism.
S7: helps with the EU import methane MRV narrative.
Stripper operators sell voluntarily at fair value.
who_loses:
Royalty owners of plugged wells (small income loss).
States (small severance-tax loss).
The stripper-well industry lobby, as its segment shrinks.
If high emitters turn out to be intermittent malfunctions, buyers overpay compared with simple repair.
closest_known_work:
- Omara et al. 2022 (Nature Communications): diagnosis of the problem.
- IIJA orphan-well plugging ($4.7bn).
- IRA Methane Emissions Reduction Program marginal-well grants. OBBBA rescinded the remaining MERP funds (map).
- ACR orphan-well plugging carbon-credit methodology; Well Done Foundation.
- EDF/Ceres work on emissions transferred through oil and gas asset sales.
why_different: Existing programmes plug orphaned (already abandoned) wells with public money, and their per-well emissions are about 10x lower than producing marginal sites (Omara). This idea targets producing high emitters, selected by measurement and priced per tonne. It uses private incumbent capital and crews and makes the cheap tail of the heavy-tailed distribution investable.
cheapest_falsifying_test:
1. Partner with one Appalachian or Oklahoma stripper operator, or a state agency, and run truck-based surveys of about 300 low-production sites, with each site re-measured three times over 3 months (about $50-100k).
2. Kill criteria:
   - The top 10% of sites carry less than 35% of emissions; or
   - more than half of the high emitters are fixed by repairs costing under $10k. In that case run a repair programme, not plugging.

title: Store the reservoir CO2 that existing LNG trains already strip and vent (the simple baseline)
one_line: Every LNG train must strip reservoir CO2 to meet spec, and most vent it. Dehydrate, compress and inject it, Sleipner-style, and sell the cargo with a measured-CI premium that costs a few cents per MMBtu. This is the cheap-tonnes baseline that every fancier idea must beat.
conventional_core: Acid-gas removal plus CO2 injection at gas processing and LNG plants (Sleipner since 1996, Snohvit, Gorgon, Qatar's Ras Laffan CCS, Santos' Moomba CCS).
graft: Product carbon-intensity differentiation from green steel and CBAM-style accounting: a per-cargo, physically measured lifecycle CI, replacing offset-based 'carbon-neutral LNG' cargoes.
mechanism:
1. Inventory every liquefaction train by feed-gas CO2 content and distance to injectable storage, often the producing field itself or a depleted neighbour.
2. Retrofit dehydration, compression and injection for the AGRU stream.
3. Certify cargo CI with measured methane (OGMP 2.0 Level 5) plus metered stored CO2.
4. Contract a CI-indexed premium with Asian or EU buyers so the buyer, not a subsidy, pays for it.
target: Reservoir CO2 vented at global liquefaction and gas processing: the cheapest concentrated tonnes.
quantitative_claims:
All figures are my calculations from the same script.

Per tonne of LNG by feed CO2 content:
- 2%: 56 kg CO2/t; 4%: 114; 6%: 175; 10%: 305; 14% (Gorgon-like): 447.
- On roughly 411 Mt/yr of LNG (IGU, 2024 trade, quoted from memory), average feed CO2 of 2-10% gives 23-125 Mt/yr. A few Mt/yr is already stored.

Premium per MMBtu:
- At $25-45/t, $0.03-0.39/MMBtu, i.e. 0.3-3.5% of an $11 LNG price.
- Even at Gorgon's realised cost of about $200/t (a press figure via IEEFA), a 4% feed costs about $0.44/MMBtu.
- Lifecycle CI falls 2-13% (against about 3.4 t CO2e per t LNG well-to-combustion, assumed).

Energy: separation about 0 (already done for spec); compression floor 0.28 GJ/t (1 to 150 bar). Scale check: 50 Mt/yr at 0.4 GJ/t is 20 PJ/yr (0.003% of world primary energy).
who_gains:
S3 LNG sellers and NOCs (QatarEnergy, Woodside, Petronas, Shell, Chevron): differentiated product and market access.
S7 importers (Japan, Korea, EU): verifiable Scope 3 cuts.
S9: about 1% price impact.
S6 and S8 producer-country jobs.
S1/S2: physical abatement replaces offsets.
who_loses:
Offset sellers.
High-CO2-field projects that cannot reach storage (they would face a discount).
S1 hard-liners, who see it as greening LNG expansion.
Risk to S10: storage execution, since Gorgon injected only 25% of reservoir CO2 in FY2024-25 against an 80% condition. That failure mechanism still applies.
closest_known_work: Sleipner, Snohvit, Gorgon, Qatar LNG CCS, Santos Moomba (reported start-up 2024), Petronas Kasawari (in development), and offset-based 'carbon-neutral LNG' cargoes (from about 2019). The idea is known; the map flags the global inventory as not yet computed.
why_different: Little novelty, deliberately. It is the simple baseline the OptiLex evidence says to keep. The added pieces are a global per-train ranking (feed CO2 against storage distance) and a buyer-paid CI premium sized to cents per MMBtu instead of a state subsidy.
cheapest_falsifying_test:
1. Desk study (about 1 month): compile feed-gas CO2 and injection options for the roughly 25 largest liquefaction plants from operator reports and environmental approvals.
   - Kill criterion: the vented total is under 15 Mt/yr, or the median train lacks storage within 100 km.
2. In parallel, run a buyer survey or RFQ with 3-5 Asian utilities.
   - Kill criterion: no willingness to pay $0.10/MMBtu for metered, stored-CO2 cargoes.

title: Per-tonne throughput royalty for CO2-pipeline landowners (the oil-and-gas royalty model applied to CCS pipelines)
one_line: Replace one-time easements backed by eminent domain with a recurring per-tonne royalty paid to every landowner a CO2 pipeline crosses, as oil wells and wind turbines already pay. This aims to unlock fermentation CCS (separation work about 0), which is blocked by landowner politics, not physics.
conventional_core: CO2 pipelines from ethanol plants to Class VI storage (Summit-type networks), with 45Q at $85/t.
graft: The mineral-royalty and wind-lease model: recurring, production-linked payments that kept landowners aligned with oil and gas in Texas and with wind farms in Iowa.
mechanism:
1. The pipeline operator pays each crossed landowner $1-3 per tonne transported, prorated by the length on their land, for the life of the line.
2. The royalty is recorded as a property-attached interest, so it is bankable and transferable with the land.
3. Easements become voluntary; no eminent domain is used.
4. Oil-major land departments, who manage royalty accounting today, administer it.
target: The roughly 43-46 Mt/yr US fermentation CO2 pool (map). The South Dakota eminent-domain ban of March 2025 stalled Summit's network (about 2,500 miles, 57 ethanol plants, up to about 18 Mt/yr; figures from memory).
quantitative_claims:
All figures are my calculations from the same script.

Cost to the operator:
- $1-3/t on 18 Mt/yr is $18-54M/yr, or $7,200-21,600 per pipeline mile per year.
- That is $1,190-3,560 per easement acre per year (50 ft permanent easement assumed), while the land stays farmed. Iowa cropland cash rent is about $250/acre/yr (assumed, ISU survey order of magnitude).
- It is 1.2-3.5% of 45Q's $85/t. For the full US ethanol pool at $2/t: $90M/yr, against $3.8bn/yr of 45Q value.

Energy: separation floor about 0; compression floor 0.28 GJ/t (1 to 150 bar).

Acceptance claim: voluntary easement acceptance rises enough to route around holdouts without eminent domain. This is an assumption to test.
who_gains:
S11 landowners: a durable income stream.
S4 ethanol producers and S9/S6 Midwest farm economies: access to low-carbon-fuel markets.
S3: pipeline and storage operators get a buildable network.
S7: state politics de-escalate.
S2: cheapest-physics removals (biogenic CO2) get built.
who_loses:
Pipeline equity (1-3.5% of credit revenue).
Anti-pipeline coalitions lose their strongest argument (eminent domain), although safety concerns remain unaddressed (Satartia 2020 rupture).
Parts of S1, who oppose propping up corn ethanol.
Non-crossed neighbours, who bear perceived risk without payment. That is a fairness gap and may require a county-level share.
closest_known_work:
- Oil and gas mineral royalties.
- Wind-turbine land leases (recurring per-turbine payments).
- Per-tonne pore-space lease payments for CO2 storage.
- Summit and Navigator's lump-sum easements; Navigator Heartland Greenway was cancelled in 2023.
- Recurring payments for linear infrastructure are uncommon in the US; I did not verify specific transmission-line examples.
why_different: The rest of this map treats CCS pipelines as an engineering and permitting problem. This idea treats the measured binding constraint, landowner property-rights politics, with the incentive design that made the US oil patch and Iowa wind politically durable. It costs about 2% of the subsidy.
cheapest_falsifying_test:
Run a discrete-choice (conjoint) survey of about 400 landowners on proposed CO2-pipeline routes in Iowa and South Dakota (about $30-50k, 2 months). Compare a lump-sum easement with a recurring royalty of equal present value, and with royalties of $1, $2 and $3/t.

Kill criterion: the recurring royalty raises the stated voluntary-signing probability by less than 10 percentage points over an equal-PV lump sum. That would mean safety or ideology, not money, is binding, and the idea should be dropped.

title: Default-factor rule for HFC-23 in fluoropolymer product footprints (sibling: N2O in nylon-66)
one_line: Buyers of PTFE and other fluoropolymers would charge every unverified supplier the unabated IPCC Tier-1 HFC-23 factor in their Scope 3 product footprints. Unabated HFC-23 alone makes PTFE about 380-1,120 t CO2e per tonne, so suppliers would rush to prove destruction, which costs about $0.4/t CO2e.
conventional_core: HFC-23 by-product destruction by thermal oxidation. It has been TRL 9 since the CDM era and is already a legal obligation under Kigali Article 2J.
graft: CBAM's default-value rule (if you cannot prove it, you pay a punitive default), moved into private product-carbon-footprint data exchanges such as Catena-X (autos), TfS (chemicals), SEMI (semiconductors) and outdoor apparel (ePTFE). Verification would use plant CEMS and destruction logs, cross-checked against regional atmospheric inversions.
mechanism: PTFE is made via 2 CHClF2 -> C2F4 + 2 HCl. HCFC-22 feedstock production has no Montreal Protocol cap, and making it co-produces HFC-23 (GWP100 14,600). Product footprints rarely reveal whether that by-product was destroyed. If an unverified supplier must be booked at the unabated default, the footprint penalty (hundreds of t CO2e per t of product) is far larger than the destruction cost, so verified destruction becomes a condition of market access. No credits are issued, which avoids the CDM failure where credit revenue exceeded product revenue and encouraged extra output. The same rule applies to adipic-acid N2O embodied in PA66.
target: Measured 2023 HFC-23 emissions are 14.0 Gg, about 5x reported (map, CEE 2024). Chinese adipic-acid N2O is the map's 'cheapest large tonnes' open problem. Both are MRV/compliance bottlenecks, not technology bottlenecks.
quantitative_claims:
All figures executed in climate/runs/2026-10-05/scripts/anti_availability_ideas.py.
(1) Stoichiometry: 1.73 t HCFC-22 per t TFE at 100% yield, 1.92 t at 90%. At HFC-23 generation of 1.5-4% (assumed IPCC-style range) that gives 26-77 kg HFC-23, or 380-1,120 t CO2e per t PTFE.
(2) Destruction cost: an assumed CDM-style incinerator ($10M capex, 10%/10 yr, $0.5M/yr opex, 350 t/yr) works out to about $6/kg HFC-23, or $0.42/t CO2e. That is $170-470 per t PTFE, about 1-6% of an assumed $8-15k/t price.
(3) Gap: 14.0 Gg measured minus about 2.8 Gg reported leaves 11.2 Gg, or 163 Mt CO2e/yr. That equals the unabated HFC-23 from about 145-430 kt/yr of PTFE-equivalent. Destroying it costs about $34-136M/yr.
(4) N2O sibling: 0.301 t N2O per t adipic acid (stoichiometric; IPCC 0.300), and 0.646 t adipic acid per t PA66, gives 53 t CO2e per t PA66 unabated. That is 6.6-8.2x an assumed 6.5-8 t/t abated footprint. Abating 95% at $0.25-4/t (NRDC 2026) costs $13-202 per t PA66. China's adipic N2O is about 78 Mt CO2e (AR6).
(5) Combined: about 240 Mt CO2e/yr for about $53-440M/yr ($0.2-1.8/t), against about $97bn/yr for the same tonnage by DAC at $400/t.
The 14.0 Gg figure is a measured atmospheric inversion. All cost figures are modelled.
who_gains: Producers that already destroy HFC-23 or abate N2O (S4, including compliant Chinese plants) gain share and a premium. Downstream buyers (autos, semiconductors, apparel) get Scope 3 cuts for under 1% of input cost. S1 and S2 get about 0.24 Gt CO2e/yr of near-free cuts. S7 China already published an industrial-N2O Action Plan in Aug 2025 (per NRDC 2026), so the rule fits its policy direction. S9 sees negligible price effects.
who_loses: HCFC-22, PTFE and adipic producers that vent pay small costs and risk losing export buyers (S4 subset). S7 China may resist inversion-based attribution as a sovereignty issue. PFAS critics within S1 may object to anything that makes fluoropolymers look 'green'. Footprint consultancies whose datasets omit by-product gases lose credibility.
closest_known_work: NRDC, July 2026, 'Toward near-zero industrial N2O' (read this run). It already proposes automaker clean procurement of nylon, citing about 1 t CO2e of embodied N2O per vehicle and about $5 per vehicle to abate. It also proposes extending CBAM to N2O, and modelling a Montreal Protocol N2O control on HFC-23. ClimeCo is running three Chinese adipic projects with a 90% baseline. Other precedents: the CDM HFC-23 and adipic projects and their gaming; Kigali Art. 2J; the EU ETS, which covers adipic and nitric N2O; and CBAM default values. Prior-art search on HFC-23-specific product footprints was not completed (search budget exhausted).
why_different: NRDC proposes voluntary 'clean procurement' for N2O. This idea adds a binding default factor inside the PCF data standards themselves, and inversion cross-checks. It also extends the rule to HFC-23 in fluoropolymers. There the default multiplier (about 380-1,120 t CO2e per t product) is roughly 10-20x the N2O case per tonne of product, and the measured-versus-reported gap (163 Mt CO2e) is documented.
cheapest_falsifying_test: Two desk checks, 2-6 weeks. (a) Audit 10-15 published PCFs, EPDs and eco-profiles for PTFE, PFA, FEP and PA66, plus the ecoinvent datasets. If they already book HFC-23 and N2O at unabated defaults unless destruction is verified, the lever already exists and the idea is moot. (b) Overlay the published HFC-23 inversion hotspots (eastern China, about 40%) on the locations of HCFC-22 plants serving feedstock versus emissive uses. If the excess does not co-locate with fluoropolymer-feedstock plants, a buyer lever on fluoropolymers targets the wrong product.

title: CO2 as the voidage-replacement fluid in Smackover lithium and bromine brine fields
one_line: Lithium and bromine producers in the Smackover pump out tens of Mm3 of brine a year. Filling part of that pore space with CO2 instead of reinjected spent brine earns $44-51 of 45Q credit per m3, as much as or more than the lithium in most cases ($7-53/m3). It also avoids the pressure build-up that made Gorgon underperform.
conventional_core: Smackover brine production with spent-brine reinjection for pressure support. Arkansas has done this for bromine for decades (Wikipedia, 2015: the only US commercial bromine source). Direct lithium extraction (DLE) projects are being added: the SWA project targets 22,500 t LCE/yr and was designated a Priority Critical Mineral Project in Apr 2025.
graft: Pressure maintenance by gas injection, imported from oilfield practice and from LLNL's 'active reservoir management' concept, run in reverse: the brine is produced for its minerals, and CO2 is the replacement fluid.
mechanism: Each m3 of brine withdrawn creates pore volume that can take about 0.52-0.57 t of supercritical CO2 at Smackover conditions. Injecting CO2 into that volume in place of spent brine keeps the pressure balanced. That removes the binding storage constraint the map identifies (Gorgon was pressure-limited to 25% of its target). The field is already characterised and drilled, with operators and ammonia CO2 nearby (El Dorado, from memory). The spent brine then goes to a separate saline disposal zone, or carries dissolved CO2 itself in a smaller, safer variant.
target: Map bottleneck: subsurface pressure management and produced-water handling (Gorgon at 1.33 of 5.22 Mt), and the storage-side open problem of co-optimising brine production with injection. It also gives near-zero-separation CO2 from Gulf Coast ammonia, ethanol and gas processing a home without new pressure build-up.
quantitative_claims:
Executed in climate/runs/2026-10-05/scripts/anti_availability_ideas.py.
(1) CO2 density from the Peng-Robinson EOS (reads about 3% low against NIST at check points) at assumed 25-33 MPa and 110-135 C: 524-568 kg/m3. So 0.52-0.57 t CO2 per m3 of voidage. My initial guess of 0.7 was wrong.
(2) 45Q at $85/t is worth $44-51 per m3 of voidage. Lithium at 200-582 mg/L (582 is the 2025 Lafayette County average), 85% recovery and an assumed $8-20/kg LCE is worth $7-53 per m3.
(3) An SWA-size project (22,500 t LCE/yr) at 400-582 mg/L produces 8.5-12.4 Mm3/yr of brine. Its voidage equals 4.5-7.1 Mt CO2/yr if fully replaced by CO2, about 7-11% of all CCS operating worldwide today (64 Mtpa).
(4) Disposing spent brine elsewhere at an assumed $3-15/m3 costs $5-29 per t CO2.
(5) Ideal isothermal compression floor from 1 to 300 bar: 0.32 GJ/t. Separation work for ammonia or fermentation CO2 is about 0.
(6) Dissolved variant (CO2 dissolved in the reinjected spent brine at an assumed 0.4-0.8 mol/kg): 0.21-0.42 Mt/yr per 10 Mm3/yr of reinjection. That is smaller, but adds no free-phase plume and no new pressure.
who_gains: S3: Gulf Coast majors already hold Smackover lithium positions and storage businesses (Exxon; Equinor with Standard Lithium; from memory). S4: ammonia and chemical emitters in south Arkansas and Texas get a storage outlet without a long pipeline. S7: critical minerals plus 45Q, with bipartisan appeal. S6: oilfield and brine-industry workers in a high-carbon region. S11 faces lower induced-seismicity and pressure risk than pure injection, because the reservoir stays pressure-balanced.
who_loses: Lithium and bromine operators carry risk if CO2 or acidified brine reaches their producers (scaling, sorbent damage, lower Br/Li grade), so injection and production must be spatially segregated. Operators of the brine-disposal formation absorb the pressure that moves there. S1 is split: this is not EOR, but it stores fossil-derived CO2. It is also a lithium-mining expansion that some S11 groups contest.
closest_known_work: LLNL Active CO2 Reservoir Management (Buscheck et al., about 2011-2016): extract brine to manage pressure and use it for desalination or cooling. Gorgon's produced-water pressure management is a realised precedent, and a troubled one. Oilfield gas injection for pressure maintenance. Smackover DLE projects (SWA, verified via Wikipedia; Exxon from memory). Not checked: whether any published study already co-optimises Smackover lithium with CO2 voidage replacement (search budget exhausted). Treat this as an open prior-art risk.
why_different: ARM treats extracted brine as a waste or water resource. Here the brine is already being produced and paid for by mineral recovery, the wells and reservoir data already exist, and the comparison per m3 shows the pore space is worth as much as or more than the lithium. That reverses which product is the by-product in most price and grade cases.
cheapest_falsifying_test: (a) A 2-4 week bench test: run a commercial-type DLE sorbent (Li-Al layered double hydroxide or ion exchange) on synthetic Smackover brine equilibrated with CO2 at reservoir pCO2. If lithium capacity drops by more than 30% or the sorbent degrades, co-mingling is ruled out and only segregated layouts remain. (b) A 1-2 month open-source simulation (OPM Flow CO2STORE or MRST co2lab) of a Smackover sector with lithium producers and CO2 injectors. If CO2 breaks through within a 20-30 year project life at well spacings that keep lithium output within 10% of plan, the simple scheme fails.

title: Silted hydropower reservoirs as the clay mine for LC3 calcined-clay cement
one_line: The fine, often kaolinitic sediment that is filling reservoirs near dam intakes could be dredged, calcined in cement kilns and sold as clinker substitute. The scheme could pay for the dredging and avoid about 1 t CO2 per t of calcined clay.
conventional_core: Limestone calcined clay cement (LC3-50). Map: 14 calcination plants with 3.45 Mt/yr capacity in 2023, enabling under 1% of global cement; the map calls it the largest near-zero-cost cement lever.
graft: Reservoir sediment management (dredging and flushing near intakes, a standard hydropower operation) recast as a clay-mining operation feeding cement plants.
mechanism: Turbidity currents carry the finest clays to the deepest zone near the dam, where operators already have to dredge or flush to protect intakes. Tropical catchments weather to kaolinite-rich laterites. Calcined at about 800 C, kaolinitic clay replaces clinker. Kilns can dry the sediment with waste heat. Dam owners (S5) recover storage and avoid sediment costs. Cement makers (S4) get supplementary cementitious material as fly ash and slag supply falls with coal and blast-furnace closures, which is a map open problem.
target: Map open problem: SCM supply as fly ash and slag decline, and mapping clay deposits against cement plants. The second bottleneck is reservoir sedimentation, which costs dams about 0.5-1% of storage a year (assumed typical range).
quantitative_claims:
Executed in climate/runs/2026-10-05/scripts/anti_availability_ideas.py.
(1) Clinker process CO2 by stoichiometry: 0.51 t/t at an assumed 65% CaO. Adding assumed fuel at 3.4 GJ/t and 0.095 t/GJ gives 0.83 t/t clinker.
(2) LC3-50 (50% clinker, 30% calcined clay, 15% limestone) emits 0.49-0.50 t/t cement against 0.79 for OPC. That saves 0.29-0.30 t/t cement, or 0.96-1.01 t CO2 per t of calcined clay, counting the limestone the clay enables.
(3) Drying penalty at 30-50% moisture: 1.1-2.6 GJ/t dry, which is 0.11-0.25 t CO2/t if fuel-fired and about 0 with kiln or cooler waste heat. Hauling 100-300 km by truck adds 10-30 kg CO2/t.
(4) A 1 km3 reservoir losing 0.5-1%/yr traps 6-12 Mt/yr. One 1 Mt/yr LC3 plant needs only about 0.33 Mt/yr of dry clay.
(5) Economics (assumed values): net SCM value of $30-45/t is worth $33-50 per m3 removed, against dredging at $5-10/m3. Sediment removal could pay for itself if the kaolinite content is adequate.
(6) Scale: 0.3 Gt/yr of calcined clay (about 25% of cement as LC3) avoids about 0.3 Gt CO2/yr. Full adoption could reach about 0.9 Gt/yr (map's upper bound).
who_gains: S5: hydropower owners regain storage and protect intakes, turning a cost centre into revenue. S4: cement makers secure SCM and lower costs while keeping their kilns. S8: tropical, kaolinitic regions such as India, Brazil, Ghana and Cameroon, where LC3 leaders already are. S11: dam-safety and flood-capacity benefits. S6: dredging and quarry jobs. S9: neutral to lower cement prices.
who_loses: Delta and floodplain communities (S11/S8) are harmed if sediment that would otherwise be flushed downstream is removed from the river system for good, which worsens delta starvation (for example the Mekong). This needs a sediment-budget rule. Fly-ash and slag marketers lose some share. Clinker volume falls, though the same S4 firms make LC3.
closest_known_work: The LC3 programme (EPFL/Scrivener; Cuba, India; map). Lab studies of calcined dam and harbour sediments as pozzolans (Algerian dam sediments; French dredged harbour sediments, Dunkirk), from memory and not re-verified because the search budget was exhausted. Reservoir sediment management practice (dredging and flushing; Kondolf et al. 2014, from memory). I know of no deployment that pairs dam desilting with LC3 supply, but the prior-art search was incomplete.
why_different: Earlier work tests sediments as a disposal problem one sample at a time. This idea treats the dam operator as a clay supplier. It targets the fine-sediment zone near intakes, where removal is already an operating need, and screens tropical kaolinitic reservoirs against nearby cement plants. That turns two separate bottlenecks into one market.
cheapest_falsifying_test: Core fine sediment near the intakes of about 10 reservoirs, tropical and temperate. Measure kaolinite by TGA (dehydroxylation mass loss at 450-600 C), calcine at 800 C, and run the ASTM C1897 R3 reactivity test. Cost is about $100-300 per sample, over a few weeks. If most samples show under about 20% kaolinite or R3 reactivity below what LC3-50 strength parity needs, the idea shrinks to a minor blend component.

title: In-storage slurry acidification paid per tonne of methane, targeted by IPCC methane-conversion factor to warm, long-storage systems
one_line: Danish farms already acidify slurry to cut ammonia. Paying for the methane it also avoids, and deploying only where stored slurry emits a lot of methane (warm climates, long storage), cuts manure methane for about $3-28/t CO2e in acid cost. My own check shows that seasonal-only dosing does not help.
conventional_core: Slurry acidification with sulfuric acid to pH 5.5-6, in-house or in-storage. It is TRL 9 in Denmark, where ammonia rules drove adoption, with a large minority of slurry treated (from memory).
graft: A results-based methane methodology in the style of landfill-gas methodologies, with payment keyed to the IPCC Tier-2 methane conversion factor (MCF) by climate zone and storage time, and verified by logged pH. This steers deployment to systems where each m3 of slurry would emit at least about 3 kg CH4.
mechanism: Holding stored slurry below about pH 6 inhibits methanogens and shifts ammonium away from NH3 volatilisation. The acid dose is set by buffer capacity, roughly per m3. The methane avoided per m3 scales with MCF, which runs about 10-80% from cool to warm climates. Cost per tonne CO2e therefore falls about 6x from cool to warm systems. Revenue should follow MCF, not volume.
target: Liquid manure methane, a lesser-discussed slice of agricultural methane (the map covers enteric 3-NOP at $44-117/t). It applies the map's lesson that abatement with no revenue stream needs a payment designed against gaming.
quantitative_claims:
Executed in climate/runs/2026-10-05/scripts/anti_availability_ideas.py.
(1) Acid-only cost assumes a 70% CH4 cut, 2-8 kg H2SO4 per m3 and acid at $80-200/t. It is $2.8-28/t CO2e for slurry emitting 3 kg CH4/m3, and $17-169/t for slurry emitting 0.5 kg CH4/m3 (GWP100 biogenic 27).
(2) Negative result: with Danish slurry temperatures and emptying pattern (assumed), May-October accounts for 67-82% of annual CH4 for an Arrhenius activation energy of 63-112 kJ/mol. Dosing only in those months still needs about 68% of the acid, so it avoids only 0.98-1.20x the CH4 per kg of acid. Seasonal dosing is not a lever.
(3) Sulfur load at 40 m3/ha: 26 kg S/ha at 2 kg acid/m3, 105 kg S/ha at 8 kg/m3, against an assumed crop need of 15-40 kg/ha. Doses must therefore be capped at about 3 kg/m3, or the scheme targeted at sulfur-deficient soils.
(4) Scale: liquid-system manure CH4 of about 4.5-7 Mt/yr (assumed 50-70% of an assumed 9-10 Mt total) gives 85-132 Mt CO2e/yr at a 70% cut.
The 60-90% CH4 reductions in storage trials are from memory, not re-verified.
who_gains: S11 gains from less ammonia (a PM2.5 precursor), odour and nitrogen deposition. That offers Dutch and Danish farms a compliance route other than herd buyouts (hypothesis). S1 and S2 get methane cuts. S3 and S4 refiners and acid producers gain a small new outlet for by-product sulfur. S7 gets help with methane-pledge and nitrogen-crisis targets. Farmers are not a listed group; the closest are S6 and S11.
who_loses: Digester and RNG developers whose economics depend on raw slurry, such as those earning California LCFS dairy credits, because acidifying before digestion cuts biogas yield. Farm workers face acid-handling and H2S risks during mixing, which need engineering controls. S1 groups opposed to intensive livestock may see it as entrenching the practice. Farmers lose if the methane payment falls below cost in cool climates.
closest_known_work: Danish commercial in-house, in-storage and in-field acidification. Storage studies report large CH4 reductions (e.g. Petersen et al. 2012, J Environ Qual; Fangueiro et al. 2015 review, both from memory). IPCC 2019 Tier-2 MCF tables. Verra and CDM manure methodologies are aimed at digesters and covers, not acidification (from memory, unverified).
why_different: Acidification is deployed today for ammonia in a cool climate where the methane benefit per m3 is smallest. This idea relocates and pays for it on methane where MCF is high. The executed check removes an attractive but wrong design, seasonal dosing, before anyone pilots it.
cheapest_falsifying_test: A 3-6 month replicated pilot with 1-10 m3 tanks at a warm-climate dairy, testing three pH targets with dynamic-chamber CH4 measurement and logged acid use. A reanalysis of published storage trials could run in parallel. If the CH4 cut falls below 40% at pH 6 by month 3 (pH rebound), or if holding pH at or below 6 in flushed-lagoon effluent takes more than 6 kg acid per m3, cost exceeds about $30/t CO2e and the targeting case fails.

title: Capture methane at the hydropower tailrace and oxidise it in a coal-mine ventilation-air oxidiser
one_line: Turbines already depressurise methane-rich deep reservoir water, which then releases its methane just downstream. Enclosing that degassing zone and sending the headspace at about 0.5% CH4 to a regenerative thermal oxidiser (RTO) of the kind used on coal-mine ventilation air could destroy it for about EUR 7-8/t CO2e (RTO only), with no pumping and no need for fuel-grade gas.
conventional_core: An existing hydropower plant, its draft tube and its tailrace.
graft: Regenerative thermal oxidisers for ventilation air methane, TRL 8-9 at coal mines (map). They run autothermally above about 0.11-0.18% CH4.
mechanism: Tropical stratified reservoirs build up dissolved CH4 in the anoxic deep water that intakes draw from. When that water leaves the turbine at atmospheric pressure it is strongly supersaturated, and a large share degasses immediately downstream. A ventilated hood over the draft-tube outlet or stilling basin can collect the released gas. Ventilation dilutes the headspace to about 0.5% CH4, well below the 5% lower explosive limit and above the autothermal threshold, and the RTO oxidises it. Earlier proposals pumped deep water to recover fuel gas. This design uses only the depressurisation the turbine already provides.
target: Reservoir methane is a lesser-discussed non-CO2 source. Bottom-up estimates run from about 10-20 Tg CH4/yr (recent) to 104 Mt (older figure cited on Wikipedia). Degassing below dams is a major pathway at some tropical reservoirs; Balbina emits 39 kt CH4/yr (Kemenes & Forsberg, via Wikipedia). It also applies the map's surprise that methane must be destroyed at concentrated sources: fan work for ambient-air removal is 9.8 GJ/t CO2e.
quantitative_claims:
Executed with the OptiLex verifier in climate/runs/2026-10-05/scripts/anti_availability_ideas.py.
(1) At an assumed 0.02-0.5 mmol/L CH4 at intake depth and 1,000 m3/s, turbines pass 10-253 kt CH4/yr. Capturing 50% avoids 0.14-3.4 Mt CO2e/yr (GWP100 biogenic 27).
(2) The equilibrium headspace pCH4 is 1.5-38% (Henry's law at 28 C). The design therefore dilutes to 0.5%, which gives a 126 K adiabatic rise and is comfortably autothermal.
(3) Ventilation fan work at an assumed 4 kPa through the RTO: 2.1 GJ/t CH4, or 0.078 GJ/t CO2e. That is about 125x below ambient-air methane removal (9.8 GJ/t CO2e, verifier).
(4) RTO cost: one MATEC-design unit (EUR 9.52M capex, EUR 0.87M/yr opex, 100 m3/s) destroys about 10 kt CH4/yr at 0.5%. That is EUR 6.8-7.8/t CO2e (8-10%, 15-20 yr). The cost of the enclosure civil works is not included and is the main unknown.
(5) Generation penalty: 0.1-0.3 m of tailwater back-pressure costs 0.9-2.6 MW per 1,000 m3/s, or 0.08-0.24 GJ/t CO2e at 0.05 mmol/L and 50% capture.
who_gains: S5: hydro utilities in Brazil, Laos, West Africa and elsewhere keep the climate legitimacy of existing dams and earn methane revenue at about EUR 7-8/t plus civil works. S8: tropical countries, where most reservoir methane is. S7: national inventories and methane pledges. S2: a measurable, bounded intervention. S10: high-integrity destruction credits with a clear monitoring boundary.
who_loses: Some S1 groups opposed to dams (e.g. International Rivers) may see this as legitimising new large dams, a moral-hazard concern. Generation falls by about 0.1-0.3% of head. Downstream river ecology needs checking for changes to the oxygen and degassing regime (S11). Plant operators take on new gas-handling safety duties.
closest_known_work: Ramos et al. 2009 (Climatic Change, DOI 10.1007/s10584-008-9542-6; title confirmed via Crossref, abstract not read) and Lima et al. 2008 proposed extracting deep-water methane from tropical reservoirs as an energy source; neither was built. KivuWatt (26 MW, operating 2016, Wikipedia) extracts dissolved gas from Lake Kivu at roughly 100x the concentration. Aeration weirs below Petit Saut and Nam Theun 2 strip CH4 to the air rather than destroying it (from memory). Coal-mine VAM RTOs (map).
why_different: There is no pumping and no fuel-grade gas requirement. The design captures only the methane the turbine already liberates, at the one place it is concentrated, and uses a dilute-stream oxidiser proven at coal mines. The idea pairs a hydropower bottleneck with a coal-mine technology, which the map treats as unrelated.
cheapest_falsifying_test: Field campaigns at 2-3 tropical dams, over weeks, for about $50-100k. Measure dissolved CH4 at intake depth and at 0, 50, 200 and 1,000 m downstream, and put a floating flux hood over the draft-tube outlet. If less than 30% of the dissolved load leaves the water within the enclosable first ~100 m, or intake CH4 is below about 0.02 mmol/L, the capturable mass is under about 0.05 Mt CO2e/yr per 1,000 m3/s and the enclosure cost will not pay back.

title: Pay for compost biocovers on large open dumps only when satellites verify the cut
one_line: Large Global South dumps emitting more than 1 t CH4/h are visible to point-source satellites. Paying municipalities for compost biocovers only when satellite plume quantification confirms a cut of at least 40-50% makes about $3-15/t CO2e methane oxidation verifiable without trusting inventories. Those inventories underestimate dump emissions 5.3x.
conventional_core: Methane-oxidising compost biocovers and intermediate covers on inactive dump faces, a technology established on landfills in Europe.
graft: Satellite point-source quantification of super-emitters (the oil and gas MARS model) used as the payment trigger, with a payment rule derived from statistical power.
mechanism: Methanotrophs in a 0.6-1 m compost layer oxidise CH4 passing up through it. Big dumps are discrete, persistent, satellite-visible plumes. A results-based contract pays per verified reduction. Because per-overpass estimates are noisy, the contract pays only for large cuts at large sites, which is where power analysis shows verification is achievable. That avoids credit inflation. Payment flows to the operator, not to an inventory, so the main failure of MARS, where 88% of alerts go unanswered, does not apply.
target: Open-dump methane is underestimated 5.3x in EDGAR v8, and satellite estimates do not correlate with reported emissions (map, Nature Climate Change 2025). The binding constraints are MRV and municipal finance in S8 countries.
quantitative_claims:
Executed in climate/runs/2026-10-05/scripts/anti_availability_ideas.py.
(1) Power analysis (log-normal, alpha 0.05, power 0.8). At a combined per-overpass CV of 50-70%, verifying a 50% cut needs 8-14 quantified overpasses per period, or 19-33 attempts at an assumed 40% usable rate under tropical cloud. A 30% cut needs 28-50 (69-124 attempts). At 100% CV, 23 and 86. So only cuts of about 40-50% or more are bankable on satellite data alone.
(2) Load: 1-3 t CH4/h over 50 ha is 48-144 g CH4/m2/day, inside the range reported for compost biocover oxidation capacity (from memory; field rates vary widely).
(3) Cost (assumed 0.8 m of compost at $12/m3, 8-yr life, $0.3M/yr O&M): $2.5-15/t CO2e at 30-60% oxidation, avoiding 0.07-0.43 Mt CO2e/yr per site (GWP100 biogenic 27).
(4) Context (map, modelled): converting dumps and diverting organics is worth about 760 Mt CO2e/yr.
who_gains: S8 municipalities gain a revenue line for sanitation they already need. S11 neighbours gain from fewer dump fires, less odour and less leachate. Informal waste workers can be paid to produce compost from incoming organics, but only if that is written into the contract. S1 and S2 get verifiable methane cuts. S10 buyers get credits whose quantity is independently measured. S7 gets methane-pledge delivery.
who_loses: S7 national inventories have to be revised upward, which is politically awkward. Intermediaries in paper-based credit verification lose business. Landfill-gas-to-energy developers lose sites that are covered rather than piped. Waste pickers lose access to covered areas if they are not included.
closest_known_work: Compost biocovers and biowindows on landfills (Austrian and Danish practice; Scheutz et al. 2009 review; Danish biocover programme), from memory. Maasakkers et al. 2022 (Science Advances), satellite detection of large landfill plumes in Delhi, Lahore, Mumbai and Buenos Aires, from memory. The map's 151-site satellite survey (Nature Climate Change 2025). UNEP IMEO MARS alert-response (map). Satellite-triggered results-based payment schemes for waste were not checked (search budget exhausted).
why_different: Components exist separately. What is new is making an independent satellite measurement the payment unit, with an executed statistical rule for which site sizes and reductions can be paid. That replaces modelled first-order-decay baselines, which are wrong by about 5x for dumps.
cheapest_falsifying_test: A 1-2 month retrospective check, using public time series of satellite plume quantification (Carbon Mapper, GHGSat, TROPOMI/EMIT) for 10-20 large dumps. Compute the real per-overpass CV and the number of usable overpasses per 6 months. If CV exceeds 100% or there are fewer than about 10 usable quantifications per 6 months, satellite-only verification of a 50% cut fails within a year and ground sensors are needed, which raises cost. Separately, a 1 ha biocover pilot on an inactive face with surface flux chambers tests whether oxidation reaches 30% or more under tropical loading.

title: Carbonated disposal water: dissolve Permian gas-plant CO2 into produced water that is already being injected
one_line: Permian gas plants vent their separated CO2. Dissolve it into the produced water that saltwater-disposal (SWD) wells already inject, at up to 50% of saturation. Storage then needs no new wells, no supercritical compression and no buoyant CO2 plume, and the CO2 can earn 45Q through the existing Class II plus Subpart RR route.
conventional_core: Saltwater disposal of produced water: about 20-23 Mbbl/d is injected in the Permian through existing wells and pipelines. Amine CO2 removal at gas plants, which already happens to meet sales specification.
graft: Surface dissolution and dissolved-phase injection (Burton & Bryant 2009; the Carbfix and BRGM CO2-DISSOLVED approach), moved from purpose-drilled doublets and basalt onto the oilfield's existing produced-water stream.
mechanism: Gas-plant CO2 (separation floor about 0.004 GJ/t) is compressed only to about 30-60 bar and mixed into produced water at SWD hubs. The loading is capped at 50% of saturation at the lowest far-field pressure, so the CO2 never forms a free phase. CO2-laden brine is denser than formation brine, so the plume sinks. The injection volume barely changes (+1.1-1.3%), so the brine adds no new pressure or seismic load. The same 'ride an existing reinjection loop' approach also works for geothermal doublets and DLE lithium plants, but at much smaller scale (see claims).
target: Concentrated CO2 at Permian gas-processing plants, which is now largely vented: about 5-16 Mt/yr (my estimate). A secondary host is geothermal brine re-injection. Smackover DLE re-injection is only a marginal host.
quantitative_claims:
All figures are calculated in climate/runs/2026-10-05/scripts/sysint/idea1_brine_loops.py, which uses the OptiLex verifier plus a Henry/Peng-Robinson/Sechenov solubility model (about ±25%; it underestimates solubility above 60 C, which makes it conservative).
(1) Design loading. Permian zones: 13-18 kg CO2/m3 (saturation 0.62-0.87 mol/kg at 2-2.5 m NaCl-equivalent and 110-380 bar), which is 55-78 m3 of brine per tonne. Hypersaline Smackover brine (about 5 m): only 6-10 kg/m3, or 105-177 m3/t.
(2) Permian capacity. Produced water of 20-23 Mbbl/d (an industry-tracker figure, not verified this run) is 1.16-1.33 km3/yr. At the design loading that can carry 15-22 Mt CO2/yr, which exceeds the gas-plant CO2 supply of 4.8-16 Mt/yr (25-28 bcf/d at 1-3% CO2; gas volume and CO2 content are from memory).
(3) Energy. Compression is 0.19-0.23 GJ/t ideal (0.30-0.36 GJ_e/t real, 82-99 kWh/t), against 0.28 GJ/t ideal for conventional 150-bar injection. The separation floor is about 0.004 GJ/t. Brine pumping adds no energy, because the water is pumped anyway.
(4) Added fluid volume is 0.7-2.2% for 10-30 kg/m3, compared with 1.4-4.3% if the same CO2 were stored as free supercritical CO2.
(5) Incremental cost is $19-25/t: compressor energy about $5, capex $6-12, MRV $5 and corrosion-resistant tubing $3 (my assumptions). Against 45Q at $85/t that leaves a margin of about $60/t, roughly $0.6bn/yr at 10 Mt/yr.
(6) The DLE add-on is not a driver. With Smackover lithium at 582 mg/L (the 2025 Lafayette County, Arkansas well average), each tonne of lithium carbonate equivalent (LCE) carries only 2.0-3.4 t CO2. A 22.5 kt/yr LCE plant could store only 0.05-0.08 Mt CO2/yr, and 45Q would add about 1.4-2.4% to a $12k/t LCE price.
(7) Scale is niche: about 0.01-0.02 Gt/yr in the Permian. The ceiling across all US produced water (about 24 bn bbl/yr, from memory) is about 50-70 Mt/yr.
who_gains: S3: gas processors (for example Targa, which already has EPA-approved Subpart RR plans on Class II wells at Red Hills, Copperhead, Bull Moose and Wildcat) can monetise vented CO2, and water-midstream SWD operators earn a per-tonne fee on assets they already own. S6: Permian workforce. S7: Texas, New Mexico and the US gain a faster, lower-cost route to 45Q tonnes. S2: storage is solubility-trapped from day one, with no buoyant plume. S11: no new wells or pipeline rights-of-way. S10: little first-of-a-kind capex risk.
who_loses: S1: CAN opposes public support (45Q) for fossil-linked CCS, so this fails its red line even though it is not EOR. S11 is at risk wherever the shallow Delaware Mountain Group disposal zone is over-pressured: acidic CO2-laden brine could surface through legacy or orphan wells, where operators have reported breakouts (not re-verified here). Deep zones avoid this but face seismic-response-area limits. Dedicated acid-gas-injection well developers lose business.
closest_known_work: (a) Burton & Bryant 2009, 'Surface dissolution', Energy Procedia, doi 10.1016/j.egypro.2009.02.169, and SPE 124711 (2009): extract brine, saturate it at surface, re-inject. (b) BRGM CO2-DISSOLVED (Energy Procedia 2014, doi 10.1016/j.egypro.2014.11.488; reactive transport 2017): dissolved CO2 from small emitters in geothermal doublets. (c) A 2023 EarthArXiv global inventory of dissolved-CO2 storage in geothermal systems (doi 10.31223/x52d52). (d) Carbfix, which uses about 25 t of water per t CO2 in basalt. (e) Permian acid-gas injection into Class II wells with EPA Subpart RR approvals: Targa, DKL Libby, Frontier Maljamar, Stakeholder Gas Services (EPA Subpart RR page, checked 2026-10-05).
why_different:
Earlier dissolution concepts produce brine specifically to carry the CO2 (Burton & Bryant, CO2-DISSOLVED) or bring in water (Carbfix). Here the host is a km3-per-year waste stream that is already pumped, permitted and piped, so the main cost of dissolved-phase storage, moving 50-80 m3 of water per tonne, is already sunk. Compared with acid-gas-injection wells, it needs no new wells and no free-phase plume monitoring.
Generator note on a rejected candidate: I also tested time-sharing one capture plant between a cycling gas plant (NGCC) and a baseload industrial flue gas, using cheap off-hour power for the reboiler. My NETL-calibrated hourly model (idea2_timeshare.py) falsified it: the shared plant cost $68-103/t, against $61-91/t for two separate plants, because the industrial gas is captured only during the gas plant's off-hours (36-63%). Using the idle absorber for direct air capture fails on fan work alone: 5.9-14.7 GJ/t at 2-5 kPa (verifier).
cheapest_falsifying_test: (1) Desk GIS, about 2 weeks: Permian gas plants venting CO2 against SWD hubs and produced-water pipelines within 20 km, with zone pore pressures. (2) A PHREEQC run plus an autoclave test: synthetic Delaware brine with 15 kg/m3 CO2 at 40-60 C, measuring bubble point, calcite and barite scaling, and carbon-steel versus coated-tubing corrosion. (3) A written query to the Texas RRC and EPA Region 6 on whether co-mingled CO2 and brine in Class II SWD wells can carry a Subpart RR plan. Kill the idea if the bubble point exceeds the minimum far-field pressure in zones that are both pressure-safe and seismically unrestricted, or if Class VI permitting is required.

title: Electric lime-mud calciner at kraft pulp mills: low-cost biogenic CO2 from wood the mill already processes
one_line: Replace the fossil-fired rotary lime kiln of a kraft pulp mill with a Leilac-type indirectly heated electric calciner, run on the mill's own surplus biomass electricity. This removes the kiln's fossil fuel and releases the lime-mud CO2, which is biogenic because its carbon comes from black liquor, as an almost pure stream that needs only drying and compression for BECCS.
conventional_core: The kraft chemical-recovery loop: causticising, plus reburning lime mud (CaCO3 to CaO) in a lime kiln.
graft: Indirect, electrically heated calcination from cement and lime decarbonisation (Calix Leilac), which keeps process CO2 separate from combustion gas.
mechanism: Lime mud (CaCO3) is filtered and then dried with low-pressure mill steam. It is calcined in an indirectly heated electric calciner, so the CO2 leaves undiluted. The power comes from the mill's back-pressure turbines, which burn black liquor and bark, and this power is now often exported. Because the lime-mud carbon originated in the wood, the captured CO2 counts as biogenic removal. The fossil fuel the kiln used to burn is eliminated at the same time.
target: Lime-kiln process CO2: about 0.20-0.24 t of biogenic CO2 per air-dry tonne (ADt) of pulp, plus 0.08-0.16 t/ADt of fossil kiln-fuel CO2, at roughly 120-140 Mt/yr of global kraft pulp.
quantitative_claims:
Calculated in climate/runs/2026-10-05/scripts/sysint/idea2_pulp_limekiln.py.
(1) Lime use of 0.25-0.30 t CaO/ADt (literature range, from memory) gives 0.196-0.235 t pure biogenic CO2/ADt. Kiln fuel of 5.5-7.0 GJ/t CaO gives 0.077-0.155 t fossil CO2/ADt, which is avoided.
(2) The calcination enthalpy floor is 3.17 GJ/t CaO (4.04 GJ/t CO2). I assume an electric calciner with heat recovery uses 4.0-4.5 GJ/t CaO, about 1.3-1.4 times the floor. That is 0.28-0.37 MWh/ADt, or 35-47 MW average for a 1 Mt/yr mill. Drying the lime mud (25-30% moisture) takes 1.5-2.0 GJ/t CaO of low-pressure steam, not electricity.
(3) Separation floor from the verifier: 0.004 GJ/t for the calciner off-gas, against 0.124 GJ/t for amine capture from a 20% CO2 kiln flue and 0.150 GJ/t from recovery-boiler flue.
(4) The energy swap roughly pays for itself under EU prices. Electricity no longer sold, valued at $40-80/MWh, costs $12-28/ADt. Kiln fuel saved at $8-12/GJ is worth $11-25/ADt, and ETS allowances at EUR 70-80 are worth $6-10/ADt. The net is -$5 to -$7/ADt, or -$26 to -$30 per t of biogenic CO2.
(5) The full chain costs $63-102/t: a calciner premium of $150-300 per t/yr, liquefaction about $14/t, and transport and storage $35-60/t. That compares with durable BECCS offtakes at $200-600/t (map).
(6) Global potential is 24-33 Mt/yr of pure biogenic CO2 plus 11-16 Mt/yr of fossil CO2 avoided. The kraft tonnage is an unverified order of magnitude. This stream is only about 12-15% of a mill's biogenic CO2; the recovery boiler is the bulk (about 1.4-1.8 t/ADt, from memory).
who_gains: S4: pulp producers gain a removal-credit revenue line, lose fossil kiln fuel and its ETS exposure, and keep their mills; this matters for S8 too, since Brazil, Chile and Indonesia are big exporters. S1: no extra biomass is harvested, because the carbon is already in the mill's liquor cycle, which avoids the Drax-type sourcing objection. S6: mill jobs are kept. S10: CDR buyers get lower-cost durable tonnes. S7: the Swedish and Finnish BECCS ambitions get a low-cost first tranche.
who_loses: Fuel suppliers to lime kilns (gas, fuel oil). Grid buyers of exported mill power. Rotary-kiln service revenue. Those S1 groups that oppose all forestry-linked BECCS. Mills without a power surplus would have to buy grid power, which raises their costs.
closest_known_work: Calix/Leilac: indirect calcination for cement and lime with hybrid electric heating; its site lists no pulp or lime-mud application (checked 2026-10-05). Kuparinen et al. 2017, BioResources (renewable lime-kiln fuels). Klüh 2022, SSRN (recycling lime-kiln CO2 via methanation). Wu et al. 2024, Fuel, doi 10.1016/j.fuel.2024.132372: kinetics of lime-mud calcination in high-CO2 atmospheres. Ind. Eng. Chem. Res. 2025: flash calcination of lime mud under different atmospheres. CO280: retrofits pulp mills for biogenic CO2 capture, with projects averaging 0.8 Mt/yr and Microsoft and Frontier among the buyers listed on its site. Onarheim et al. 2017 (from memory): post-combustion capture on recovery boilers.
why_different: Pulp-mill BECCS so far means amine scrubbing of recovery-boiler or kiln flue gas, and kiln decarbonisation means switching fuel. This combines the two: the indirect calciner makes the process stream solvent-free and nearly pure, and the mill's own biomass power replaces the fossil fuel. The lowest-cost biogenic tonnes and the removal of fossil kiln fuel come from a single piece of equipment.
cheapest_falsifying_test: A bench study of 4-8 weeks. Calcine real lime mud from 3-5 mills in an electrically heated tube furnace under about 100% CO2 at 900-950 C. Measure slaking reactivity, residual CaCO3 and causticising efficiency against the same mills' rotary-kiln lime; Wu 2024 gives the kinetic baseline. In parallel, run a desk power balance for 10-20 mills (surplus MWh/ADt). Kill the idea if reactivity loss needs more than about 20% extra lime or makeup, or if typical mills have less than 0.3 MWh/ADt of surplus power.

title: Cane distilleries on the Deccan Traps: mineralise fermentation CO2 in basalt using the sugar mill's surplus condensate water
one_line: Many Indian molasses distilleries sit on the Deccan basalt and beside sugar mills that have surplus cane-juice condensate. Dissolve the distillery's pure biogenic fermentation CO2 in that condensate and inject it into deep basalt flows, Carbfix-style. The CO2, the water and the reactive rock are all already on site.
conventional_core: Molasses or B-heavy ethanol distilleries attached to sugar mills, with bagasse cogeneration, under India's E20 programme. Fermentation off-gas is already more than 98% CO2.
graft: Carbfix in-situ mineralisation of dissolved CO2 in basalt, where more than 95% mineralised within 2 years at the Hellisheiði pilot.
mechanism: Fermentation CO2 (separation floor 0.0025 GJ/t) is dried and compressed to 25-40 bar with bagasse-cogeneration power. It is dissolved in the mill's surplus evaporator condensate, cane being about 70% water, at Carbfix ratios of 17-27 t of water per t CO2. The CO2-charged water is injected into deep vesicular basalt flows, well below the shallow aquifers used for drinking water, where calcium, magnesium and iron leached from the rock precipitate it as carbonate. Because the carbon is biogenic, this is durable BECCS removal.
target: Pure biogenic fermentation CO2 from cane-route ethanol in Maharashtra and north Karnataka (about 2 Mt/yr), and across India (about 3-4 Mt/yr from cane, about 7.5 Mt/yr from all E20 ethanol). Volumes are unverified orders of magnitude.
quantitative_claims:
Calculated in climate/runs/2026-10-05/scripts/sysint/idea3_cane_basalt.py.
(1) Fermentation gives 0.753 kg CO2 per litre of ethanol (stoichiometric). The separation floor is 0.0025 GJ/t. Compression to 25-40 bar is 0.18-0.21 GJ/t ideal (77-89 kWh/t real). Water injection at 3 MPa adds about 0.09 GJ/t. The total is about 0.38 GJ_e/t (106 kWh/t). On bagasse power that is near-zero carbon; on a 0.7 kg/kWh grid it would cost 7% of the removal.
(2) Water balance. C-molasses ethanol (10-12 L/t cane) needs 0.13-0.24 t water/t cane and B-heavy ethanol (20-25 L/t) needs 0.26-0.51 t, against an assumed condensate surplus of 0.30-0.45 t/t cane, so the water is self-sufficient for molasses routes. Juice-route ethanol (70-80 L/t) needs 0.9-1.6 t/t and is not covered.
(3) Cost is $36-63/t: wells at $1.5-3M serving 10-20 kt/yr, energy about $10/t, MRV $10/t and other $8/t. That compares with about $25-30/t for Carbfix at Hellisheiði (a geothermal gas stream) and $150-600/t for durable CDR offtakes.
(4) About 3.3 t of basalt reacts in situ per t CO2.
who_gains: S8: cooperative sugar mills and their cane farmers, the dominant ownership model in Maharashtra, receive the removal revenue. S7: India gains an E20 co-benefit, a domestic durable-CDR supply and a reason to strengthen its carbon market (CCTS). S4: distilleries. S1: generally positive, since the CO2 is biogenic, needs no new land and is permanently mineralised. S2: the first field data on Deccan basalt mineralisation.
who_loses: Merchant CO2 buyers (beverage and dry ice) lose a cheap supply; that is minor. S11: villages depend on Deccan basalt aquifers, so poorly isolated injection could mobilise metals or acidify groundwater. This is the decisive social-licence risk, and it needs deep targets and transparent monitoring.
closest_known_work: Carbfix (Matter et al. 2016, Science; commercial in Iceland). Punnam et al., reactive-transport modelling of CO2 mineralisation in Deccan basalt: EAGE 2025, doi 10.3997/2214-4609.202570014, and Fuel 2026, doi 10.1016/j.fuel.2026.139483. Fermentation BECCS into sandstone at ADM Decatur and Red Trail (US) and FS (Brazil). Indian distilleries already capture CO2 for beverage use, but that CO2 is re-emitted.
why_different: Carbfix's binding constraint at scale is water (17-27 t per t CO2), and Deccan field work has stayed at the modelling stage. Here the water is a waste by-product of the same agro-industrial site, the CO2 needs no capture plant, and the power is bagasse cogeneration. Carbfix is placed where all three inputs are free, which also routes removal revenue to Global South smallholder cooperatives.
cheapest_falsifying_test: (1) Batch and column reactors, 4-8 weeks: crushed Deccan basalt cores plus real mill condensate charged with CO2 at 25-40 bar. Track pH, cation release, carbonate formation and biofilm growth from residual organics and ethanol in the condensate. (2) Desk GIS: distilleries against basalt thickness above 500 m and depth to potable aquifers, using public CGWB data. Kill the idea if condensate organics cause biofouling or clogging that pretreatment cannot remove cheaply, or if fewer than about 20 distilleries sit over basalt sections deep enough to isolate injection from aquifers.

title: VAM as boiler air: duct coal-mine ventilation air into nearby boilers so the boilers destroy the methane
one_line: Many high-gas coal mines sit next to mine-mouth power or industrial boilers. Ducting the methane-bearing ventilation exhaust (0.1-0.7% CH4) into the boiler's combustion-air intake destroys the methane with no oxidiser capex, no autothermal threshold, and a small fuel credit.
conventional_core: A pulverised-coal or gas boiler's forced-draught combustion-air system. A 600 MWe unit draws about 1.84 Mm3/h of air.
graft: Mine ventilation air methane (VAM) as a supplementary 'fuel-in-air'. This was done with on-site gas engines at BHP's Appin and Tower collieries in the 1990s-2000s (from memory).
mechanism: A booster fan and duct connect the ventilation shaft's evasé to the boiler's secondary or overfire air intake. The methane, far below its 5% lower explosive limit (Chinese mine rules already keep return air under about 0.75%), burns out in the furnace. When the boiler is down, a damper returns the VAM to atmosphere, or to a small regenerative thermal oxidiser (RTO) or flare. Unlike an RTO, the boiler holds flame temperature on its own fuel, so even 0.1-0.2% shafts qualify.
target: Coal-mine VAM, about 70-80% of underground coal-mine methane, at shafts within about 2-5 km of a boiler: mine-mouth plants in Shanxi, Guizhou and Inner Mongolia, Silesian combined-heat-and-power plants, and NSW.
quantitative_claims:
Calculated in climate/runs/2026-10-05/scripts/sysint/idea4_vam_boiler.py.
(1) Combustion air of 0.97, 1.84 and 2.85 Mm3/h for 300, 600 and 1000 MWe coal units at least matches a typical 0.5-1.5 Mm3/h VAM shaft.
(2) A 1.0 Mm3/h shaft at 0.4% CH4 supplies 37 MWth (2-3% of a 600 MWe unit's fuel). At a boiler capacity factor of 0.55 it destroys 12.9 kt CH4/yr, which is 0.38 Mt CO2e at GWP100 and 1.06 Mt at GWP20 (fossil 29.8/82.5).
(3) Net cost runs from -$6/t CO2e (2 km duct, capex about $11M) to +$7/t CO2e (5 km, about $53M), with ducts assumed at $4-10M/km and a fuel credit of $10/t CO2e at $6/GJ. That compares with EUR 8.5-9.8/t CO2e for a stand-alone RTO (MATEC 2025 design case).
(4) Moving the air 3 km takes 1.65 GJ per t CH4 of fan work, against about 263 GJ/t CH4 to process ambient air at 1.93 ppm (verifier). An RTO needs at least about 0.18% CH4; the boiler needs no threshold.
(5) Global envelope: if 5-20% of global VAM (about 27 Mt CH4/yr) lies within duct reach, at a capacity factor of 0.55, that is 0.75-3.0 Mt CH4/yr, or 22-90 Mt CO2e/yr at GWP100. The reachable share is the unknown that matters.
who_gains: S4/S5: coal and power operators get compliance with China's coal-mine methane standards and the EU's 2031 VAM rules at roughly zero net cost, plus a 2-3% fuel saving. S6: miners and plant workers, with no job impact. S7: China's methane targets and the Global Methane Pledge. S2/S1: a fast methane cut. S11: neutral.
who_loses: RTO vendors. S1 groups wary of any measure that touches coal, although it does not extend plant life. Joint safety and liability between two operators (mine ventilation and boiler) needs contracts. Abatement ends when the boiler retires or is idle, unless a backup oxidiser is installed.
closest_known_work: BHP Appin and Tower collieries used VAM as combustion air for on-site gas engines (from memory; not re-verified). A 2025 CFD study of boiler combustion with VAM mixed into secondary air (ETEP 2024 proceedings, doi 10.1117/12.3064271). US DOE/NETL reports 'Capture and Use of Coal Mine Ventilation Air Methane' (2003, doi 10.2172/823123; 2008, doi 10.2172/969298). The MATEC 2025 RTO design case.
why_different: VAM abatement is stuck because an RTO earns no revenue (only about 7 coal sites worldwide). This turns existing utility boilers into zero-capex oxidisers and gives the methane a fuel value. The open question is not the chemistry but the share of shafts within duct reach, which a GIS exercise can answer within weeks.
cheapest_falsifying_test: (1) A GIS study using public mine and plant databases: VAM shafts against boiler air intakes within 5 km in Shanxi, Guizhou, Silesia and NSW, giving the reachable share of VAM. (2) A boiler-OEM or CFD check of CH4 slip and flame stability with 0.2-0.7% CH4 in secondary air. (3) A 2-week trial ducting one small shaft to an industrial boiler, with FTIR on the stack. Kill the idea if less than 5% of VAM is within reach or if methane slip exceeds about 2%.

title: Enclosed degassing weir: capture reservoir methane that degasses below tropical hydro dams and oxidise it like VAM
one_line: Below tropical dams, methane dissolved in deep reservoir water degasses after the turbines. Enclosing the existing kind of aerating weir and drawing a controlled air sweep through it concentrates that methane to 0.4-4% in air, which a regenerative thermal oxidiser can destroy autothermally.
conventional_core: Hydropower tailrace aerating or regulating weirs (as at Petit Saut and Nam Theun 2), which are already built to oxygenate the turbined water.
graft: The VAM regenerative thermal oxidiser (RTO), plus air stripping from water treatment. The weir becomes an enclosed stripping cascade whose exhaust is treated as ventilation-air methane.
mechanism: Turbined hypolimnetic water flows over a cascade inside an enclosure. A fan draws air through it at about 0.13 m3 per m3 of water (stripping factor about 4), which strips about 75% of the dissolved CH4. The exhaust, at 0.4-4% CH4 and kept below 25% of the lower explosive limit by extra dilution, feeds an RTO or a nearby boiler. The cost is 2-4 m of head, plus a bypass in low-methane months.
target: Downstream degassing at young or deep-intake tropical reservoirs in Brazil, Laos, West Africa and Guyana. At Nam Theun 2 this was 10-30% of reservoir CH4 (measured), concentrated in a few months.
quantitative_claims:
Calculated in climate/runs/2026-10-05/scripts/sysint/idea5_hydro_weir.py, assuming a dimensionless Henry coefficient of about 30 for CH4.
(1) At 2 mg/L CH4 and 1,000 m3/s, the sweep air carries 1.7% CH4, above the 0.18-0.2% RTO autothermal threshold. Recovering 75% gives about 47 kt CH4/yr, or 1.3 Mt CO2e at GWP100 (biogenic factor 27), if it ran all year.
(2) Energy: a 2-4 m head loss forgoes 18-35 MW, which is 0.44-0.88 GJ/t CO2e ($6-12/t at $50/MWh). At 0.5 mg/L it rises to 2.6 GJ/t ($37/t); at 5 mg/L it falls to 0.26 GJ/t ($4/t). For comparison, the verifier puts fan work alone for removing methane from ambient air at 8.8 GJ/t CO2e (GWP100).
(3) Capex for the RTO plus enclosure is about $44M (MATEC RTO unit cost plus an assumed $30M structure). That is $3.5/t CO2e at full-year operation, or about $10-14/t if the plant only runs seasonally: Nam Theun 2 measured 80% of downstream emissions within 2-4 months.
(4) Measured context from Deshmukh et al. 2016: hypolimnetic CH4 reached 1,000 µmol/L (about 16 mg/L). Turbulence at the intake shifted emissions upstream and cut downstream emissions by at least 40% through enhanced oxidation.
