who_gains: S5: hydro utilities defend the 'clean hydro' label and earn methane credits. S8: Brazil, Laos and African host countries. S7: methane-pledge accounting. S1/S2: a measurable methane cut. S11: downstream oxygenation continues. No industry is harmed.
who_loses: Hydro output falls by 0.5-3% during operating months. Some operators resist measuring reservoir emissions at all, for reputational reasons. Hydro projects counted as zero-emission in carbon markets could face scrutiny once the methane is measured.
closest_known_work: Bambace et al. 2007, Energy, doi 10.1016/j.energy.2006.09.008: proposed recovering methane from turbined water at tropical dams. The Petit Saut aerating weir, which degasses methane but vents it. Nam Theun 2 measurements and intake design (Deshmukh et al. 2016, Biogeosciences 13:1919). Lake Kivu methane extraction, which deals with natural, far higher concentrations. VAM RTOs.
why_different: Bambace proposed extracting and enriching the methane for fuel, which is hard at mg/L concentrations. This idea skips enrichment: it reuses an aerating weir, which already exists or is cheap, as the stripping contactor, and treats the dilute exhaust with mature VAM oxidiser hardware. The simple baseline to beat is Nam Theun 2's intake-turbulence and selective-withdrawal approach.
cheapest_falsifying_test: (1) Desk compilation: published dissolved CH4 in turbined water, with discharge time series, for 5-10 tropical reservoirs. Compute annual capturable kt CH4 and the seasonal capacity factor, and compare with intake-design mitigation. (2) A bench cascade flume, 1-5 m, using CH4-spiked water, to measure stripping efficiency against air-to-water ratio. Kill the idea if most large dams have turbined-water CH4 below about 0.5 mg/L for most of the year, or if intake-mixing or selective-withdrawal designs achieve similar cuts at under $5/t.

title: Sell the water you don't pump: grid-tied solar irrigation pumps make alternate wetting and drying (AWD) pay in kWh, with pump telemetry as MRV
one_line: For groundwater-irrigated rice, connect farmers' solar pumps to feeders that pay for exported power. Each cubic metre not pumped then becomes saleable electricity, so alternate wetting and drying (AWD, which cuts rice methane by 40-48%) earns money without carbon credits. Pump telemetry plus Sentinel-1 flood mapping supplies the field-level MRV that rice credits lack.
conventional_core: AWD irrigation, which is TRL 9 agronomy, plus India's PM-KUSUM solar pumps and feeder solarisation.
graft: Feed-in metering as a resource-conservation incentive: IWMI's 'Solar Power as a Remunerative Crop' (Dhundi cooperative, Gujarat; from memory). The pump's own energy log serves as an MRV sensor.
mechanism: With a feed-in tariff, a farmer who keeps fields continuously flooded forgoes power sales, and one who uses safe AWD (re-irrigating at about -15 kPa or 15 cm below the surface) earns them. The pump controller logs run-hours and kWh per field. Combined with Sentinel-1 SAR flood detection, that classifies continuous flooding against AWD for credit aggregation, addressing the MRV integrity problem behind Verra's 2023 suspension of a CDM rice methodology.
target: Groundwater-pumped rice: Bangladesh boro (about 4.8 Mha) and Punjab-Haryana kharif (about 4.5 Mha). Areas are unverified orders of magnitude.
quantitative_claims:
Calculated in climate/runs/2026-10-05/scripts/sysint/idea6_solar_awd.py.
(1) Using the IPCC default of 1.19 kg CH4/ha/day for continuous flooding and an AWD scaling factor of 0.52-0.60 (from memory), AWD saves 48-69 kg CH4/ha/season. That is 1.3-1.85 t CO2e/ha at GWP100 (biogenic 27) or 3.8-5.5 at GWP20, before an assumed N2O penalty of 0.1-0.4 t CO2e/ha.
(2) Water saved is 2,400-4,500 m3/ha (20-30% of 1,200-1,500 mm). At 15-40 m lift and 35-40% pump efficiency that is 245-1,400 kWh/ha, worth INR 740-4,200/ha ($9-50) at an INR 3/kWh feed-in tariff. Methane credits at $10-20/t add $16-32/ha.
(3) Where diesel pumpsets are used instead, the same water saving avoids 0.22-1.25 t CO2/ha.
(4) Full adoption would cut about 7 Mt CO2e/yr in each region; 10% adoption would cut about 1.5 Mt/yr.
who_gains: S8: smallholders gain power income and water savings, and their wells last longer. S7: Indian states (Punjab, Haryana) cut farm-power subsidies and slow groundwater depletion. S5: distribution companies (DISCOMs) get daytime solar and lower agricultural loss. S1/S2: real, measured methane cuts. S9: neutral, since safe AWD is yield-neutral in the literature.
who_loses: Diesel pumpset sellers. DISCOMs pay feed-in tariffs, although subsidy savings may offset this. Farmers who manage AWD badly risk yield loss, and N2O partly offsets the methane cut. Carbon-credit intermediaries would be held to stricter MRV.
closest_known_work: IWMI's Solar Power as a Remunerative Crop (Shah et al. 2017, Economic & Political Weekly; from memory). India's PM-KUSUM components A and C. Punjab's 'Paani Bachao Paisa Kamao' pilot paying farmers for unused power (from memory). An IoT-automated AWD system field-evaluated at ASABE AIM 2026 (doi 10.13031/aim.202600052). Verra VM0051 (the An Giang project, 116,000 ha, modelled).
why_different: Past AWD programmes relied on carbon finance or extension work, and their MRV broke down. Here the energy system already present on the farm supplies both the incentive (feed-in revenue for unpumped water) and the measurement (pump telemetry), so the methane cut is a side effect of a power sale that farmers already understand.
cheapest_falsifying_test: Use existing telemetry from KUSUM-C feeders or the Dhundi cooperative for a few hundred rice fields over 1-2 seasons, together with free Sentinel-1 flood time series. Test (a) whether feed-in metering lowers pumping by at least 20% compared with flat-tariff neighbours, and (b) whether telemetry plus SAR classifies AWD against continuous flooding with at least 80% agreement with field water-tube checks. Kill the idea if there is no behavioural response or classification fails.

title: Prepaid-pump AWD: volumetric irrigation pricing unlocks alternate wetting and drying in dry-season rice
one_line: Turn rice-methane abatement from a practice farmers have no reason to adopt into one they profit from. Convert fixed-fee tubewell commands to hourly prepaid-card pricing, and use the methane credit to make up the pump owner's lost revenue.
conventional_core: Alternate wetting and drying (AWD) in irrigated dry-season (boro) rice, credited under Verra VM0051 (TRL 9 agronomy; first VM0051 project at An Giang covers 116,000 ha).
graft: Volumetric (marginal) water pricing using prepaid smart-card pump meters, imported from Bangladesh's BMDA deep-tubewell card system and from the water-pricing RCT literature. Card logs double as auditable activity data for MRV.
mechanism: Under seasonal fixed fees, a farmer who saves water saves nothing; the pump owner keeps the diesel savings. Chakravorty, Dar and Emerick (AEJ: Applied 2023, two randomized trials in Bangladesh) found that water-saving technology cut use only when farmers faced marginal prices, and that merely offering an hourly option saved nothing. The design has four parts. (1) Fixed fees are replaced by hourly prepaid cards. (2) AWD is introduced at the mild threshold: water no lower than 15 cm below the surface. (3) Methane credits are split between the farmer and the pump owner so the owner's lost hourly sales are covered. (4) Card logs (pump-hours per field) plus Sentinel-1 flood detection verify the drying events. Physics: CH4 is avoided at the source, and the practice saves pumping energy instead of consuming it.
target: Pump-irrigated dry-season rice in Bangladesh (boro), the Vietnamese Mekong delta, and eastern India. Partners: BMDA or other prepaid-meter operators, pump owners' cooperatives, VM0051 developers.
quantitative_claims: Measured: in the GCB 2024 global meta-analysis (doi 10.1111/gcb.17581), AWD cut CH4 by 51.6% and net CH4+N2O GWP by 46.9%, while N2O rose 44%. Measured: in the Carrijo 2017 meta-analysis (56 studies, 528 comparisons), mild AWD caused no significant yield loss in most cases; severe AWD cost 22.6%. Modelled: using IPCC 2019-refinement defaults (recalled, not re-verified this run: 0.85 kg CH4/ha/day for South Asia, 1.22 for SE Asia, multiple-drainage scaling factor 0.55) over 100-120 days, the cut is 38-66 kg CH4/ha/season. That is 1.0-1.8 t CO2e/ha (GWP100, biogenic 27) or 3.0-5.3 t (GWP20). It sits inside the map's field-trial range of 1.5-5. Computed energy: saving 200-400 mm of irrigation is 2,000-4,000 m3/ha. On 8 m shallow diesel tubewells (12% fuel-to-water) that saves 36-73 L diesel/ha (1.3-2.6 GJ, 0.10-0.19 t CO2). On 25 m electric deep tubewells it saves 454-908 kWh/ha (0.30-0.59 t CO2). Net energy is therefore -1.1 to -2.1 GJ per t CO2e avoided. Verifier contrast: stripping the same methane back out of ambient air costs at least 263 GJ/t CH4 in fan work alone, about 11 GJ for one hectare-season's avoided 42 kg. Economics: farmer diesel savings of about $36-73/ha at $1/L (assumed) plus credits of $10-36/ha at $10-20/t. Scale: 5-15 Mha of pump-irrigated dry-season rice gives 5-30 Mt CO2e/yr (GWP100).
who_gains: S8 smallholders, through lower water bills, diesel savings and a credit share. S7, through groundwater conservation, lower diesel import bills and Bangladesh's Barind aquifer stress. S2/S1: the abatement is measured at the field rather than modelled. S9: rice prices are unchanged because mild AWD protects yields. S5: electric tubewell load falls in peak irrigation months. S10/carbon buyers: VM0051 credits gain hard activity data (card logs), addressing the integrity failure behind Verra's 2023 suspension of AMS-III.AU.
who_loses: Pump owners and water sellers lose fixed-fee rents and hourly volume; credit-sharing is the compensation. Diesel retailers (S3 downstream) lose a trivial amount. Farmers on light or high-pH soils face yield risk if drying turns severe; the meta-analysis shows the largest losses at pH ≥7. Net warming benefit falls where N2O rises the most.
closest_known_work: Chakravorty, Dar and Emerick (AEJ: Applied 2023) showed the pricing-and-AWD interaction in RCTs but did not attach methane finance. Verra VM0051 and the An Giang project (116,000 ha, 590,682 t CO2e/yr expected, modelled) use remote sensing and models with no price change. BMDA prepaid cards in Barind have run for years with no carbon link. IRRI and Mitti Labs-style satellite AWD MRV is another neighbour. What is different: the abatement contract is designed around the incentive failure the RCT identified. Credit revenue buys the switch to marginal pricing, and pump-card logs give per-field activity data rather than a modelled practice claim.
why_different: Most AWD credit projects assume adoption follows payment. The RCT evidence says adoption follows marginal water price. This idea pays to change the price, not the practice.
cheapest_falsifying_test: Computation only, about 2-3 months. Take existing prepaid-card command areas and comparable fixed-fee command areas in one district, with BMDA card logs or a pump cooperative's records. Run a Sentinel-1 VV/VH time series of flooded/non-flooded state per field for one boro season. Prediction: volumetric-priced fields show at least 2 more dry-down events per season and at least 20% fewer pump-hours. If they show no difference, the graft fails. Optional second step: a one-season pilot of about 40 versus 40 commands with closed-chamber CH4 and N2O on about 60 fields (about $50-80k). It is falsified if the CH4+N2O GWP reduction is below 25% or mild-AWD yield loss exceeds 5%.

title: Husk-to-char parboiling mills: run the steam on pyrolysis gas and return silica-rich char to paddies, credited only for husk with no fuel use
one_line: Treat rice-mill husk as 'point-source biomass': already collected and dry. Pyrolyse it ahead of the existing boiler so the gas still raises the mill's steam and the char goes back to paddies as a silicon amendment. Credit removal only where the husk was being dumped or open-burned, because elsewhere the verifier shows leakage cancels the gain.
conventional_core: Husk-fired boilers at parboiling rice mills (TRL 9, ubiquitous in South and Southeast Asia). Japanese carbonised rice husk ('kuntan') is already a traditional paddy and nursery amendment.
graft: A continuous pyrolysis front end, as used in the charcoal and activated-carbon industries, coupled to the existing boiler, which burns the pyrolysis vapours. This applies the CCS 'cheap concentrated stream first' logic to biomass: no collection logistics, no drying.
mechanism: Paddy is about 20% husk. Pyrolysing husk at 450-650 C keeps 35-42% of its mass as char that is 40-50% carbon. The volatiles carry about 43-60% of the husk's energy and are burned in the mill's existing boiler. A parboiling mill that currently burns no more than about 53% of its husk energy for steam can therefore char all of its husk and still meet steam demand. A mill burning 70% can char about 64%. The char is roughly 45% amorphous silica, which suits silicon-depleted, intensively cropped paddies; rice accumulates silicon. Holding peak temperature at or below about 650 C avoids crystalline cristobalite, a respiratory hazard.
target: Parboiling and husk-surplus mills in Bangladesh, eastern India, Myanmar, Cambodia, the Mekong delta and West Africa, where husk is dumped, open-burned or landfilled. Pilot partners: mill owners' associations and an artisanal or industrial C-sink certifier.
quantitative_claims:
Computed (OptiLex script; inputs assumed: husk 38% C, LHV 13.5 MJ/kg, char yield 35-42%, char C 40-50%):
- 0.51-0.77 t CO2 per t husk before the permanence discount; 0.38-0.69 t after a factor of 0.75-0.9 (central about 0.5).
- The char holds 34-51% of husk energy (central 42%).

KEY VERIFIER RESULT: stored carbon costs about 11.2 GJ of forgone fuel energy per t CO2 across all cases. That exceeds typical real DAC (5-10 GJ/t) and is 24x the 0.47 GJ/t DAC floor. If the husk used to be sold as boiler fuel displacing coal (94.6 kg CO2/GJ), leakage is 0.43-0.65 t CO2/t husk and net removal is about zero (-0.02 to -0.04 t/t). Only husk with no fuel fate generates net removal.

Scale: about 776 Mt paddy/yr (FAOSTAT, recalled) gives about 155 Mt husk. If 20-40% is genuinely surplus, that is about 16-31 Mt CO2/yr.
Revenue: $50-75 per t husk at $100-150/t CO2, against assumed husk prices of $20-60/t.
Mill energy: neutral for eligible mills, with no purchased fuel.
who_gains: S8: mill owners and paddy farmers gain a char revenue line plus a silicon amendment. S11: communities near mills get less smoke from open husk piles and less husk dumped in rivers. S1/S2: a durable, weighable removal (weigh the char and test H/Corg) rather than a modelled one. S10/CDR buyers: a low-cost biochar supply (biochar averaged about $177-250/t in 2025) from the Global South.
who_loses: Buyers of surplus husk (brick kilns, small boilers) lose cheap fuel where husk was being sold, which is why that husk is excluded. Rice-husk-ash sellers (steel tundish insulation, pozzolan) lose feedstock only if mills switch away from full combustion. No major industry is harmed.
closest_known_work: Husk Power Systems (Bihar) and Cambodian husk gasifiers produce char as a by-product. Japanese kuntan is traditional carbonised husk. Artisanal and industrial biochar is credited under the CSI Global Artisan C-Sink, Puro and Isometric standards. Rice-husk biochar papers are numerous. What is different: (1) integration with the mill's existing steam demand, shown by computation to balance at at most about 53% of husk energy for steam; (2) an explicit eligibility rule from the verifier's leakage result (about 11 GJ forgone fuel per t CO2), which most biochar crediting ignores; (3) the char is sold on agronomic silicon value to the same paddy farmers who supply the mill.
why_different: It shows when biochar is thermodynamically worse than DAC: whenever its feedstock energy would otherwise displace fossil fuel. It then restricts credits to the case where it is not.
cheapest_falsifying_test: Bench and survey, about 3 months, about $15-30k. (a) Pyrolyse husk from 3 mills at 450, 550 and 650 C. Measure char yield, C, H/Corg, the energy balance (bomb calorimetry on husk and char) and XRD for cristobalite. (b) Survey about 30 parboiling mills on steam fuel use as a share of husk produced, and on the fate of surplus husk (sold as fuel, dumped, open-burned). The idea is falsified if the median mill's steam demand exceeds about 75% of husk energy (so less than 50% of husk can be charred), or if less than 10% of surveyed husk is genuinely surplus (so leakage cancels the removal), or if H/Corg exceeds 0.7 at temperatures that avoid cristobalite.

title: Swap carbonate aglime for silicate fines in tropical estates, and apportion alkalinity with river-geochemistry mixing models
one_line: Replace part of the carbonate lime and dolomite on Brazilian cane and soy and Southeast Asian palm estates with quarry silicate fines. Credit the avoided carbonate CO2 at once, and credit silicate removal only when a carbonate-versus-silicate source-apportionment model shows it above detection. This fixes the measured failure in the Sabah palm trial.
conventional_core: Agricultural liming of acidic tropical soils (TRL 9; Brazil uses tens of Mt of lime a year, about 35-50 Mt, recalled). Ground magnesium limestone and dolomite on palm estates. Brazil's remineralizer (rochagem) law recognises silicate rock powders as inputs (recalled).
graft: End-member mixing and source apportionment from global river weathering budgets (Gaillardet et al. 1999 style), imported into field ERW MRV. It uses Ca/Na, Mg/Na and Sr/Ca ratios, 87Sr/86Sr, δ13C-DIC and nitrate to split alkalinity between carbonate fertilizer and silicate rock, and between carbonic-acid and nitric-acid weathering.
mechanism: In heavily N-fertilised tropical soils, nitrification makes nitric acid. Carbonate lime dissolved by nitric acid releases CO2 (IPCC Tier 1 counts all of it as emitted). Silicate weathered by nitric acid releases none, and silicate weathered by carbonic acid removes CO2. Swapping part of the lime for silicate fines therefore avoids an emission and may add removal. The measurement problem is that carbonate weathering swamps the silicate signal. Larkin et al. (2022) applied andesite at 50 t/ha/yr for 3 years on a Sabah oil-palm estate and measured catchment CDR of 3.8±0.8 t CO2/ha (treated) against 3.7±0.6 (untreated). The signal was driven mainly by the estate's carbonate fertilizer. Mixing models separate the two sources, so the credit can be split into avoided carbonate CO2, read from purchase records and confirmed by tracer chemistry, and measured silicate CDR.
target: Corporate cane, soy and palm estates, each a single counterparty with drain or catchment outlets, located within about 50 km of basalt or andesite quarries producing fines. Examples: Paraná and São Paulo basalt, and Sabah/Sumatra palm estates. Partners: estate agronomy teams, quarries, an isotope lab.
quantitative_claims:
IPCC 2006 Tier 1: 0.44 t CO2/t limestone and 0.48 t/t dolomite. A West and McBride-type net estimate (recalled) is about 0.22 t/t, 49% of Tier 1. Brazil at 35-50 Mt lime/yr: 15-22 Mt CO2/yr at Tier 1, 8-11 Mt on the net estimate. A 30% swap is about 2.5-7 Mt/yr avoided.

Computed substitution logistics: at 10-30% CaCO3-equivalence, 3-10 t of rock replaces 1 t of lime. Trucking at 30-100 km costs 10-100 kg CO2 per t lime replaced, against 216-440 kg avoided. Using existing quarry fines avoids 18-26 kWh/t of Bond grinding (P80 100-50 µm, Wi 20).

Silicate CDR is credited only if measured. The Illinois field rate of about 0.05 t CO2/t rock is the optimistic reference; in tropical andesite (Larkin 2022) the signal was not detectable. Process energy is near zero beyond haulage.
who_gains: S4 quarries and aggregates producers: fines become a product. S8/S9: estates and farmers get a liming, K, Mg and Si input that may be cheaper per hectare near quarries. S7 (Brazil): less reliance on imported potash (partial K substitution) and lower reported agricultural emissions. S2: a measurement method that resolves the main confound in tropical ERW. S1: credits are tied to measured signals rather than models.
who_loses: Agricultural limestone and dolomite suppliers lose part of their market. Estates face agronomic risk if silicate neutralizes acidity too slowly in Al-toxic Cerrado or Ultisol soils, so the swap must stay partial (25-50%). S11: dust and trace metals if mafic fines are poorly characterised.
closest_known_work: Larkin et al. 2022 (Frontiers in Climate) ran the catchment method on a palm estate but did not swap out the carbonate, and that is why the method failed. The map's open problem proposes Midwest aglime substitution 'credited on the difference'. Brazilian ERW firms (InPlanet, Terradot; recalled) apply remineralizers on top of liming. Hubbard Brook's 1999 wollastonite catchment addition is the measurement precedent. What is different: the swap plus a tracer-based apportionment is aimed at the specific failure Larkin measured. The nitric-acid question also decides whether the avoided-lime credit is real.
why_different: It turns the dominant noise source in tropical ERW, carbonate fertiliser, into a lever: remove it, and measure what remains.
cheapest_falsifying_test: A 12-16 week soil-column experiment (about $10-20k) on a urea-fertilised tropical Oxisol or Ultisol. Treatments: control, GML, basalt fines, GML+basalt, and a blind known-proportion spike. Measure leachate cations, alkalinity, Sr isotopes, δ13C-DIC, nitrate, headspace CO2 flux and pH. It is falsified if (a) the mixing model misassigns the known silicate fraction by more than ±50%, or (b) GML under urea shows no net CO2 efflux (the avoided-emission claim then shrinks toward zero), or (c) basalt at swap rates raises pH by less than 0.2 units in 16 weeks, so farmers would need lime anyway. Larkin's archived stream chemistry, if obtainable, gives a zero-cost first pass.

title: Verified ration balancing: co-op dairy methane intensity measured from the bulk-milk spectra the plant already takes
one_line: Scale India's cooperative ration-balancing programme, which measurably raises milk yield and cuts methane per litre. Verify it at near-zero marginal cost with mid-infrared (MIR) methane predictions run on each village society's daily bulk-milk sample, and pay a per-litre premium through the co-op's existing payment rail.
conventional_core: NDDB-style ration balancing for smallholder cows and buffaloes: local feeds are rebalanced by trained village resource persons using software (TRL 9; field-measured).
graft: Milk mid-infrared spectra as a methane proxy. Canada already uses MIR-predicted methane in national genetic evaluation (JDS 2026 abstracts). It is applied here to pooled society-level bulk milk rather than individual cows.
mechanism: Garg et al. (Animal Feed Sci Tech 2013; 1,131 buffaloes and 540 cows under field conditions) found that balanced rations raised milk yield by 2-14%. They also raised feed-conversion efficiency and cut enteric CH4 per kg milk by 15-20% (P<0.05). Per-cow methane measurement is too costly for smallholders. Every society's milk is already sampled daily at the chilling centre or plant. A calibrated MIR model applied to bulk milk would give a society-level methane-intensity trend. Payments are made per litre through the co-op, and only absolute per-animal reductions beyond a baseline are credited.
target: Indian dairy co-op unions (and East African dairy hubs) with FTIR-equipped plant labs. Partners: a dairy union lab, an animal-nutrition institute holding SF6 or GreenFeed reference data.
quantitative_claims:
Measured: 15-20% lower CH4 per kg milk and 2-14% more milk (Garg 2013). Computed (assumed 50-70 kg CH4/yr per lactating animal, biogenic GWP100 27): 0.20-0.38 t CO2e per animal-year on an intensity basis, worth $3-11 per animal-year at $15-30/t. The absolute per-animal reduction is likely smaller and unverified.

Computed MRV cost: monthly per-cow MIR at $0.5-1.5 per sample is $6-18 per animal-year, which exceeds the carbon value. Daily bulk-milk MIR at society level (200-500 animals) is $0.4-2.7 per animal-year, so only the pooled design pays.

Scale: 10-30 M animals gives 1.5-11 Mt CO2e/yr (intensity basis, an upper bound). Energy: no process energy; feed efficiency improves.
who_gains: S8/S6 smallholder dairy households: more milk and lower feed cost (the main driver; carbon is a small add-on). S4 dairy processors gain a verified Scope 3 reduction without a Bovaer-style mandate backlash. S7 gains an inventory improvement and livestock-mission outcomes. S2 gains low-cost, population-scale methane data from tropical breeds. Mineral-mixture makers gain sales.
who_loses: Sellers of excess protein concentrate lose some sales, because ration balancing often cuts over-fed crude protein (71% of animals were over-supplied in Garg 2013). If the herd grows with productivity, absolute emissions may not fall. That is a rebound risk the credit design must exclude.
closest_known_work: NDDB's Ration Balancing Programme (Garg 2013; scale recalled at millions of animals). Canadian Lactanet/MIR methane index for Holsteins. European MIR-CH4 equations (e.g. the Austrian and Swiss 2026 JDS studies on silage/TMR diets). A 2026 faecal-NIRS study suggests MIR may miss additive-driven changes. What is different: MIR applied to pooled bulk milk as programme MRV for results-based payments in tropical buffalo and crossbred systems on crop-residue diets, where no calibration yet exists.
why_different: It reuses a measurement stream the co-op already generates daily, rather than adding chambers or GreenFeeds. It credits absolute rather than per-litre reductions to avoid rewarding herd growth.
cheapest_falsifying_test: About 3-4 months, with lab access only. Collect paired milk samples from animals with existing SF6 or GreenFeed methane measurements before and after ration balancing (an NDDB- or ICAR-type dataset), or from about 60 animals measured with a hand-held laser methane detector. Apply published MIR-CH4 equations, then recalibrate locally with cross-validation. It is falsified if the cross-validated prediction error exceeds the 15-20% treatment effect, or if bulk-milk spectra cannot separate balanced from unbalanced societies at p<0.05 with about 20 societies per arm.

title: Methane-burning retort kilns for Africa's charcoal trade, credited on measured kiln methane and weighed yield instead of disputed fNRB
one_line: Fix the cooking-fuel supply chain rather than the stove. Retort and afterburner kilns burn the methane-rich smoke that earth-mound kilns vent, and raise charcoal yield by 40-70%. Both effects can be measured by weighing and spot gas sampling, which sidesteps the fNRB assumption behind the 9.2x over-crediting of cookstove offsets.
conventional_core: Charcoal production for urban cooking: an informal industry of roughly 50 Mt charcoal a year (FAOSTAT, recalled), about two-thirds of it in Africa. Earth-mound kilns are the norm.
graft: Retort or afterburner carbonisation from the industrial charcoal and biochar sector (e.g. the Adam retort, 2009). Pyrolysis vapours are recirculated and burned, removing CH4 and supplying carbonisation heat.
mechanism: Earth-mound kilns let pyrolysis gases escape, and these contain CH4, CO and condensables. A retort burns them, so the wood needs less partial combustion: yield rises and CH4 falls. The methane benefit is a direct, measurable non-CO2 reduction that holds regardless of whether the wood is renewable. That matters because Gill-Wiehl et al. (Nature Sustainability 2024) found fNRB the largest source of cookstove over-crediting (sample over-credited 9.2x). The wood saving is credited only conservatively, or not at all.
target: Charcoal producer associations in Kenya, Tanzania, Zambia, Ethiopia, Uganda and Mozambique, where transport permits already exist. Partners: a forestry department, a producer cooperative, a kiln fabricator.
quantitative_claims:
Measured (Ethiopian field studies, Heliyon 2023 and Environ Monit Assess 2024):
- Earth-mound conversion efficiency is 23.6-24%; improved kilns reach 28-42%.
- Improved kilns cut CH4 by 29.6-57% and CO2 by 36-58%.
- Income per hectare of plantation rose from 71,580 ETB (traditional) to 284,824 ETB (best kiln).
- Traditional kilns in Awi zone had a primary GWI of 7.6 kg CO2e/kg charcoal (wood CO2 included).

Assumed emission factor: 30-60 g CH4 per kg charcoal for traditional kilns (IPCC 1996 default about 30 g/kg, recalled; field values higher, not re-verified). Computed methane-only benefit: 0.28-1.22 t CO2e/t charcoal (GWP100) or 0.84-3.6 (GWP20).

Computed yield effect: 24% to 34-40% means 29-40% less wood, 19-26 GJ of wood saved per t charcoal. That is 0.65-1.76 t CO2/t at fNRB 0.3-0.6 (not credited by default).

Verifier: CH4 in kiln smoke at about 2-5% has a separation floor of 0.57-0.71 GJ/t CH4, against 2.07 from air, and an afterburner needs no separation at all. Removing the same CH4 from ambient air later would cost at least 263 GJ/t CH4 in fan work (9.8 GJ/t CO2e).

Scale: 25-50% of the trade gives 4-52 Mt CO2e/yr (GWP100; the methane-only low end is 4-8 Mt). Net energy is positive.
who_gains: S8 charcoal producers: 40-70% more charcoal per tree, a 2-4x income rise per hectare in the Ethiopian data, and shorter burns. S9 urban cooks: more supply per hectare stabilises prices. S11 producers' villages: less smoke exposure at kiln sites. S7 forestry departments: less forest loss per tonne and auditable levies. S1/S2: a measurable reduction not resting on fNRB. Buyers: high-integrity non-CO2 credits.
who_loses: Wood sellers and cutters see lower wood demand per tonne of charcoal. Clean-cooking advocates (part of S1) may object that it entrenches charcoal over LPG or electric cooking; household air pollution is unchanged. LPG distributors (S3 downstream) lose a little demand growth. Informal permit-rent collectors lose opaque margins if weighing is formalised.
closest_known_work: CDM small-scale methodology AMS-III.K (methane avoidance by shifting to mechanised charcoaling; recalled). Adam retort (Renewable Energy 2009). UNDP/GEF green-charcoal programmes (Uganda, Kenya) and Brazil's Siderurgia Sustentável (pig-iron charcoal; recalled). Ethiopian kiln trials. Gold Standard's metered cookstove methodology, the only one Gill-Wiehl found close to reality (1.5x). What is different: crediting is built only from measured kiln methane (carbon-balance method) and weighed yield at producer-association aggregation points. The disputed fNRB term is excluded, and the methane value is framed explicitly at GWP20 for near-term warming.
why_different: It moves the measurable climate benefit of cooking fuel from household behaviour, which is unmeasurable at scale, to a smokestack-like production step that can be weighed and sampled.
cheapest_falsifying_test: About 3 months, about $20-40k. Run 10 earth-mound and 10 retort or afterburner batches with one producer association. Weigh wood (moisture-corrected) and charcoal. Sample smoke with a portable CH4/CO2/CO analyser using the carbon-balance method from the Ethiopian studies. Track adoption at 6 months. It is falsified if the retort's CH4 cut per kg charcoal is below 30%, if the yield gain is below 20%, or if more than half the producers revert because of cost or labour.

title: Pay plantation companies to fully rewet deep-peat blocks, measured by InSAR-detected subsidence arrest against paired drained blocks
one_line: Rewetting drained tropical peat avoids about 35-70 t CO2e/ha/yr, so a carbon price of $4-26/t beats palm-on-peat margins. Pay the plantation owner per centimetre of subsidence arrested, measured by Sentinel-1 InSAR against adjacent still-drained blocks. This replaces REDD+-style counterfactual baselines with physics.
conventional_core: Peatland rewetting by canal blocking. Indonesia's BRG/BRGM programme has run since 2016. Indonesia's water-table regulation (PP 57/2016, recalled) sets a 0.4 m water-table requirement.
graft: Satellite InSAR ground-deformation monitoring, imported from oil-and-gas and CCS reservoir surveillance (e.g. In Salah CO2-storage uplift monitoring), with Hoyt et al. 2020 as the peat-science precedent. It is used as a payment-grade MRV signal, because peat subsidence is mostly carbon oxidation.
mechanism: Hooijer et al. (Biogeosciences 2012) measured large-scale subsidence in Acacia and oil-palm plantations: about 5 cm/yr after year 5 at a 0.7 m water table, with 92% of subsidence from oxidation after 18 years. That equals about 73 t CO2e/ha/yr. Better water management inside a working plantation cuts this by at most 20%, so real abatement requires taking deep-peat blocks out of drained production. Subsidence converts to CO2 through bulk density and carbon content, so a paired-block InSAR time series measures the avoided emission directly. Payment flows to the concession holder, with a share for communities or paludiculture, such as sago or jelutong.
target: The 4.3 Mha of industrial plantations on peat in Sumatra, Borneo and Peninsular Malaysia (oil palm 3.1 Mha, pulpwood 1.1 Mha; Miettinen 2016). The first targets are deep-peat, low-yield and flood-prone blocks near the end of their drainability. Partners: a palm or pulp company with a no-peat commitment, BRGM, and an InSAR group.
quantitative_claims:
Measured: Hooijer 2012 gives 73 t CO2e/ha/yr after year 5 and 178 t in years 1-5. Plantation water management alone saves at most 20%.

Computed check: 3-5 cm/yr subsidence × 0.75-0.92 oxidative share × 80-100 kg/m3 bulk density × 55-57% C gives 36-96 t CO2/ha/yr, consistent with Hooijer.

Assumed residual CH4 after rewetting: 20-60 kg/ha/yr, i.e. 0.5-1.6 t CO2e/ha/yr. Net avoided: about 35-70 t CO2e/ha/yr.

Computed break-even: at an assumed palm-on-peat net margin of $300-900/ha/yr, the break-even carbon price is $4-26/t CO2e.

Scale: rewetting 0.5, 1 or 2 Mha gives 18-35, 35-70 or 70-140 Mt CO2e/yr. Process energy is near zero (earth or plank canal blocks). Verifier DAC-equivalent for 50 Mt: 0.3 EJ/yr at 6 GJ/t (0.048% of world primary energy) against a 0.023 EJ floor.

Assumed InSAR detection: about 0.5-1 cm/yr precision per pixel-year, against a 3-5 cm/yr drained signal. That is an SNR of about 3-10 before spatial averaging over blocks of 100 ha or more.
who_gains: S7 Indonesia and Malaysia: fire and haze suppression (the 2015 fires cost about $16bn per the World Bank, recalled) and avoided subsidence-driven coastal flooding of undrainable peat. S11 and S8: haze health, plus community payment shares and paludiculture jobs. S4: plantation companies are paid more than their margin on a depleting asset that will become undrainable. S10: insurers face lower fire-risk exposure. S3: subsurface-monitoring and InSAR service firms gain a new market. S1/S2: abatement is measured physically rather than against REDD+ baselines.
who_loses: S4 plantation and pulp output on rewetted blocks falls, with lower mill throughput. S6 plantation and mill workers on those blocks lose jobs unless paludiculture or restoration work replaces them. Some of the 3.5 Mha of smallholder peat holdings face pressure if rewetting raises water tables on neighbouring land, so hydrological units must be negotiated as a whole. Downstream refiners lose a marginal amount of supply.
closest_known_work: Indonesia's BRG/BRGM canal blocking (no payment-by-measurement). Katingan Mentaya and other peat REDD+ projects under Verra VM0007's peat module, which protect forest against modelled baselines. Hoyt et al. 2020 (Nature Geoscience) used InSAR to estimate SE Asian peat subsidence and emissions as science, not payment; numbers not re-verified this run. Deltares drainability assessments. What is different: (1) the seller is the company holding already-drained plantation land, not a forest protector; (2) payment is indexed to measured subsidence relative to paired drained blocks, not a counterfactual deforestation baseline; (3) full rewetting is required, because Hooijer shows 0.4 m-type management saves at most 20%.
why_different: It is the largest per-hectare abatement in land use (tens of t CO2e/ha/yr), on land already converted. It brings an oil-and-gas measurement tool to land MRV, and it pays a high-carbon industry to stop rather than offset.
cheapest_falsifying_test: Computation only, about 2-3 months. Process Sentinel-1 SBAS or PS-InSAR for 2017-2025 over known BRG canal-blocked areas and adjacent drained concessions. Cross-check against published subsidence-pole and dipwell records where available. It is falsified if InSAR cannot separate rewetted from drained subsidence by more than 2σ (about 1-2 cm/yr) at a 100 ha block scale, or if canal-blocked blocks show no subsidence slowdown compared with drained ones. That outcome would mean rewetting did not raise water tables, or that InSAR coherence over vegetated peat is too poor for payment-grade MRV.
